relationshipDescription: Jesus repeats Genesis' statement that God created male and female while teaching about marriage.
Jesus refers to God's creation of male and female when answering a question about marriage.
Hebrews quotes the account of God resting on the seventh day while discussing God's rest.
Paul quotes Adam becoming a living soul and contrasts the first Adam with Christ, the last Adam.
Paul quotes the two becoming one flesh to explain the seriousness of sexual union.
Paul quotes Genesis' marriage statement and applies it to his teaching about Christ and the church.
Jesus quotes the instruction to leave father and mother and become one flesh when teaching about marriage.
Jesus quotes Genesis' words about a man and wife becoming one flesh in his teaching about marriage.
After Adam and his wife hide from the Lord in Genesis, Job refers to hiding transgressions 'as Adam,' echoing the account of concealed sin.
Adam first calls his wife 'Woman' because she was taken out of man, then later gives her the name Eve because she is the mother of all living.
Genesis records the tree of life in Eden, while Revelation describes access to the tree of life in the final city for those who do God's commandments.
Genesis describes access to the tree of life after the fall; Revelation promises the overcomer the right to eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.
Genesis records Abel bringing an offering from his flock; Hebrews commends Abel's more excellent sacrifice as an act of faith.
Genesis records Cain killing Abel; John identifies Cain's evil works and hatred of his brother while warning against hatred.
Genesis records Cain's murder of Abel; Jude refers to the 'way of Cain' as an example of wrongdoing without recounting the murder itself.
Genesis recounts Cain killing Abel, while Jesus names Abel as righteous when speaking of blood shed on the earth.
Genesis names Enos as Seth's son; Luke includes Enos and Seth in the genealogy tracing Jesus' ancestry back to Adam.
Genesis 5 repeats the creation of male and female described in Genesis 1 and says God called their name Adam.
Genesis 5 identifies Seth as Adam's son and continues the family line introduced when Eve bore Seth in Genesis 4.
Chronicles begins its genealogy with Adam, Seth, and Enos, the same early family line recorded in Genesis 5.
Genesis records that Enoch walked with God and was taken; Hebrews attributes his being taken to faith and says he pleased God.
Genesis calls Noah righteous in his generation; Peter calls him a preacher of righteousness and recalls his preservation during the flood.
God identifies Noah as righteous in Genesis 7, echoing the description of Noah as just in Genesis 6.
Genesis describes Noah as just and walking with God; Hebrews explains that he prepared the ark by faith after God's warning.
God announces that the flood will destroy living creatures that have the breath of life; Genesis 7 describes such creatures entering the ark to be preserved.
Genesis 6 says Noah did all God commanded him; Genesis 7 repeats his obedience when God directs him to enter the ark.
Genesis 6 summarizes Noah's obedience; Genesis 7 describes the animals entering the ark as God commanded Noah.
God calls Noah righteous and directs him into the ark; Peter later recounts God's preservation of Noah and judgment of the ungodly during the flood.
Genesis 6 first calls Noah a just man; Genesis 7 says God has seen him righteous and instructs him to enter the ark.
God instructs Noah to enter the ark; Hebrews describes Noah preparing the ark in faith in response to God's warning.
Genesis 7 records Noah doing what God commanded, repeating the obedience summarized in Genesis 6:22.
Genesis describes the fountains of the deep and windows of heaven opening as the flood begins; Genesis 8 says these sources were stopped as the waters receded.
Genesis 2 describes God giving the man the breath of life; Genesis 7 says land creatures with the breath of life died in the flood.
Genesis records that only Noah and those with him in the ark survived; Peter likewise says eight people were saved through the water.
After the flood God commands living creatures to multiply on the earth, recalling the creation blessing to be fruitful and multiply.
Genesis 7 lists the kinds of creatures that entered the ark; Genesis 8 commands Noah to bring them out so they can multiply again.
God blesses Noah and his sons with the command to be fruitful and multiply, echoing the blessing given to humanity at creation.
Genesis 9 names Noah's sons after the flood; Genesis 10 introduces the generations descended from those same sons.
Genesis 9 identifies Ham as Canaan's father; Genesis 10 lists Canaan among Ham's sons.

Genesis names Magog, Meshech, and Tubal among Japheth's sons; Ezekiel names these same peoples or places in his prophecy concerning Gog, without establishing that the passages describe the same event.
Genesis lists Gomer among Japheth's sons; Ezekiel names Gomer among the peoples associated with Gog's forces, without narrating the same event.
Genesis 10 places Babel in the land of Shinar; Genesis 11 describes people settling in Shinar and building a city and tower.
Genesis places the beginning of Nimrod's kingdom in Babel in Shinar; Genesis 11 explains why the city was called Babel after the confusion of languages.
Genesis names Peleg, son of Eber, and Chronicles repeats the same genealogy and the statement that the earth was divided in Peleg's days.
Genesis 9 names Noah's three sons through whom the earth was populated; Genesis 10 traces the nations descended from their families.
Genesis locates the builders of Babel in Shinar; Daniel describes treasures from Jerusalem being taken to the land of Shinar, a later reference to the region.
Genesis 11 locates the tower builders in Shinar; Genesis 14 also identifies Shinar as the kingdom of Amraphel.
Genesis 11 explains the name Babel through the confusion of languages; Genesis 10 had already named Babel among the beginnings of Nimrod's kingdom.
Genesis 11 introduces Abram's wife as Sarai; Genesis 17 records God changing her name to Sarah.
Genesis 11 begins the family's journey toward Canaan and records their stop in Haran; Genesis 12 continues Abram's departure from Haran toward Canaan.
Genesis 11 describes Terah's family leaving Ur and stopping in Haran; Joshua recalls Abraham's family living beyond the Euphrates and God's calling him to Canaan.
Genesis 11 describes Abram's family leaving Ur of the Chaldees; Nehemiah recalls God choosing Abram and bringing him out of Ur.
Stephen recalls God's command for Abraham to leave his land and relatives.
Peter repeats God's promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring.
Paul cites God's promise to bless all nations through Abraham while explaining justification by faith.
God promised Abram the land for his descendants; Joshua later says Israel possessed the land God had sworn to give their fathers.
Abram returns to the altar he built between Bethel and Ai and calls on the Lord again, returning to the place first described in Genesis 12.
Genesis 12 notes the Canaanites were already in the land; Genesis 13 mentions Canaanites and Perizzites dwelling there when Abram's and Lot's herdsmen disputed.
Genesis 13 describes Lot settling among the cities of the plain near Sodom; Genesis 14 reports that he was living in Sodom when he was captured.
Genesis 13 says Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom; Genesis 19 later finds him living in Sodom when the angels arrive.
Abram settles by Mamre near Hebron in Genesis 13; Genesis 14 locates him there when a survivor reports Lot's capture.
Abram pitches his tent by the oaks of Mamre in Genesis 13; the Lord later appears to Abraham at the same location in Genesis 18.
Abram settles near Mamre at Hebron; Genesis 35 identifies Mamre and Hebron as the place where Jacob later comes to his father Isaac.
Genesis 14 names the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah; Deuteronomy recalls the later overthrow of those cities as an example of judgment.
Genesis 14 identifies Horites living in Mount Seir; Deuteronomy 2:12 explains that Esau's descendants later displaced them.
Genesis 14 locates the Horites in Mount Seir; Deuteronomy 2:22 recalls the Horites being driven out of Seir before the descendants of Esau.
Genesis 14 describes Abram dwelling by Mamre when he hears Lot was taken captive, continuing the location introduced in Genesis 13.
Genesis 14 calls the northern location Dan; Judges explains that the city was formerly called Laish and later renamed Dan, clarifying the place-name.
Genesis introduces Melchizedek as king of Salem and priest of the most high God; Psalm 110 speaks of a priest forever after Melchizedek's order.
Genesis names Melchizedek king of Salem; Psalm 76 names Salem as the place of God's tabernacle and associates it with Zion.
Paul recalls God's promise that Abraham's descendants would be numerous despite his circumstances.
Paul quotes Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness to explain justification by faith.
James quotes Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness in his discussion of faith and works.
Paul quotes Abraham's belief being counted as righteousness to explain his argument about faith.
Stephen recounts God's warning that Abraham's descendants would live as strangers and suffer oppression before deliverance.
God foretold Abraham’s descendants would endure four hundred years of affliction in a foreign land; Exodus records Israel leaving Egypt after a 430-year sojourn, using a different time figure.
God promised Abraham that his descendants would depart with great possessions; Exodus records the Israelites receiving silver, gold, and clothing from the Egyptians.
God covenanted to give Abram’s descendants land with named boundaries; Joshua later reports Israel possessing the land sworn to the fathers, without repeating those boundaries.
Genesis 16 introduces Sarai's Egyptian handmaid Hagar after earlier passages report that Abram and Sarai had no child and Abram lacked an heir.
Genesis 16 introduces Sarai's servant Hagar; Genesis 21 recounts Sarah's demand that Hagar and her son be sent away.
Paul quotes God's declaration that Abraham would be the father of many nations.
God promised that Sarah would bear Isaac at the appointed time the next year; Genesis 21 records her bearing Abraham a son at that set time.
Sarah was promised a son despite her age; Genesis 21 opens by saying the LORD did for her exactly as he had spoken.
Paul recalls God's promise that Sarah would bear a son at the appointed time.
Genesis 18 says the men turn toward Sodom while Abraham remains before the Lord; Genesis 19 describes two angels arriving in Sodom that evening.
Genesis 13 describes the men of Sodom as exceedingly wicked; Genesis 19 depicts the city's men surrounding Lot's house and demanding his visitors.
Genesis 18 reports the great outcry over Sodom's sin; Genesis 19 describes the conduct of the city's men toward Lot's visitors.
Genesis 13 describes the well-watered Jordan plain extending toward Zoar; Genesis 19 identifies Zoar as the town to which Lot is permitted to flee.
Genesis 14 names Bela and identifies it as Zoar; Genesis 19 describes Lot's escape to the town called Zoar.
Genesis 19 recounts the Lord raining brimstone and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah; Deuteronomy recalls their overthrow when describing a devastated land.
Genesis records the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah; Isaiah compares Babylon's coming downfall to that destruction.
Genesis describes Sodom and Gomorrah's destruction; Jude cites those cities as an example of divine judgment.
Genesis names Moab as Lot's son by his elder daughter; Deuteronomy later identifies Moab as land granted to Lot's descendants.
Genesis names Benammi as the father of the Ammonites; Deuteronomy identifies the children of Ammon as descendants of Lot.
Paul quotes Sarah's demand to send away Hagar and Ishmael in his illustration about the two covenants.
Hebrews quotes God's promise that Abraham's descendants would be reckoned through Isaac while discussing Abraham's faith.
Paul quotes God's promise that Abraham's descendants would be named through Isaac.
Hebrews recalls God's oath to Abraham, highlighting that God swore by himself when promising blessing.
Peter recalls God's promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring.
Paul refers to the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham; Genesis repeats that promise here.
Abraham asks for a burial possession as a stranger in Canaan; Genesis 49 later identifies the cave and field he purchased as the family burial place.
Genesis 23 records Abraham purchasing the field and cave of Machpelah; Genesis 25 says Isaac and Ishmael buried Abraham there.
Genesis 23 records Abraham's purchase of the field and cave of Machpelah; Genesis 50 records Jacob's burial in that same family tomb.
Genesis 11 identifies Milcah as Nahor's wife; Genesis 24 identifies Rebekah as the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Milcah and Nahor.
Genesis 24 introduces Laban as Rebekah's brother in Nahor's family; Genesis 29 again identifies Laban with Nahor's household when Jacob seeks him.
Genesis 24 sends Rebekah away with her nurse; Genesis 35 records the death and burial of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse.
Genesis 24 places Isaac near the well Lahairoi; Genesis 25 says Isaac later dwelt by that same well.
Genesis lists the sons Keturah bore to Abraham; 1 Chronicles repeats Keturah's sons and their descendants in its genealogy.
God tells Abram he will die in peace at a good old age; Genesis 25 records Abraham dying in a good old age.
Isaac and Ishmael bury their father Abraham together; later Esau and Jacob bury their father Isaac, continuing the family burial narrative.
Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham in the cave of Machpelah; Genesis 50 records Jacob's burial in the same family tomb.
Genesis 23 records Abraham paying for the field and cave of Machpelah; Genesis 25 identifies that purchased property as Abraham’s burial place.
God promises to establish his covenant with Isaac before his birth; after Abraham’s death, Genesis records God blessing Isaac.
Genesis 24 places Isaac near Beer-lahai-roi before meeting Rebekah; Genesis 25 says he lived there after Abraham’s death.
God promises Abraham that Ishmael will father twelve princes; Genesis 25 names Ishmael’s twelve sons and calls them princes.
Genesis 24 introduces Laban as Rebekah’s brother; Genesis 25 identifies Rebekah as Isaac’s wife and again names Laban as her brother.
Genesis records Isaac praying for Rebekah and her conception of twins; Paul recalls Rebekah’s pregnancy in his discussion of God’s choice before their birth.
Genesis describes Esau as hairy at birth; Jacob later contrasts Esau’s hairy skin with his own smooth skin during the plan to obtain Isaac’s blessing.
Genesis says Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for food; Hebrews uses Esau as a warning against treating a birthright lightly.
Genesis 21 records Abraham’s dealings and covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba; Genesis 26 introduces Isaac’s later dealings with Abimelech during a famine.
Abraham names the place Beersheba after his agreement with Abimelech; later Isaac gives a well the name Shebah and the city is again called Beersheba.
Genesis 26 names Esau’s Hittite wives Judith and Bashemath; Genesis 36 gives a later list of his wives, including Adah daughter of Elon, with differing names that should not be silently equated.
Esau’s Hittite wives bring grief to Isaac and Rebekah; Rebekah later tells Isaac she does not want Jacob to marry a daughter of Heth.
Genesis describes Esau as hairy and Jacob as smooth; Jacob cites this distinction when he fears Isaac will discover the deception.
Isaac blesses Jacob using the words that those who curse him will be cursed and those who bless him blessed; Balaam uses a closely related blessing-and-curse formula for Israel.
Genesis records Isaac’s words of blessing to Esau; Hebrews recalls that Isaac blessed both Jacob and Esau concerning things to come.
Rebekah expresses distress over the possibility of Jacob marrying a Hittite woman; Isaac then sends Jacob to his mother’s family to find a wife.
Genesis 25 identifies Rebekah’s father Bethuel and brother Laban; Isaac later directs Jacob to that same family in Padan-aram to seek a wife.
Genesis 28 says Esau married Mahalath, Ishmael’s daughter; Genesis 36 lists Bashemath, also a daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth, but uses a different name.
Jacob sees angels ascending and descending on a ladder in his dream; Jesus speaks of angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
God promises Jacob the land on which he lies; this continues the land promise God had earlier given to Abraham and his descendants.
God identifies himself to Jacob as the God of Abraham and Isaac; he had previously appeared to Isaac and reaffirmed his promise to Abraham’s descendants.
God promises Jacob and his descendants the land in Genesis 28 and repeats that land promise when he later appears to Jacob in Genesis 35.
God promises Jacob that all families of the earth will be blessed through him and his seed, repeating the promise made earlier to Abraham.
The promise that all families of the earth will be blessed through Jacob’s seed recalls God’s earlier oath that all nations would be blessed through Abraham’s seed.
Jacob calls the place Bethel after his dream; God later tells him to return to Bethel and build an altar there.
Jacob names the place Bethel, formerly called Luz; years later he recalls that God appeared to him at Luz and blessed him.
Jacob names the place Bethel after his encounter with God; Hosea later recalls Jacob’s encounter with God at Bethel.
Laban runs to meet Jacob, his nephew; earlier Laban ran to meet Abraham’s servant when he arrived seeking a wife for Isaac.
Genesis introduces Leah as Laban’s elder daughter; Jacob later identifies Leah as buried in the family burial place at Machpelah.
Genesis introduces Leah and Rachel as Laban’s daughters; Ruth later names Rachel and Leah as the women who built the house of Israel.
The Lord opens Leah’s womb while Rachel has no children; Rachel later envies Leah and asks Jacob for children.
Genesis identifies Reuben as Jacob and Leah’s firstborn; Genesis 46 includes Reuben and his sons among Jacob’s family who went into Egypt.
Leah names her firstborn son Reuben; Jacob later addresses Reuben as his firstborn when speaking over his sons.
Jacob says that God has withheld children from Rachel; the psalm likewise describes children as a gift and heritage from the Lord.
Genesis records Leah naming her son Gad; Jacob later addresses Gad by name in his words about his sons’ futures.
God opens Leah’s womb while Rachel is barren; later God remembers Rachel and opens her womb as well.
Genesis describes the flocks bearing marked young; Jacob later recounts a dream involving marked animals when explaining his years of labor for Laban.
Jacob names the place Mahanaim after encountering God’s angels; 2 Samuel later names Mahanaim as the place to which Abner brought Ish-bosheth.
Jacob sends messengers to Esau in Edom; Genesis earlier explains Esau’s name Edom in connection with the red food he requested.
Jacob sends messengers to Esau in the land of Seir; Joshua later says that God gave Mount Seir to Esau as his possession.
Jacob’s messengers report that Esau is coming with four hundred men; in the next chapter Jacob sees Esau approaching with those four hundred men.
Jacob addresses the God who appeared to him at Bethel and promised him the land and descendants; he now asks that God to deliver him from Esau.
Jacob prays to the God of Abraham and Isaac, whom he previously acknowledged as the one who protected him during his years with Laban.
Jacob invokes the God of his fathers in prayer; he had earlier sworn by the fear of his father Isaac when making his covenant with Laban.
Jacob crosses the Jabbok during his return home; Deuteronomy later names that river as part of the boundary of land assigned to Reuben and Gad.
God changes Jacob's name to Israel; later at Bethel God repeats that Israel will be his name.
Jacob sees Esau approaching with four hundred men, confirming the earlier report that made him afraid.
Jacob names his encampment Succoth; Joshua later places Succoth among the towns allotted east of the Jordan.
Jacob buys a field near Shechem; Joshua later records that Joseph's bones were buried in the parcel Jacob had purchased.
Genesis first records Leah giving birth to Dinah; the later account identifies Dinah as Leah's daughter when she goes to see the women of the land.
Simeon and Levi attack the men of Shechem after Dinah is violated; Jacob later condemns their violent anger in his words about the brothers.
God tells Jacob to return to Bethel and build an altar, recalling the earlier encounter in which God identified himself as the God of Bethel.
Jacob is told to return to Bethel; Hosea later recalls Jacob's encounter with God at Bethel.
Jacob returns to the place he previously named Bethel after his dream of the ladder and God's promise.
Genesis 24 introduces the nurse who accompanied Rebekah when she left home; Genesis 35 names her Deborah and records her death and burial.
God again promises Jacob the land given to Abraham and Isaac, repeating the promise spoken to him during his earlier vision at Bethel.
Genesis describes Rachel's death and burial on the way to Ephrath, or Bethlehem; Jacob later recalls that burial when speaking to Joseph.
Jacob sets a pillar over Rachel's grave; Samuel later directs Saul past Rachel's sepulchre as a known landmark.
Genesis records Reuben lying with Bilhah, his father's concubine; Chronicles later identifies that offense as the reason his birthright passed to Joseph's sons.
Jacob returns to Isaac at Mamre near Hebron, where Abraham had earlier settled and built an altar.
Jacob returns to Isaac near Hebron; Genesis earlier identifies nearby Machpelah as the burial place Abraham purchased for his family.
Jacob and Esau bury their father Isaac; Jacob later identifies Isaac and Rebekah among those buried in the family cave of Machpelah.
Genesis names Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah among Esau's sons; Chronicles preserves the corresponding family list.
Genesis 32 identifies Seir as Esau's land when Jacob sends messengers; Genesis 36 again states that Esau lived in Mount Seir.
Genesis identifies Esau with Mount Seir; Malachi later speaks of judgment on Esau's mountains and Edom's territory.
Genesis records the descendants of Seir the Horite; Deuteronomy recalls that the Horites had formerly inhabited Seir before Esau's descendants took their place.
Genesis lists the Horite family of Seir; Deuteronomy later says Esau's descendants dispossessed the Horites who had lived there.
Genesis 14 places the Horites in Mount Seir; Genesis 36 lists Seir the Horite and his descendants in the region.
Genesis names Saul of Rehoboth by the river as a king of Edom; Chronicles repeats the same name in its Edomite king list.
Jacob lives in Canaan, the land where his father had sojourned; God had promised that land to Abraham and his descendants.
Joseph tends the flock with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah; Genesis 35 names those sons as Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher, Joseph's half brothers.
Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his; years later his brothers bow before him when he governs grain distribution in Egypt.
Joseph dreams of his brothers bowing before him; when they later bow in Egypt, he remembers his dreams.
Jacob sends Joseph from the valley of Hebron to find his brothers; the preceding family account says Jacob had returned to his father Isaac near Hebron.
Reuben intervenes to keep his brothers from killing Joseph; years later he reminds them that he had warned against harming the boy.
Genesis records Judah's firstborn son Er; Numbers later lists Er and Onan as Judah's sons and says they died in Canaan.
Genesis says the Lord slew Er, Judah's firstborn, because he was wicked; Chronicles repeats that account in Judah's genealogy.
Genesis records Er's death at the Lord's hand; Jacob's family register later confirms that Er and his brother Onan died in Canaan.
Chronicles identifies Perez (Pharez) and Zerah as the twin sons born to Judah and Tamar.
The census traces the clans descended from Judah's son Perez (Pharez) and his twin brother Zerah.
Joseph's sale to traders in Canaan leads to his being brought to Egypt and purchased by Potiphar.
Genesis first names Potiphar as Joseph's purchaser in Egypt, then resumes Joseph's story in his household.
The chief cupbearer later tells Pharaoh about the dreams he and the baker had on the same night in prison.
Joseph tells both the prisoners and Pharaoh that interpreting dreams belongs to God, not to himself.
The cupbearer recounts to Pharaoh the same prison dreams recorded in Genesis 40.
Jacob's family list names Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and their mother Asenath, as first recorded during Joseph's years in Egypt.
Simeon, whom Joseph had bound during the brothers' first visit, is released when they return to Joseph's house.
Judah recalls Joseph's earlier demand that the brothers bring Benjamin to Egypt before appearing before him again.
Judah repeats Jacob's fear that losing Benjamin would bring his gray hairs down to the grave in sorrow.
Exodus repeats the names of Simeon's sons from the family list of Jacob's descendants.
Numbers lists Gad's later clans, corresponding to the sons named in Genesis, with some names spelled differently.
Genesis first records the birth and naming of Joseph's sons Manasseh and Ephraim, then includes them among Jacob's family in Egypt.
Genesis identifies Bilhah as Rachel's maid; Jacob's family list later counts the descendants born through Bilhah.
Jacob's arrival in Goshen follows Joseph's invitation for his father and household to settle there.
Joseph's brothers ask Pharaoh to settle in Goshen, as Joseph had instructed them to explain their work as shepherds.
Joseph settles Jacob's family in the land of Rameses; generations later, the Israelites depart from Rameses in the Exodus.
Jacob recalls the promise of descendants and land that Isaac had earlier pronounced over him as Abraham's blessing.
Jacob's blessing over Joseph's sons recalls God's earlier promise to multiply his descendants and remain with him.
Jacob's rebuke of Simeon and Levi recalls their violent attack on Shechem after their sister Dinah was defiled.
Jacob and Moses each pronounce a blessing on Zebulun, with references to maritime life and resources.
Jacob and Moses both speak about the tribe of Dan, though Jacob mentions judging and a serpent while Moses uses a lion image.
Chronicles recounts how the Gadites and their allies defeated enemy forces, a later example of Gad prevailing in battle.
Jacob describes Gad overcoming attackers, while Moses blesses Gad with strength and a leading place among the tribes.
Jacob describes Asher's rich food, and Moses likewise blesses Asher with abundance and strength.
Jacob and Moses both bless Naphtali, using different language: Jacob speaks of a released hind and goodly words; Moses of favor and land.
Jacob directs his sons to bury him in the family cave at Machpelah, and Genesis records their carrying out his command.
Jacob names the burial cave at Machpelah that Abraham had purchased from the sons of Heth.
Jacob identifies Abraham's burial place at Machpelah, where Isaac and Ishmael had buried him.
Jacob recalls Isaac's burial among the ancestors; Genesis earlier records that Esau and Jacob buried their father.
Jacob is buried in the Machpelah cave purchased by Abraham, whose acquisition of the family burial ground is recorded earlier.
Genesis names Machir as Joseph's grandson through Manasseh; Numbers later records Machir's descendants taking Gilead.
Joseph foretells God's deliverance from Egypt; God later tells Moses he has visited Israel and will lead them into the promised land.
Joseph's assurance that Israel will return to the promised land recalls God's earlier land promise to Jacob at Bethel.
Joseph recalls the land promised to the patriarchs, including God's renewed promise to Jacob at Bethel.
Moses takes Joseph's bones out of Egypt, fulfilling the oath Joseph required of the Israelites.
Joshua records the burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem, completing the return Joseph requested before his death.
Stephen repeats Exodus' account that a new Egyptian king arose who did not know Joseph, preceding Israel's oppression.
Exodus later names Amram and Jochebed as the parents of Aaron and Moses, identifying the Levite couple first mentioned at Moses' birth.
Exodus first identifies Moses' parents only as Levites; Numbers names them Amram and Jochebed and also names his siblings.
The daughters of Midian's priest become part of Moses' household; the next chapter shows Moses tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro.
Stephen recounts God's command for Moses to remove his sandals because he stood on holy ground.
Jesus refers to God's words at the burning bush identifying himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Jesus quotes God's declaration at the burning bush that he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Jesus quotes God's words identifying himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to discuss the resurrection.
God first turns Moses' rod into a serpent as a sign; Aaron later performs a similar sign with his own rod before Pharaoh.
After Moses flees because Pharaoh seeks to kill him, God tells him to return because the men seeking his life are dead.
Moses and Aaron repeat to Pharaoh the request God instructed them to make: a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice.
Exodus repeats the names of Reuben's sons previously listed among Jacob's family who entered Egypt; Pallu is spelled Phallu in Genesis.
Both passages list descendants of Simeon, but Chronicles uses different forms and omits Ohad; the lists should not be treated as identical.
Exodus repeats the six sons of Simeon named in Jacob's family list in Genesis.
The genealogy in Exodus repeats the three sons of Levi previously listed among Jacob's descendants entering Egypt.
Numbers names Gershon, Kohath, and Merari as Levi's sons while organizing the Levite families for service.
Chronicles repeats the sons of Gershon (called Gershom there), Libni and Shimei, with minor spelling differences.
Chronicles repeats Kohath's sons Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel in its Levite genealogy.
Chronicles again names Mahli and Mushi as Merari's sons and continues with the descendants of Mahli.
Chronicles repeats the two sons of Merari, Mahli and Mushi; Exodus spells the first name Mahali.
Numbers identifies Mahli and Mushi as the family branches descended from Merari during the Levite census.
Numbers identifies Jochebed as Amram's wife and Aaron and Moses' mother, also naming their sister Miriam.
Aaron's brother-in-law Nahshon, son of Amminadab, is named as the leader of Judah's camp in Numbers.
Elisheba, Aaron's wife, is identified as Nahshon's sister; Ruth includes that same Nahshon in the family line leading to David.
Exodus identifies Phinehas as Eleazar's son; Joshua later records Eleazar's burial in a hill belonging to his son Phinehas.
God warns that Pharaoh will not listen; later he explains that Pharaoh's refusal will allow his wonders in Egypt to multiply.
God's stated purpose in bringing Israel out of Egypt is repeated at the Red Sea, where Pharaoh's pursuit will make the Egyptians know he is the LORD.
Aaron's rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, echoing the earlier sign God performed with Moses' rod.
Moses demands Israel's release to worship in the wilderness, carrying out the instruction God gave him at the burning bush.
Moses insists on the three-day journey into the wilderness that God earlier directed him to request from Pharaoh.
Paul quotes God's statement to Pharaoh that his power would be shown and his name proclaimed throughout the earth.
Exodus summarizes Pharaoh's continued refusal after the signs and plagues, including the hardening of his heart following the locust plague.
The Israelites receive favor from the Egyptians and are given valuables as they prepare to depart, as Exodus 11 had described.
The favor the Israelites receive from the Egyptians fulfills God's earlier promise that they would not leave Egypt empty-handed.
Moses foretells the death of Egypt's firstborn; Exodus 12 records the judgment occurring at midnight, though its description of the lowest household differs.
The summary of Pharaoh's hardened heart follows the specific refusal recorded after the plague of darkness.
The Passover law forbids breaking the lamb's bones; John describes Jesus' unbroken bones as fulfillment of Scripture.
Luke cites the law requiring every firstborn male to be set apart for the Lord when describing Jesus' presentation.
Moses carried Joseph’s bones out of Egypt in keeping with Joseph’s request; Joshua records their eventual burial at Shechem.
Numbers retraces the same encampment at Pihahiroth near Migdol and Baalzephon, then continues with Israel's crossing of the sea.
God's earlier warning that he would harden Pharaoh's heart continues when Pharaoh pursues Israel after their departure.
Joshua recalls the Israelites' cry to the LORD when Pharaoh's forces pursued them to the Red Sea.
Isaiah repeats Moses’ words that the LORD is his strength, song, and salvation, using the same praise in a later song of thanksgiving.
The psalm repeats the declaration in Moses’ victory song that the LORD is strength, song, and salvation.
Micah names Miriam alongside Moses and Aaron as people God sent before Israel during the deliverance from Egypt; Exodus shows Miriam leading the women in praise.
Numbers identifies Miriam as the sister of Aaron and Moses and names their parents, adding family detail to the woman leading the song in Exodus.
Numbers retraces Israel’s journey from the sea through three days in the wilderness to Marah, the place of bitter water.
Numbers repeats Israel’s arrival at Elim and its twelve springs and seventy palm trees in the wilderness itinerary.
Moses calls manna the bread God gave Israel in the wilderness; Jesus’ listeners recall that manna as bread from heaven during his teaching.
Paul quotes the manna account, where those who gathered much had nothing left over and those who gathered little had no lack.
Paul describes Israel’s spiritual drink in the wilderness and identifies the spiritual Rock as Christ, recalling the water God gave from the rock at Horeb.
Moses later lists Massah among the places where Israel provoked the LORD, recalling the people’s testing of God in Exodus.
Both places are called Meribah because Israel quarreled, but Numbers 20 describes a later water-from-the-rock incident at Kadesh, not the event at Rephidim.

David's lament recalls Jonathan's extraordinary love; the earlier narrative says Jonathan loved David as his own soul and renewed their oath.
David mourns Jonathan's devoted friendship; earlier, Jonathan sought David in hiding and strengthened his trust in God.
David is directed to settle in Hebron after Saul's death, a town he had recently included among recipients of recovered spoil.
David takes Ahinoam and Abigail to Hebron; the earlier account tells how Abigail became his wife and names Ahinoam as his other wife.
When Judah anoints David king, he learns that men from Jabeshgilead buried Saul; the earlier account tells how they retrieved and buried Saul's remains.
Abner son of Ner, identified earlier as commander of Saul's army, later brings Saul's son Ishbosheth to Mahanaim.
Samuel gives David's reign in Hebron over Judah as seven years and six months; Kings summarizes his Hebron reign as seven years within forty years total.
Abner kills Asahel with a spear during battle; Joab later kills Abner at Hebron in revenge for his brother Asahel.
David demands Michal back, recalling the promised bride-price of one hundred Philistine foreskins; the earlier account says he delivered two hundred.
David later recalls Joab's killing of Abner as bloodshed in peace; Samuel tells how Joab killed Abner at Hebron to avenge Asahel.
Joab kills Abner by striking him under the fifth rib; later he kills Amasa with a similar concealed, fatal stroke. These are different victims and incidents.
The earlier account explains how Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth became lame while fleeing after Saul and Jonathan died; Ziba later identifies him to David.
Chronicles also records the tribes of Israel coming to David at Hebron, where he is anointed king.
Chronicles also recounts David and his men taking Jerusalem from the Jebusites.
Chronicles recounts the ark being brought to Jerusalem and Michal watching David celebrate as it arrives.
Chronicles also recounts Nathan’s message to David about the enduring rule of his descendants.
God promised David that his son would succeed him; Solomon later declares that he has taken David’s throne and built the house promised by God.
God promised David a descendant whose kingdom would be established; Peter applies God’s promise of a descendant on David’s throne to the risen Christ.
God promised that David’s son would build a house for his name; Solomon explicitly recalls that promise as he prepares to build the temple.
Hebrews quotes God’s promise to be a father to David’s son and applies the words to the Son.
Chronicles recounts David’s defeat of Moab and its resulting tribute, while Samuel adds the details of David’s harsh treatment of the captives.
Saul previously fought against the kings of Zobah; David later defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, near the Euphrates. These are distinct campaigns.
Both accounts describe David capturing Hadadezer’s chariots and foot soldiers and disabling horses, but Samuel says 700 horsemen and Chronicles says 7,000.
Both passages say David stationed garrisons, received submission, and was preserved by the LORD; Samuel names Syria of Damascus, while this Chronicles verse names Edom.
The two accounts report the king of Hamath hearing of David’s defeat of Hadadezer; Samuel calls him Toi and Chronicles Tou, and Hadadezer is also spelled Hadarezer.
Both accounts describe a victory of 18,000 in the Valley of Salt; Samuel credits David and names Syrians, while Chronicles credits Abishai and names Edomites.
Chronicles repeats that David ruled all Israel and administered judgment and justice among his people.
Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud is identified as recorder under David and is still listed as recorder among Solomon’s officers.
David seeks a survivor of Saul’s house to honor Jonathan, reflecting the covenant in which David and Jonathan pledged loyalty between their descendants.
David’s desire to show kindness to Jonathan’s family follows the deep affection for Jonathan expressed in David’s lament after his death.
Ziba, introduced as a servant of Saul’s household, later brings supplies to David during Absalom’s rebellion and accuses Mephibosheth of disloyalty.
Ziba, first introduced as a servant of Saul’s household, later approaches David’s returning party with his sons and servants.
Ziba’s report that Jonathan left a son lame in his feet refers to Mephibosheth, whose childhood injury is explained in the earlier account.
Machir son of Ammiel of Lodebar, whose household sheltered Mephibosheth, later brings food and supplies to David during Absalom’s rebellion.
Mephibosheth is called Meribbaal in Chronicles’ genealogy, which likewise identifies him as a son of Jonathan.
Mephibosheth, introduced as Jonathan’s son under David’s care, later has his possessions awarded to Ziba after Ziba accuses him during Absalom’s rebellion.
Chronicles recounts the same conflict that began when the Ammonites mistreated David’s messengers and hired Aramean forces.
Chronicles recounts the same campaign against Ammon and siege of Rabbah, including David’s remaining in Jerusalem while Joab led the army.
Uriah the Hittite, named as Bathsheba’s husband, is also counted among David’s mighty men.
David orders Uriah exposed to death in battle; Nathan later explicitly holds David responsible for killing Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites.
Chronicles recounts David’s treatment of the captured Ammonites after Rabbah fell; both passages describe saws and iron implements, though their wording differs.
Chronicles’ list of David’s children separately names their sister Tamar, who is identified in Samuel as Absalom’s sister.
The earlier family list identifies Amnon as David’s firstborn and Absalom as his third son, providing their family relationship in the account of Tamar.
After killing Amnon, Absalom flees to Talmai king of Geshur; the earlier genealogy identifies Talmai as Absalom’s maternal grandfather.
David’s longing for Absalom after Amnon’s death explains why Joab recognizes that the king’s heart is turned toward his exiled son.
Samuel lists three sons born to Absalom, but later quotes Absalom saying he had no son to preserve his name when he erected a monument; the text does not explain the difference.
Absalom and later Adonijah each set up chariots and horses with fifty men running before them while pursuing royal status; these are separate attempts.
The Cherethites and Pelethites, earlier identified as troops under Benaiah, accompany David when he flees Absalom.
Ittai the Gittite, whom David initially urges to return rather than follow him into exile, later commands one-third of David’s forces against Absalom.
Zadok and Abiathar accompany the ark as David leaves Jerusalem; an earlier list names them in connection with the priesthood of David’s reign, with Abiathar’s son Ahimelech named there.
David sends Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar back with their fathers; the two later relay intelligence to David from near Enrogel.
Ahithophel, whose defection drives David to pray against his advice, had been regarded as an exceptionally authoritative counselor to both David and Absalom.
David prays that Ahithophel’s advice will be frustrated; later the LORD causes Absalom to prefer Hushai’s counsel and defeats Ahithophel’s plan.
David prays that Ahithophel’s counsel will be made foolish; after Absalom rejects that counsel, Ahithophel goes home and kills himself.
David directs Hushai to report palace news through Zadok and Abiathar; Hushai later tells those priests of Absalom’s plans so David can be warned.
Chronicles names Hushai the Archite as the king’s companion, matching Samuel’s description of him as David’s friend during Absalom’s revolt.
Hushai, David’s friend, arrives in Jerusalem as Absalom takes the city and then approaches Absalom with a greeting intended to win his confidence.
David twice rebukes the sons of Zeruiah when they urge harsh action concerning Shimei: once during Shimei’s curses and again after David returns to power.
Samuel first says Hushai reached Jerusalem as Absalom arrived; the subsequent account describes Absalom’s entry and Hushai’s greeting of him.
Ahithophel, formerly David’s counselor, joins Absalom’s conspiracy; Samuel later describes how highly both David and Absalom regarded his advice.
David sent Hushai to frustrate Ahithophel’s counsel; Absalom later accepted Hushai’s advice, and the account says the LORD had appointed Ahithophel’s counsel to be defeated.
David had named Zadok’s son Ahimaaz and Abiathar’s son Jonathan as messengers; they later waited at Enrogel to carry information from Jerusalem to David.
Ahithophel first joined Absalom’s rebellion as David’s former counselor; after Absalom rejected his counsel, he returned home and hanged himself.
Absalom had appointed Amasa commander in Joab’s place; after the revolt David promised Amasa the same position, emphasizing their family relationship.
Barzillai was among those who supported David at Mahanaim during Absalom’s revolt; David later told Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai’s sons in gratitude.
Machir son of Ammiel of Lodebar previously sheltered Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth; he later appears among those who brought aid to David at Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok was earlier designated to convey news to David during Absalom’s revolt; he later offered to run to David with word of the battle’s outcome.
David’s anguish after Absalom’s death continues across the two passages: he weeps for his son at the gate and later covers his face and cries out again.
After Absalom’s defeat, the Israelites recall that David had fled because of him; the earlier passage records David ordering his household to leave Jerusalem to escape Absalom.
Absalom had made Amasa commander instead of Joab; after Absalom’s defeat, David sought to replace Joab with Amasa and appealed to their family ties.
David’s final instructions to Solomon recall Shimei son of Gera of Bahurim coming to meet him at the Jordan and the oath by which David spared him.
David rebukes the sons of Zeruiah on two occasions involving Shimei: first when Shimei curses David, and later when they urge his execution after David’s return.
Barzillai escorted David across the Jordan after supporting him during his flight; David later instructed Solomon to reward Barzillai’s sons for that kindness.
Barzillai offers his servant Chimham to accompany David; Jeremiah later names a habitation of Chimham near Bethlehem, though these verses do not explain its origin.
Sheba’s rebellion and the later northern tribes’ rejection of Rehoboam use nearly the same declaration: they claim no share in David or inheritance in Jesse’s son and call Israel to its tents.
Amasa, whom Absalom had appointed commander during his revolt, is subsequently ordered by David to assemble Judah’s forces, showing his continuing military role under David.
David had promised Amasa command of the army in Joab’s place; he now gives Amasa his first recorded order to assemble Judah’s men.
The Cherethites and Pelethites join the pursuit of Sheba; an earlier list identifies them as David’s forces commanded by Benaiah son of Jehoiada.
Both lists identify Joab as commander of Israel’s army and Benaiah son of Jehoiada as leader of the Cherethites and Pelethites during David’s reign.
David spares Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth because of his oath to Jonathan; the earlier passage records the covenant formed out of Jonathan’s love for David.
David spares Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth because of their oath before the LORD; the earlier account records David and Jonathan renewing their covenant.
The Mephibosheth David spared is Jonathan’s son, whose lameness and childhood escape after Saul and Jonathan’s deaths are described in the earlier account.
The earlier account names Merab as the daughter of Saul given to Adriel; 2 Samuel 21:8 associates five sons of Adriel with Michal, with a KJV marginal alternative reading “Michal’s sister.”
Rizpah daughter of Aiah, first named as Saul’s concubine in Ishbosheth’s dispute with Abner, is later identified as the mother of two of Saul’s sons delivered to the Gibeonites.
David later retrieves Saul’s and Jonathan’s bones from Jabeshgilead, whose men had earlier recovered their bodies from the Philistines at Bethshan and buried their bones.
Sibbechai the Hushathite, who killed Saph in battle against the Philistines, is also named among David’s mighty warriors in Chronicles (spelled Sibbecai).

Both accounts credit Elhanan with defeating a Philistine giant whose spear was like a weaver’s beam; Chronicles names the victim Lahmi, brother of Goliath, while Samuel’s KJV main text includes a supplied “brother of.”
Chronicles repeats Samuel’s conclusion that four descendants of the giant in Gath fell by David and his servants in their battles against the Philistines.
David’s song in 2 Samuel 22 is also preserved in Psalm 18; both verses call the LORD David’s rock, fortress, and deliverer.
Psalm 18 repeats David’s words that he cried to the LORD in distress and was heard from God’s temple; the wording closely parallels his song in 2 Samuel.
Both versions of David’s song describe the earth shaking under God’s anger; Samuel speaks of the foundations of heaven, while Psalm 18 speaks of the foundations of the hills.
Both passages picture the LORD moving on the wings of the wind: David’s song describes him riding a cherub, while Psalm 104 describes him moving on the wind and clouds.
Psalm 18 preserves the same striking image from David’s song: the LORD riding upon a cherub and flying upon the wings of the wind.
Psalm 18 repeats David’s description of darkness and thick clouds as the LORD’s pavilion, with slightly different wording from 2 Samuel.
The two versions of David’s song both contrast God’s dealings with the pure and the froward; Samuel’s KJV says “unsavoury,” while Psalm 18 says “froward.”
Psalm 18 repeats David’s declaration that God enabled him to run through a troop and leap over a wall.
Both versions of David’s song declare God’s way perfect, his word tried, and his protection like a shield for those who trust him.
Both versions of David’s song credit God with giving David strength and making his way perfect, though their wording for God’s strength differs.
Psalm 18 repeats David’s praise that the LORD gave him the shield of salvation and that divine gentleness made him great; the psalm adds that God’s right hand upheld him.
Psalm 18 repeats David’s promise to thank the LORD among the nations and sing praises to his name, using nearly the same wording as his song in Samuel.
Chronicles identifies Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite as one of David’s three mighty men and expands the account of his stand against the Philistines when Israel’s men fled.
David’s warriors later met him at the cave of Adullam, the same refuge where he had earlier gathered his family and followers while escaping Saul; the texts do not date the visits as one event.
Chronicles repeats Benaiah son of Jehoiada’s feats against two Moabite warriors and a lion in a snowy pit, and continues with his defeat of an Egyptian.
Both accounts say Benaiah seized an Egyptian’s spear and killed him with it; Chronicles adds that the Egyptian was five cubits tall and carried a spear like a weaver’s beam.
David’s list of mighty men names Asahel as Joab’s brother; the earlier account identifies Asahel among Zeruiah’s three sons and describes his remarkable speed.
Both books recount David’s census and the resulting judgment; Samuel attributes the incitement to the LORD’s anger, while Chronicles names Satan.
Both Absalom and Adonijah advanced their royal ambitions with chariots, horses or horsemen, and fifty runners ahead of them; the accounts describe separate attempts to gain power.
The earlier list identifies Adonijah as David’s son by Haggith; the later account tells how that son declared his intention to reign.
Kings says Adonijah was born after Absalom, while Samuel lists Absalom third and Adonijah fourth among David’s sons born at Hebron.
Abiathar, previously named alongside Zadok as a priest in David’s administration, later sided with Joab in supporting Adonijah’s claim to the throne.
Benaiah, whom Samuel names as leader of David’s Cherethites and Pelethites, accompanies those same troops as they escort Solomon to his public anointing.
Kings records Zadok anointing Solomon with oil and the people acclaiming him; Chronicles later describes Solomon being made king a second time and Zadok being anointed priest.
Jonathan son of Abiathar, once appointed to carry reports to David during Absalom’s rebellion, later brings news to Adonijah of Solomon’s accession.
Adonijah and Joab each seize the altar’s horns out of fear after Solomon’s accession; their actions occur separately, and the outcomes differ.
David also recalls Joab’s killing of Amasa; the earlier account describes Joab striking Amasa with a concealed sword while the army pursued Sheba.
David’s warning to Solomon about Joab’s killing of Abner recalls the account in which Joab privately lured Abner aside at Hebron and fatally stabbed him.
David tells Solomon to honor Barzillai’s sons because Barzillai helped him during Absalom’s revolt; Samuel describes the provisions Barzillai and others brought to David at Mahanaim.
David’s command to feed Barzillai’s sons at the royal table continues his gratitude for Barzillai’s support; Samuel records Barzillai declining David’s invitation to live in Jerusalem.
David tells Solomon to remember Shimei’s curse; Samuel records Shimei son of Gera cursing David and throwing stones as the king fled through Bahurim.
Solomon sends Abiathar to his fields at Anathoth rather than executing him; Joshua lists Anathoth as a Levite city within Benjamin’s territory.
Kings explicitly identifies Abiathar’s removal from the priesthood as fulfillment of the LORD’s earlier judgment against Eli’s priestly house, announced by a man of God.
Samuel receives another divine warning that Eli’s house will be judged for his sons’ wrongdoing; Kings later identifies Abiathar’s removal as fulfillment of the word against that house.
Joab flees to the altar and grasps its horns after Solomon’s accession, echoing Adonijah’s earlier appeal for protection at the same altar; they were different men and occasions.
Joab’s support for Adonijah is first recorded among the prince’s allies; Kings later cites that allegiance as Joab flees to the altar after Solomon secures the throne.
Chronicles also recounts Solomon’s sacrifice at Gibeon and God’s invitation to ask for a gift, leading Solomon to request wisdom.
Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud served as recorder under David and is still listed in that position among Solomon’s officers.
After Solomon installs Benaiah in Joab’s place over the army and Zadok in Abiathar’s place as priest, both men appear in his roster of officials.
Solomon’s officer Baana administers Bethshean, Taanach, and Megiddo, towns also named in Joshua’s account of Manasseh’s territorial allotment.
The district assigned to Solomon’s officer includes sixty fortified cities in Argob, Bashan, recalling the sixty cities taken from Og’s kingdom in Deuteronomy.
Solomon’s district includes the towns of Jair in Gilead, recalling Numbers’ account of Jair son of Manasseh capturing towns there and naming them Havothjair.
Solomon’s reign is described as a time when people lived safely under their vines and fig trees; Micah uses the same picture to describe a future time of peace and security.

Kings names Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda among the wise men surpassed by Solomon; Chronicles lists Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara among Zerah’s sons. The lists resemble each other but differ in lineage wording.
Kings explains that Hiram king of Tyre had long been friendly to David; Chronicles records Hiram sending David cedar, builders, and craftsmen for his house.
Solomon’s contact with Hiram of Tyre continues the relationship Hiram had with David; Chronicles explicitly recalls the cedar Hiram had supplied for David’s house.
Hiram’s friendship with David, mentioned when he sends word to Solomon, is demonstrated earlier when he supplied cedar and skilled workers to build David a house.

Hiram describes transporting Lebanon timber by sea for Solomon’s building work; generations later the returned exiles likewise arranged for timber from Lebanon to reach Joppa by sea for rebuilding the temple.
Chronicles also describes Solomon building the temple, giving overlapping details about its construction.
Solomon’s house of the forest of Lebanon, described as a great cedar-pillared building, later housed the three hundred gold shields he made.
Both passages describe court construction using three rows of hewn stones and a row of cedar beams; Kings 6:36 specifically describes the temple’s inner court.
Jeremiah describes the temple pillars taken apart by the Babylonians; their eighteen-cubit height and twelve-cubit circumference match Solomon's pillars in Kings.
Chronicles confirms that Solomon placed two pillars at the temple entrance and named the right one Jachin and the left one Boaz.
Both histories describe Solomon's large cast-bronze basin, the sea, as ten cubits across, five high, and thirty around.
Both passages describe two rows of decorations beneath the bronze sea's rim; Kings calls them knops, while Chronicles describes oxen.
Chronicles repeats the arrangement of twelve oxen supporting Solomon's bronze sea, with three facing each of the four directions.
Both accounts describe the bronze sea's handbreadth thickness and lily-shaped rim, but Kings gives its capacity as 2,000 baths and Chronicles as 3,000.
Chronicles likewise credits Huram (called Hiram in Kings) with completing the bronze vessels and other furnishings for Solomon's temple.
Chronicles gives a parallel description of the two temple pillars and their decorated capitals, using somewhat different terms for their ornaments.
The pots, shovels, and basins made for Solomon's temple echo the bronze utensils previously made for the tabernacle altar; these are different sets of furnishings.
Both accounts locate the casting of Solomon's bronze furnishings in clay ground in the Jordan plain, but Kings names Zarthan and Chronicles Zeredathah.
Kings and Chronicles both emphasize that Solomon made so many bronze furnishings that their total weight was not determined.
Chronicles also records the ark being brought into the temple and the glory of the LORD filling the house.
Chronicles also preserves Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple.
Kings explicitly calls this God's second appearance to Solomon and recalls the earlier encounter at Gibeon, where God invited Solomon to ask for a gift.
Chronicles repeats God's condition for establishing Solomon's royal line: Solomon must follow David's example by obeying God's commands.
Chronicles repeats the warning that covenant unfaithfulness would bring Israel's removal from the land and rejection of the temple Solomon built.
God's warning that disobedient Israel will become a proverb and byword echoes the covenant curse Moses announced in Deuteronomy.
Both accounts say the coming devastation will be explained by Israel's abandonment of the LORD who brought their ancestors from Egypt and their worship of other gods.
Solomon's building program included the Millo and Jerusalem's wall; David had earlier fortified the city of David from the Millo inward.
Joshua lists Megiddo among the towns associated with Manasseh's inheritance; Solomon later included Megiddo in his royal building program.
Kings counts 550 chief overseers of Solomon's work, while the parallel account in Chronicles counts 250; the passages do not explain the numerical difference.
Kings first notes Solomon's construction of the Millo; later it identifies that construction and repair of Jerusalem as the occasion for Jeroboam's opposition.
Hezekiah later repaired the Millo in the city of David, a fortification Kings says Solomon built after moving Pharaoh's daughter to her own house.
Solomon established ships at Eziongeber on the Red Sea; generations later Jehoshaphat's ships were broken at the same port before reaching Ophir.
Solomon's ships brought gold from Ophir, a source of fine gold that David had previously designated for the future temple.
Both accounts describe Solomon's voyage with Huram's seamen to Ophir, but Kings records 420 talents of gold and Chronicles records 450.
Chronicles also recounts the queen of Sheba visiting Solomon to test his wisdom with questions.
Jesus recalls the queen of Sheba traveling to hear Solomon’s wisdom and says that one greater than Solomon is present.
Numbers identifies Chemosh with Moab; Kings says Solomon later built a high place for this Moabite god near Jerusalem.
Kings explains Hadad's flight from Edom against the backdrop of David and Joab's campaign there; Samuel records David's conquest and garrisons in Edom.
Kings first reports Jeroboam's rebellion against Solomon; the later account explains that he had fled to Egypt before the accession of Rehoboam.
Chronicles later recalls Jeroboam as Solomon's servant who rebelled against his ruler, confirming the revolt first reported in Kings.
Kings links Jeroboam's opposition to Solomon's building of the Millo, the same project mentioned after Pharaoh's daughter moved into her house.
Jeroboam later sends his wife to Ahijah, explicitly identifying him as the prophet who had foretold that Jeroboam would become king.
Chronicles lists a prophecy of Ahijah among the records of Solomon's reign; Kings describes Ahijah meeting Jeroboam and announcing the kingdom's division.
Ahijah predicts that ten tribes will be given to Jeroboam; Kings later says Rehoboam's refusal to listen fulfilled that word from the LORD.
God conditionally promises Jeroboam an enduring dynasty if he obeys, echoing the earlier conditional instruction to Solomon to walk in God's ways.
Chronicles also tells how Rehoboam rejected the people’s request for lighter burdens, leading to the division of the kingdom.
The man of God confronts Jeroboam at Bethel while the king burns incense at the altar he had established for his unauthorized feast.
During Josiah's reforms, the people identify the tomb of the man of God from Judah who had earlier denounced Jeroboam's altar at Bethel.
The man of God names Josiah and foretells the burning of bones on Bethel's altar; Kings later explicitly describes Josiah doing this in fulfillment.
The declaration that Jeroboam's sin would destroy his house is developed into Ahijah's explicit prophecy that God would cut off his dynasty.
The warning that Jeroboam's house would be destroyed is fulfilled when Baasha kills its surviving members; Kings attributes the judgment to Jeroboam's sins.
Jeroboam asks his disguised wife to seek Ahijah because that prophet had previously promised him rule over ten tribes of Israel.
The warning that Jeroboam led Israel into sin develops the earlier statement that his unlawful worship would bring destruction upon his own dynasty.
The later account says Jeroboam's own sins, and his leading Israel into sin, provoked God's anger—the same wrongdoing already identified in the warning of judgment.
Baasha continued the idolatry that Jeroboam introduced; the later account explicitly says he walked in Jeroboam's way and made Israel sin.
Chronicles repeats Kings' account of Rehoboam's reign: he began at forty-one, ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem, and his mother was Naamah the Ammonitess.
Judah's sins provoked the LORD to jealousy, echoing Moses' warning that worshiping other gods would provoke God's jealousy and judgment.
Kings later describes the northern kingdom repeating the same practice found in Judah: setting up high places, images, and groves on hills and beneath green trees.
Judah built idolatrous high places under green trees and on hills—the very locations where Moses commanded Israel to destroy pagan worship sites.
Chronicles parallels Rehoboam's death and burial in the city of David and records that his son Abijah succeeded him, called Abijam in Kings.
Kings names the matter of Uriah as the exception to David's obedience; Samuel recounts David's orders that placed Uriah in danger, resulting in his death.
Both verses record continuing war between Rehoboam of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel; the later verse repeats the earlier account nearly word for word.
Chronicles likewise describes Asa as doing what was good and right before the LORD, confirming Kings' favorable assessment of his reign.
Jehoshaphat followed his father Asa's ways, and Kings explicitly notes that neither king removed the high places, although each is praised for doing right.
Chronicles reproduces Asa's request that Benhadad of Syria break his alliance with Baasha of Israel in exchange for silver and gold.
Benhadad attacked Ijon, Abelbethmaachah, and Naphtali in Asa's time; much later, Assyria captured some of the same northern towns under Pekah. These are separate invasions.
Both histories report Asa taking Baasha's building materials from Ramah and using the stone and timber to fortify Geba and Mizpah.
Matthew's genealogy names Asa as the father of Jehoshaphat (Josaphat), agreeing with Kings' account of Jehoshaphat succeeding his father.
The prophet Jehu son of Hanani who spoke judgment against Baasha later rebuked Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked; these were separate messages to different kings.
Chronicles credits Jehu son of Hanani with a written record of Jehoshaphat's reign; Kings earlier identifies this same prophet delivering God's word against Baasha.
The judgment against Baasha explicitly charges him with following Jeroboam's sinful example, as Kings had already said about his reign.
Jehu foretold the destruction of Baasha's house, and Kings explicitly reports Zimri destroying that household according to the LORD's word through Jehu.
Gibbethon remained a site of Israelite military activity: Baasha killed Nadab during a siege there, and later Israel's army was camped there when Zimri seized power. These are separate events.
Micah later condemns people for following the 'statutes of Omri,' connecting his name with the evil reign Kings attributes to him.
Jehu refers directly to Ahab's service of Baal when gathering its worshipers; his claim that he would serve Baal more was part of his deception against them.
Ahab's worship of Baal helped establish the idolatry later summarized among Israel's sins before its exile; the passages describe different stages of that history.
Ahab built a temple for Baal in Samaria; Jehu later assembled Baal's worshipers in that temple before destroying them and the house of Baal.
Joshua pronounced a curse concerning the rebuilding of Jericho and the builder's sons; Kings explicitly says Hiel's rebuilding fulfilled the LORD's word through Joshua.
Elijah first announces that no rain will fall except by his word; later the LORD sends him to Ahab and promises to restore rain to the land.
James recalls Elijah's prayer that rain would cease and gives the drought's duration as three years and six months, expanding the account of Elijah's announcement to Ahab.
Jesus specifically recalls Elijah being sent to the widow of Zarephath (Sarepta) near Sidon during the famine, the event recorded in Kings.
The later command to Elijah to announce returning rain follows his earlier declaration that rain would cease; both verses concern the same drought.
Ahab calls Elijah the one who troubles Israel and later calls him his enemy; both encounters show Ahab's hostility when confronted by the prophet.
Elijah invokes the LORD as God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel (Jacob), the same patriarchal identification God gave Moses at the burning bush; these are distinct settings.
Paul quotes Elijah’s complaint that Israel had killed God’s prophets and torn down his altars while discussing a faithful remnant.
Paul quotes God’s answer to Elijah that seven thousand had not bowed to Baal while discussing the remnant chosen by grace.

Ahab returns home 'heavy and displeased' after a prophet condemns his release of Benhadad; he reacts with the same words when Naboth refuses to sell his ancestral vineyard. These are separate incidents.
Ahab is 'heavy and displeased' when Naboth refuses his request, just as he was after being rebuked for sparing Benhadad. The repeated description marks two different reactions of the same king.

Elijah foretells that dogs will lick Ahab's blood, and the later account says dogs licked blood from Ahab's chariot at Samaria. Kings explicitly presents the event as fulfilling the LORD's word, though the locations are worded differently.

Ahab had earlier accused Elijah of troubling Israel; when Elijah confronts him over Naboth's vineyard, Ahab again treats the prophet as an enemy. Both encounters show their continuing conflict over Ahab's wrongdoing.
Elijah explicitly says Ahab's house will become like Baasha's; the earlier judgment against Baasha likewise promises to remove his descendants because of his sins and Israel's idolatry.

Elijah foretells that dogs will eat Jezebel by Jezreel's wall; after her death, Jehu identifies the announced judgment as fulfilled. The description of the place is not worded identically in both accounts.

Kings earlier reports Ahab's worship of Baal and the grove he made; its later assessment says Jezebel encouraged his unusually wicked conduct. The passages describe his idolatry and its influence rather than a new incident.
Ahab is condemned for following the abominations of the Amorites; the later accusation says Manasseh did greater evil than the Amorites before him. These are comparisons of separate kings' idolatry.
God delays judgment on Ahab's house until his son's days because Ahab humbled himself; Jehu later kills Ahab's son Joram and recalls the LORD's judgment over Naboth's blood.
Chronicles also recounts Ahab and Jehoshaphat’s campaign at Ramoth Gilead, including Ahab’s death.

In both episodes, fire comes from heaven in response to Elijah, but at Carmel it consumes a sacrifice to demonstrate the LORD's power, while here it consumes a king's soldiers confronting the prophet.

James and John explicitly recall Elijah's calling down fire from heaven, but Jesus rebukes their proposal to consume the Samaritan villagers. Their request and Elijah's action occur in different circumstances.

After Ahaziah dies without a son, Jehoram succeeds him as king of Israel; the next account names Jehoram as Ahab's son and describes his reign, although the regnal synchronisms are stated differently.
God named Elisha as Elijah's prophetic successor, and Elijah called him to follow and serve him. Their journey before Elijah's departure continues that relationship, with Elisha remaining beside him.
Elijah cast his mantle upon Elisha when calling him; later he uses that same distinctive mantle to divide the Jordan before departing, after which Elisha takes it up.
Elisha cries, 'My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof,' when Elijah departs; years later King Joash speaks the same words over the dying Elisha.
Ahaziah son of Ahab reigned over Israel before Jehoram son of Ahab; these notices establish the succession of the brothers, not the same king or the same accession date.

One verse records that Jehoram succeeded childless Ahaziah as king of Israel; the other begins the account of Jehoram son of Ahab's twelve-year reign. Their chronological notices use different synchronisms.
Jehoram continued the sins introduced by Jeroboam, despite removing a Baal image; the earlier prophecy had condemned Israel for the sins Jeroboam committed and taught the nation to follow.
Both verses explicitly date Moab's rebellion against Israel to the death of Ahab; the later chapter supplies the fuller account of the conflict under Jehoram.
Jehoshaphat repeats almost word for word his pledge of military support: first to Ahab against Syria, and later to Ahab's son Jehoram against Moab. These were separate campaigns.
The servant identifies Elisha as one who ministered to Elijah; the earlier account records Elisha leaving his work, following Elijah, and ministering to him.
On two different campaigns Jehoshaphat asks whether a prophet of the LORD can be consulted, first before the battle at Ramothgilead and later during the Moabite expedition.
Gehazi serves Elisha when the Shunammite woman is first introduced; later Gehazi recounts Elisha's raising of her son to the king just as that same woman comes seeking restoration of her property.
Elisha promises the Shunammite a son 'according to the time of life,' echoing the language of the promise to Sarah. These are distinct birth announcements, with different speakers and families.
Jesus explicitly recalls Naaman the Syrian as the leper cleansed in Elisha's time; Kings records Naaman washing seven times in the Jordan and becoming clean.
Benhadad king of Syria besieges Samaria in both accounts, but the siege under Ahab in 1 Kings 20 and the later famine siege in 2 Kings 6 are separate episodes, not one continuous attack.
The Syrian siege causes extreme famine and exorbitant prices in Samaria; Elisha then announces that flour and barley will be affordable at the city gate the very next day, reversing those conditions.

Benhadad, who earlier besieged Samaria and caused a severe famine, later hears that Elisha has come to Damascus while the Syrian king is ill. These are distinct episodes involving the same named ruler.

Elisha warns Hazael that he will inflict suffering on Israel; the later history records the LORD delivering Israel into Hazael's hand during Jehoahaz's reign. It confirms his oppression, without detailing every atrocity Elisha predicted.

The LORD earlier instructed Elijah to anoint Hazael king of Syria; Elisha later tells Hazael that the LORD has shown him he will become king. The text does not describe Elijah himself performing that anointing.

Both passages date royal successions using Jehoram of Judah and Joram (Jehoram) of Israel; 2 Kings 1:17 speaks of the second year of Judah's Jehoram, whereas 8:16 gives Israel's Joram's fifth year and says Jehoshaphat was then king. The chronological notices should not be silently equated.
During Jehoshaphat's reign, Edom had no independent king but was governed by a deputy; under his son Jehoram, Edom revolted against Judah and established its own king.
Jehu is commissioned to avenge the blood of the LORD's prophets on Jezebel; Kings earlier records Jezebel killing the prophets while Obadiah hid and fed one hundred of them.
The command to destroy Ahab's house repeats Elijah's earlier judgment that Ahab's posterity would be cut off. The later commission to Jehu applies that specific prophecy to the dynasty's downfall.
The sentence on Ahab's house explicitly compares it to Jeroboam's; the earlier history records Baasha destroying all Jeroboam's family in fulfillment of Ahijah's prophecy.

Jehu's conspiracy arises while Israel's army holds Ramothgilead against Hazael; the earlier account describes the battle in which Syria wounded King Joram, setting the stage for his return to Jezreel.

Chronicles also recounts Joram's return to Jezreel after being wounded by Syria. In the KJV it calls the visiting Judahite king Azariah (also called Ahaziah), whereas Kings calls him Ahaziah; the account provides context for Jehu's attack.
Both passages describe Joram returning wounded from the Syrian battle at Ramothgilead to recover in Jezreel. The later account places Jehu's plot against him during that recovery.

After Jehu kills Joram, he orders his body thrown onto Naboth's land and recalls the LORD's judgment on Ahab for Naboth's blood. Elijah's earlier pronouncement also foretold dogs licking Ahab's blood; the passages should not be reduced to an identical description of one death.
Jehu explicitly identifies Jezebel's death and the dogs' consumption of her body as fulfillment of the LORD's word through Elijah; 1 Kings records the earlier prediction at Jezreel.
Jehu declares that the LORD's judgment against Ahab's family has come to pass; Elijah had previously foretold the cutting off of Ahab's descendants.
When Ahab humbled himself, the LORD deferred the disaster on his family until his son's days; Jehu later declares that the announced judgment on Ahab's house has been carried out.

Jehu's declaration that the LORD has fulfilled Elijah's judgment follows his destruction of Ahab's family; the earlier commission explicitly ordered him to strike Ahab's house and avenge the prophets' blood.

Jehu meets Jehonadab son of Rechab, who joins him; Jeremiah later recalls Jonadab son of Rechab as the ancestor whose instructions his descendants continued to obey. The passages illuminate the same named Rechabite family in different generations.
Jehu destroys Ahab's remaining family in Samaria, and Kings explicitly says this fulfills the LORD's word through Elijah; the earlier decree ordered the complete end of Ahab's house.
Jehu pretends that he will serve Baal more than Ahab did as part of his plan to gather and kill Baal's worshipers. Kings earlier recounts Ahab's adoption of Baal worship after marrying Jezebel.
God promises Jehu that four generations of his descendants will sit on Israel's throne; after the death of Zechariah, the account explicitly states that this word to Jehu was fulfilled.

The LORD earlier names Hazael as an agent of judgment alongside Jehu and Elisha; Kings later recounts Hazael taking portions of Israel's territory by force, a concrete instance of his military threat.

Elisha foretells that Hazael will do great harm to Israel; the later record reports Hazael attacking Israel's territory. It records his aggression but does not itemize all the acts named in the warning.
Kings and Chronicles both report Athaliah's attempt to destroy Judah's royal family after Ahaziah died; Chronicles continues with the rescue and concealment of Joash.
Chronicles repeats the people's destruction of Baal's temple, altars, images, and priest Mattan after Athaliah's fall, while providing additional details of the reforms and procession.

The LORD foretells judgment involving Hazael's sword; during Jehoahaz's reign, Israel is delivered into Hazael's and his son's power. This is a connection in the prophetic and historical accounts, not an assertion that every named action occurred then.
When Elijah was taken away, Elisha cried, 'My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.' King Joash later uses those same words as he weeps over the dying Elisha.
Elisha foretells Hazael's violence against Israel; the later account says Hazael oppressed Israel throughout Jehoahaz's reign, confirming the broader warning of suffering under his rule.

Both passages explicitly appeal to God's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: Exodus says God remembered that covenant amid Israel's bondage, and Kings says he showed Israel mercy despite Syrian oppression because of it.

Kings explicitly cites the law forbidding the punishment of children for their parents' sins when Amaziah refuses to execute the children of his father's assassins. Deuteronomy states that command directly.
Chronicles repeats Joash's parable of the thistle and cedar almost word for word. In both histories, the king of Israel uses it to warn Amaziah of Judah against challenging him.

Kings and Chronicles recount the same defeat of Amaziah by Joash of Israel, followed by damage to Jerusalem's wall and the taking of temple and royal treasures; the genealogical names are not identical in the KJV accounts.

Kings reports that Azariah restored Elath to Judah; a later reign records Rezin of Syria recovering Elath and expelling the Jews. The two accounts show the city's changing control in different periods.
God promised Jehu that his descendants would rule Israel through the fourth generation; after Zechariah's reign ends, Kings explicitly declares that this promise was fulfilled.

Both accounts describe Assyria deporting Israelites under Tiglathpileser (Tilgathpilneser). Kings names captured northern towns and Naphtali; Chronicles specifies Reuben, Gad, and eastern Manasseh, describing related but distinct groups of captives.

Kings records Tiglathpileser's earlier deportation of Israelites from Galilee and Naphtali during Pekah's reign; the later passage describes Samaria's fall and another Assyrian deportation under Hoshea, not the same campaign.
Kings and Chronicles give Jotham's accession age as twenty-five, his reign as sixteen years in Jerusalem, and his mother as Jerusha or Jerushah, daughter of Zadok.
The threat from Rezin and Pekah begins in the account of Jotham's reign; the next chapter describes their joint siege of Ahaz in Jerusalem, which did not capture him.
Kings first reports Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel being sent against Judah during Jotham's days; Isaiah recounts their later joint advance on Jerusalem during Ahaz's reign and says it failed.
