Kings and Chronicles both describe Ahaz's sixteen-year reign and his unfaithfulness. Chronicles adds molten images for Baalim and describes burning his children, while Kings says he made his son pass through the fire.
Moses commanded Israel to destroy pagan worship sites on hills and under green trees; Ahaz instead sacrificed and burned incense at precisely those kinds of places.
Kings first names Rezin and Pekah as enemies sent against Judah in Jotham's days; the subsequent account describes their unsuccessful siege of his son Ahaz at Jerusalem.
Azariah (Uzziah) restored Elath to Judah, but during Ahaz's reign Rezin of Syria seized it and drove out its Judean inhabitants, reversing Judah's earlier gain.

Ahaz seeks Tiglathpileser's intervention against Syria and Israel; an earlier passage records the same Assyrian king conquering northern Israelite territory during Pekah's reign. The texts do not explicitly identify these as one campaign.

After Assyria captured Damascus, Kings says its people were taken captive to Kir; Amos names Kir as the place from which the LORD had previously brought the Syrians. The passages connect the same people and place at different stages of their history.

Both passages describe Israelites carried into Assyrian exile and name Halah, Habor, and the Gozan region. Chronicles identifies deportees from the eastern tribes; Kings recounts the later fall of Samaria, so the deportations are not presented as one event.

Hosea warns that Samaria will suffer judgment for rebellion against God; Kings records the Assyrian capture of Samaria and the exile of Israelites. Hosea's prediction includes details not described in this verse of Kings.

Deuteronomy commands Israel to destroy pagan altars, groves, and images; Kings records Israel erecting images and groves on hills, contrary to that command. The shared locations reinforce the contrast between command and practice.
Kings' review of Israel's apostasy includes service to Baal; the earlier history describes Ahab promoting Baal worship after marrying Jezebel, an identifiable part of that religious decline.

The history of Israel's downfall lists worship of Baal, groves, and the heavenly host; Manasseh later introduced the same kinds of worship into Judah, including altars for Baal and the host of heaven.
Isaiah also recounts Sennacherib’s invasion of Judah and the Assyrian spokesman’s threats against Jerusalem.
Isaiah also records Hezekiah seeking God after the Assyrian threats and the deliverance of Jerusalem.
Isaiah also records Hezekiah’s illness, his prayer, and the sign that God would extend his life.
Isaiah also recounts Hezekiah showing Babylonian envoys his treasures and receiving Isaiah’s warning about a future exile.
Isaiah foretold to Hezekiah that Judah’s stored treasures would be carried to Babylon; 2 Kings later records Babylon taking royal and temple treasures.
Chronicles gives a parallel account of Manasseh's evil reign, including his restoration of high places, altars to Baal, groves, and worship of the heavenly host. Kings gives the same basic charges.

Both histories describe Manasseh rebuilding the high places his father Hezekiah destroyed, raising altars for Baal, and worshiping the heavenly host; Chronicles also describes altars in the temple courts.

Israel's earlier apostasy included groves, Baal worship, and worship of the heavenly host; Manasseh later practiced these same forms of idolatry in Judah. These are different settings, not the same incident.
Kings and Chronicles state directly that Manasseh built altars to all the host of heaven in the two courts of the LORD's house.
Both accounts describe Manasseh passing his child or children through fire and practicing divination and dealings with familiar spirits; Chronicles adds the Valley of Hinnom as the location.
Both accounts compare royal idolatry with the abominations of the Amorites: Kings says Ahab followed them, and later says Manasseh exceeded their wickedness and led Judah into sin.
The LORD announces coming disaster on Judah for Manasseh's sins; later Kings explicitly identifies Manasseh's wickedness as a reason judgment came upon Judah.
Both prophecies announce disaster on Jerusalem with the distinctive warning that listeners' ears will tingle; Jeremiah also identifies idolatry and innocent blood as causes.
Kings and Chronicles both record Manasseh's death, burial at his own house or its garden, and succession by his son Amon. Chronicles elsewhere adds the account of Manasseh's humbling and prayer.
Chronicles also recounts the discovery of the book of the law during Josiah’s reign and Huldah’s response to the king’s inquiry.
A man of God named Josiah long before his birth as the one who would defile Bethel’s altar; 2 Kings records Josiah burning bones there as foretold.
Chronicles gives a fuller account of the Passover Josiah commanded Judah to observe.

Kings reports that Nebuchadnezzar brought Jehoiakim under Babylonian rule for three years before his rebellion; Daniel dates Nebuchadnezzar's siege to Jehoiakim's third year. The accounts supply differing chronological notices and should not be silently equated.

Kings reports Jehoiakim's submission to Nebuchadnezzar and later rebellion; Jeremiah dates a message to Jehoiakim's fourth year, identified as Nebuchadnezzar's first year, providing a dated setting for Babylon's ascendancy.

Kings records Chaldean and Syrian raiding bands sent against Judah in Jehoiakim's days; Jeremiah reports the Rechabites seeking shelter in Jerusalem out of fear of Chaldean and Syrian armies during Nebuchadnezzar's advance.

Kings says Babylon seized Egypt's former territory as far as the Euphrates; Jeremiah identifies Nebuchadnezzar's defeat of Pharaohnecho's army at Carchemish on the Euphrates, helping explain Egypt's loss of influence.

Both accounts describe Jehoiachin's brief reign before Babylonian captivity, but the KJV of Kings gives his accession age as eighteen and three months of rule, while Chronicles gives eight and three months and ten days.
Both passages state that Nebuchadnezzar installed Zedekiah in Judah after Jehoiachin (Coniah); Kings explains that he had been called Mattaniah before the Babylonian king renamed him.

Both passages name Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah as the mother of Zedekiah and Jehoahaz. Since each is also described as Josiah's son, the records identify them as brothers sharing the same mother.

Kings and Jeremiah give nearly identical dates and details for Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem under Zedekiah: it began in his ninth year on the tenth day of the tenth month and continued into his eleventh year.

Jeremiah recounts the same Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem's walls and the burning of its royal and private houses. Kings places the demolition under Nebuzaradan's command after the temple was burned.

Both accounts say the Chaldean army under the captain of the guard demolished Jerusalem's walls. Jeremiah 52:14 directly parallels this verse; the longer original target also covered later deportations and temple furnishings.
Kings and Jeremiah both record the Chaldeans breaking up Solomon's bronze pillars, bases, and sea and transporting their bronze to Babylon. Jeremiah also lists associated bronze furnishings.

Both accounts describe the decorated bronze pillars taken from Solomon's temple, but Kings gives a pillar height of eighteen cubits and Jeremiah gives thirty-five cubits. The difference is left explicit rather than reconciled.
Chronicles traces the priestly line through Seraiah to Jehozadak, who went into Babylonian captivity; Kings identifies Seraiah as the chief priest seized by the Babylonians after Jerusalem fell.
Jeremiah names Zephaniah son of Maaseiah as one of Zedekiah's messengers seeking guidance during Babylon's attack; Kings later names Zephaniah among the priests captured after Jerusalem fell.

Zephaniah the priest, whom Jeremiah names as the recipient of Shemaiah's letter, is also named among the temple officials seized after Jerusalem fell; the passages concern different stages of his ministry.
Kings says Nebuchadnezzar placed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over the people left in Judah; Jeremiah separately records the Babylonian officers committing Jeremiah to Gedaliah's care after his release.

Kings first records Jehoiachin surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar and being taken captive; its closing chapter describes his release and elevation after thirty-seven years in captivity, completing that personal history.

Kings and Jeremiah recount Evilmerodach releasing Jehoiachin in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity, speaking kindly to him, and giving him regular provision. Their dates in the twelfth month differ: the twenty-seventh in Kings and twenty-fifth in Jeremiah.
Chronicles opens its genealogy with Adam, Seth (Sheth), and Enosh (Enos); Genesis records Seth's birth to Adam after Abel's death and then the birth of Seth's son Enos.
Chronicles traces its earliest generations from Adam through Seth and Enosh; Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs back through Enos and Seth to Adam, whom Luke calls the son of God.
Chronicles lists Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; Genesis explicitly names the same three and identifies Noah as their father when he was five hundred years old.
Both genealogies identify Nimrod as Cush's descendant who became mighty on the earth; Genesis adds that he was a mighty hunter and names Babel and other early centers of his kingdom.
Chronicles repeats Genesis' genealogy of Eber's sons Peleg and Joktan and the explanation that the earth was divided in Peleg's days.
The Edomite king lists in Genesis and Chronicles both place Saul (Shaul) of Rehoboth by the river after Samlah of Masrekah and before Baalhanan son of Achbor.
Both Edomite king lists place Hadad or Hadar after Baalhanan son of Achbor, but their names differ in the KJV: Chronicles says Hadad and his wife Mehetabel; Genesis says Hadar and names Mehetabel.
Both passages enumerate the twelve sons of Jacob (Israel). Genesis groups them by their mothers, while Chronicles gives a compact list of the same sons.

Chronicles lists Israel's twelve sons; Revelation names tribes among the sealed servants of God. Its list includes Manasseh and Joseph and omits Dan, so it is not an identical repetition of the ancestral list.
Chronicles and Ruth both trace Judah's family line from Hezron through Ram, Amminadab, and Nahshon; Ruth continues through Salmon to Boaz, linking this ancestry to David's family.

Chronicles names Abigail as Amasa's mother and Jether the Ishmeelite as his father; Samuel identifies Amasa as the commander Absalom appointed and calls his father Ithra an Israelite, preserving the different forms used in the KJV.

Chronicles identifies the scribal families living at Jabez as Kenites connected with the house of Rechab; Kings names Jehonadab son of Rechab, whom Jehu meets. The passages share a named ancestral house, not a documented meeting with those scribes.
Chronicles records that David reigned seven years and six months in Hebron before thirty-three years in Jerusalem; Samuel independently gives the same length of his reign over Judah at Hebron.
Two lists in Chronicles name David's sons born in Jerusalem, including Elishama and Eliphelet (Eliphalet); the corresponding name Eliada appears as Beeliada in the later list.

Chronicles places Pharez (Perez) and Hezron within Judah's descendants; Genesis names Pharez among Judah's sons and identifies Hezron as Pharez's son, providing the generations compressed in Chronicles.
Chronicles 2:24 identifies Ashur as Hezron's son and father of Tekoa; Chronicles 4:5 returns to Ashur and names his two wives, Helah and Naarah, supplying further family details.
Chronicles names Othniel as a son of Kenaz; Joshua records Othniel son of Kenaz capturing Kirjathsepher and receiving Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife.
Chronicles traces families descended from Shelah son of Judah; Genesis records the birth of Judah's son Shelah at Chezib, providing the earlier family history.
Both lists name sons of Simeon, including Jamin, Jachin, and Shaul, but the KJV forms and membership vary: Chronicles names Nemuel, Jarib, and Zerah, while Genesis names Jemuel, Ohad, and Zohar.
Genesis records Leah bearing Jacob's first son, Reuben; Chronicles calls him Israel's firstborn but explains that his birthright was later transferred because of his offense.

Chronicles explains that Reuben lost his firstborn birthright because he defiled his father's bed; Genesis records his lying with Bilhah, his father's concubine, which is the specific offense behind the loss.
Jacob's declaration that Reuben would not excel because he defiled his father's bed directly explains the forfeiture of Reuben's firstborn privilege described by Chronicles.
Chronicles and Exodus give matching lists of Reuben's four sons: Hanoch, Pallu or Phallu, Hezron, and Carmi; Exodus includes them in the ancestral families of Israel.
Chronicles and Genesis name the same four sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu (Phallu), Hezron, and Carmi, preserving their family line across the genealogies.

Numbers divides Reuben's descendants into the families of Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi, corresponding to the four sons named in Chronicles. The original range extends into a different family's history and is narrowed.
Chronicles says Gad's descendants lived in Bashan as far as Salchah; Joshua identifies Bashan as far as Salcah within the Transjordan territory that had belonged to King Og.

Chronicles lists Jetur and Nephish among the peoples fought by the eastern Israelite tribes; an earlier genealogy lists Jetur and Naphish among Ishmael's sons, connecting those names to an ancestral line without asserting every combatant's precise descent.
Chronicles names Pul and Tilgathpilneser among the Assyrian kings associated with the eastern tribes' exile; Kings separately records Pul taking tribute from Menahem, not an exile in that verse.

Both passages name Tiglathpileser (Tilgathpilneser) in Assyrian actions against Israel. Kings details towns and Naphtali captives, while Chronicles describes the exile of Reuben, Gad, and eastern Manasseh; the captive groups differ.

Chronicles records the eastern tribes being deported to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the Gozan region; Kings names Halah, Habor, and the Gozan river for captives after Samaria's fall. These are related Assyrian exiles, not necessarily one deportation.
Chronicles and Exodus list Levi's three sons as Gershon, Kohath, and Merari; Exodus places the names within Moses' account of the ancestral Levite families.
Chronicles and Genesis give the same three sons of Levi—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—identifying the family lines from which Israel's Levites descended.
Chronicles names Levi's sons Gershon, Kohath, and Merari; the census in Numbers identifies the Levite clans descended from each of these sons.
Chronicles names Ahimaaz as the son of Zadok; Samuel identifies Ahimaaz as Zadok the priest's son when David sends the priests back to Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt.
Chronicles traces Zadok's descent from Ahitub, and Samuel independently names Zadok son of Ahitub among the priests serving during David's reign.
Chronicles names Seraiah in the priestly family line as Jehozadak's father; Kings identifies Seraiah as the chief priest taken prisoner when Jerusalem fell to Babylon.
Both passages identify Mahli and Mushi as sons of Merari; the later genealogy adds Mahli's sons Eleazar and Kish.
Chronicles traces Elkanah's descent through Jeroham and Eliab; Samuel identifies Samuel's father Elkanah as Jeroham's son but gives the preceding name as Elihu. The KJV wording differs.
Both accounts assign Golan in Bashan and a second town to the Gershonite Levites from half-Manasseh. Chronicles calls the second town Ashtaroth, while Joshua calls it Beeshterah.
Chronicles lists Naphtali's sons Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum; Numbers identifies corresponding clans, spelling the first and last names Jahzeel and Shillem.
Chronicles traces Joshua's ancestry through his father Nun, here written Non; Numbers identifies Joshua as Nun's son and records Moses changing his name from Oshea to Jehoshua.
Chronicles and Genesis record Asher's children, including his daughter Serah and sons Imnah/Jimnah, Ishuai/Isui, Isuah/Ishuah, and Beriah; the KJV spellings vary.
Both passages list descendants of Benjamin and name Bela/Belah and Ashbel, but Genesis contains a longer list; the two genealogies should not be read as identical lists of sons.
Chronicles names Lod and Ono among towns built by Shamed; Ezra records descendants from Lod, Hadid, and Ono among those returning from exile, showing these towns in the later community.
Chronicles credits Shamed with building Lod and Ono; Nehemiah later names both places as settlements and calls the surrounding area the valley of craftsmen.
Both passages place Kish within Saul's Benjaminite family: Chronicles says Ner fathered Kish and Kish fathered Saul, while Samuel calls Kish the son of Abiel. The ancestry is stated differently.
Both passages describe Israelites, priests, Levites, and Nethinims living in their towns, with Ezra adding singers and gatekeepers to the postexilic community.
Chronicles includes the Nethinims among those settled in their cities; Ezra explains that David and the princes had assigned the Nethinims to serve the Levites and records 220 by name.
Chronicles lists Israelites, priests, Levites, and Nethinims living in their cities; Nehemiah similarly describes these groups resettling their towns after the exile.
Samuel also recounts Saul and his sons falling in battle against the Philistines.
Samuel also records Israel’s elders coming to David at Hebron and anointing him king.
Samuel also recounts David and his men taking Jerusalem from the Jebusites.

Chronicles lists armed men from the tribes gathering to David at Hebron as Saul's kingdom passed to him; Samuel describes the elders of all Israel coming to Hebron and anointing David king over Israel, later than his first anointing over Judah.
Samuel explains how the ark reached Kirjathjearim after its return from the Philistines; Chronicles records David later gathering Israel to bring that same ark away from Kirjathjearim.
Chronicles and Samuel both describe David going to Baalah, also called Kirjathjearim or Baale of Judah, to bring up the ark associated with the LORD's presence between the cherubim.
Both accounts say David did not bring the ark into his own city after Uzzah died but took it to the house of Obededom; Samuel continues by reporting its three-month stay and God's blessing.
Chronicles first records God blessing Obededom's household while the ark remained there; a later genealogy names Obededom's eight sons and explicitly attributes the family's blessing to God.
Chronicles and Samuel describe David defeating the Philistines at Baalperazim and using the image of bursting waters to explain why the place received its name.
Samuel also recounts the ark’s journey into Jerusalem and Michal watching David dance as it arrived.
Chronicles names Asaph and other musicians using cymbals, harps, and psalteries in David's worship arrangements; Hezekiah later restores those instruments according to David's command.
Chronicles and Isaiah use closely matching calls to thank or praise the LORD, call on his name, and tell the peoples of his deeds; Isaiah places this praise in a future song of thanksgiving.
The opening command of David's song in Chronicles is repeated almost word for word at the beginning of Psalm 105: give thanks to the LORD, call on his name, and make his deeds known.
Psalm 105 repeats verbatim David's song's warning not to touch God's anointed or harm his prophets, in its account of God's protection of the patriarchs.
Chronicles calls worshipers to honor the LORD in the beauty of holiness; Jehoshaphat later appoints singers who praise the beauty of holiness as Judah goes to battle.
Psalm 29 closely repeats Chronicles' paired commands to give the LORD the glory due his name and worship him in the beauty of holiness.
Chronicles' call to worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness appears also in Psalm 96, whose surrounding verses closely parallel this part of David's song.
Chronicles' summons for the sea and all it contains to roar is repeated in Psalm 98, where creation is also called to rejoice before the LORD.
Both texts picture the trees rejoicing before the LORD because he comes to judge the earth; Psalm 96 expands the promise by speaking of righteous judgment and truth.
David's song declares that the LORD is good and his mercy endures forever; the people repeat that refrain at Solomon's temple dedication when fire and God's glory appear.
The people rebuilding the temple use David's song's refrain about God's goodness and enduring mercy as they praise the LORD when the new foundation is laid.
Psalm 106 repeats David's song's declaration that the LORD is good and his mercy endures forever, using the same words as a call to praise.
Chronicles places Zadok and the priests serving at the tabernacle on the high place at Gibeon; Kings later records Solomon offering sacrifices at Gibeon, described as the great high place.
Samuel also records Nathan giving David God’s promise concerning the future of his royal line.
Both accounts say David defeated Moab and made its people tributaries; Samuel adds the severe treatment of captives that Chronicles does not mention.

These parallel accounts report David capturing Hadadezer's chariots and foot soldiers and disabling most chariot horses, but the KJV main text differs on horsemen: 7,000 in Chronicles and 700 in Samuel.
Both accounts name Hamath's king, Tou or Toi, hearing of David's defeat of Hadarezer or Hadadezer; the alternate spellings refer to the corresponding figures in the two narratives.

Chronicles credits Abishai with killing 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt; Samuel reports David's victory there with 18,000 Syrians in the KJV text, then describes his garrisons in Edom. The accounts differ in the named enemy and leader.
Chronicles repeats Samuel's description of David reigning over all Israel and administering judgment and justice to his people.
Chronicles identifies Joab as David's commander of the army; an earlier account explains that Joab became chief by leading the attack against the Jebusites at Jerusalem.
Chronicles lists Zadok and Abimelech son of Abiathar as priests and Shavsha as scribe; Samuel's later list names Zadok and Abiathar as priests and Sheva as scribe. The personnel lists differ.
Both lists name Zadok son of Ahitub and a priest named as Abimelech or Ahimelech son of Abiathar, alongside a royal scribe called Shavsha in Chronicles and Seraiah in Samuel.
These parallel lists identify Benaiah son of Jehoiada as commander of the Cherethites and Pelethites and place David's sons in senior royal positions.
Samuel also recounts the conflict caused by the mistreatment of David’s messengers by the Ammonites.
Chronicles and Samuel describe David's harsh treatment of captured Ammonites and his return to Jerusalem; Samuel also mentions making captives pass through a brickkiln, a detail absent in Chronicles.

Both accounts describe Elhanan killing a Philistine associated with Goliath whose spear shaft resembled a weaver's beam. Chronicles calls the victim Lahmi, Goliath's brother; Samuel's KJV supplies 'the brother of' in italics, and the father's name differs.
Both books recount David’s census and the resulting judgment; Chronicles names Satan as the instigator, while Samuel speaks of the LORD’s anger.

David repeats to Solomon the charge to be strong, courageous, and unafraid as he prepares to build the LORD's house; the later charge adds a promise that God will be with him until the work is completed.
Chronicles identifies Aaron and Moses as Amram's sons while describing Aaron's priestly duties; Exodus also names their mother Jochebed and records their birth to Amram.
Both passages name Aaron's four sons—Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Chronicles introduces their priestly divisions, while Exodus records their mother, Elisheba.
Both priestly genealogies name the four sons of Hebron in the same order: Jeriah, Amariah, Jahaziel, and Jekameam.
Chronicles appoints Heman and his fellow musicians to minister with instruments; its earlier genealogy names Heman as a singer and traces his descent through Joel and Shemuel.
Chronicles appoints Asaph among the musicians serving under David; its earlier genealogy identifies Asaph son of Berachiah among the singers who stood beside Heman.
The Jashobeam who led David's first monthly military division is also named as chief among David's mighty men; the second passage records his feat with a spear.
Chronicles identifies Sibbecai the Hushathite as commander of the eighth monthly division; Samuel names Sibbechai the Hushathite as the warrior who killed Saph in battle with the Philistines.
Chronicles names Ahithophel as David's counsellor; Samuel records Ahithophel leaving David's service to join Absalom's conspiracy against him.
Chronicles calls Hushai the Archite David's companion, while Samuel calls him David's friend and records his return to Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion.
Chronicles names Joab as David's army commander after listing his counsellors; an earlier account explains how Joab became chief by leading the assault on the Jebusites.
Chronicles lists Abiathar among David's advisers and Joab as commander; Kings later names both Joab and Abiathar as supporters of Adonijah's attempt to take the throne.
David tells Solomon that the LORD can be found by those who seek him and warns of forsaking him; the prophet Azariah later gives Asa and Judah the same seek-or-forsake warning.
David's later charge to Solomon repeats his earlier command to be strong, courageous, and unafraid, adding assurance of God's presence throughout the temple building.
David's charge to Solomon closely echoes God's words to Joshua: be strong and courageous, do not fear, and trust that the LORD will not forsake you. The charges concern different responsibilities.
David acknowledges God's rule over all and his power to strengthen people; Jehoshaphat later prays to the same LORD whose power and might rule every kingdom.
Both records give David a forty-year reign, divided into seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
Kings also recounts Solomon offering sacrifices at Gibeon and asking God for wisdom.
Both accounts describe Solomon assigning 70,000 burden bearers and 80,000 stonecutters for temple construction, but Chronicles counts 3,600 supervisors and Kings 3,300.
Solomon reminds Hiram (Huram), king of Tyre, that he had supplied cedar timber and builders for David's house; Chronicles earlier records Hiram's assistance to David.
Solomon's statement that the heavens cannot contain God is repeated in the parallel account of his temple dedication prayer in Kings.
Before building the temple Solomon says heaven cannot contain God; at the temple's dedication he repeats that even the heaven of heavens cannot contain him.
Kings also describes Solomon building the temple, providing additional details of its construction.
Both accounts give the bronze sea's dimensions as ten cubits across, five cubits high, and thirty cubits around; this is a direct description of the same temple furnishing.

Both passages describe two cast rows of ornament beneath the bronze sea's brim. Chronicles calls the figures oxen, whereas Kings calls them knops; Kings separately describes the twelve supporting oxen.
Both passages describe the sea's handbreadth thickness and lily-shaped rim, but Chronicles says it held 3,000 baths while Kings gives 2,000 baths.
Chronicles and Kings both name Huram (Hiram) as the craftsman who completed the pots, shovels, and basins for Solomon's temple; Kings includes the same completion statement.
These parallel inventories identify the temple's two bronze pillars, their upper capitals, and the decorative networks covering them; Chronicles uses 'pommels' where Kings uses 'bowls.'
Both accounts place the casting of Solomon's bronze temple furnishings in the Jordan plain near Succoth; Chronicles names Zeredathah as the second location, while Kings names Zarthan.
Both accounts emphasize the extraordinary abundance of Solomon's bronze furnishings, whose total weight was not determined.
The temple inventories both name pure-gold snuffers, basins, spoons, and censers and describe gold fittings for the sanctuary doors; Kings specifies gold hinges.
Kings also records the ark being brought into the temple and the glory of the LORD filling it.
Kings also preserves Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication, including his appeal for God to hear prayers offered toward the temple.
At the temple dedication the people praise the LORD for his enduring mercy after witnessing fire and God's glory; earlier the singers used the same refrain as the LORD's cloud filled the temple.

Chronicles says the Levites used instruments David had appointed for praise at Solomon's temple dedication; an earlier passage records David organizing Levitical singers with harps, psalteries, and cymbals.
Both accounts say Solomon consecrated the middle of the temple court for offerings because the bronze altar could not accommodate them all during the dedication.
God's response that his eyes would be open and his ears attentive to prayer at the temple directly answers Solomon's earlier request using nearly the same words.
The LORD's response to Solomon in Chronicles parallels the conditional promise in Kings: if Solomon walks in David's ways and keeps God's commands, God will establish his royal throne.
God tells Solomon that his throne will continue according to the covenant made with David; Nathan's earlier message promises that David's house and kingdom will endure.
Kings records the same warning to Solomon: disobedience would bring removal from the land, rejection of the temple, and disgrace among the nations.
God warns Solomon that unfaithfulness will make Israel a proverb and byword among the nations, repeating the distinctive consequence Moses announced among the covenant curses.
Both records count Solomon's chief officers over the work or people, but Chronicles gives 250 while Kings gives 550; the accounts differ in their totals and description of responsibilities.
Solomon observes the three annual feasts—unleavened bread, weeks, and tabernacles—named in Moses' command for Israel's men to appear before the LORD.
Kings likewise recounts the queen of Sheba testing Solomon with difficult questions and witnessing his wisdom and prosperity.
Kings also records Rehoboam rejecting the people's request to lighten their burden, after which the northern tribes rebel.
Kings gives the parallel account of Rehoboam gathering 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to recover the northern kingdom, before God's message stops the proposed attack.
Shemaiah delivers God's warning to Rehoboam against fighting Israel; Chronicles later identifies Shemaiah as a prophet whose writings recorded Rehoboam's reign.
Chronicles first describes three years when Judah strengthened Rehoboam and followed David's and Solomon's ways; the next chapter records Rehoboam abandoning God's law after his rule became secure.
Rehoboam's abandonment of God's law after establishing his kingdom contrasts with the earlier three years when Judah strengthened him and followed David's and Solomon's ways.
Shemaiah first brings God's word forbidding Rehoboam's war against Israel; during Shishak's later invasion, the same prophet delivers a separate warning of judgment to Rehoboam.
Kings confirms that Rehoboam began reigning at forty-one, ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem, and was the son of Naamah the Ammonitess.
Chronicles refers to Shemaiah's and Iddo's writings as records of Rehoboam's reign; its earlier notice also names Iddo as a seer who recorded events concerning Solomon and Jeroboam.
Abijah calls Jeroboam a former servant who rebelled against Solomon; Kings identifies Jeroboam son of Nebat as Solomon's servant who lifted his hand against the king.
Both accounts describe Asa removing Maachah from her royal position because of her idol and destroying it by the brook Kidron; Chronicles adds that he stamped it.
Kings independently records Asa using the stones and timber taken from Baasha's unfinished works at Ramah to build Geba and Mizpah.
Hanani the seer rebukes Asa for trusting Syria; Kings later identifies Jehu, a prophet who addressed Baasha, as Hanani's son. These are different prophetic messages.
Hanani rebukes Asa for trusting a foreign king rather than the LORD; his son Jehu later rebukes Asa's son Jehoshaphat for aiding wicked Ahab. The two warnings concern different alliances.

Both verses use the distinctive image of the LORD's eyes running to and fro through the whole earth; Chronicles emphasizes God's support for faithful hearts, while Zechariah speaks of divine oversight of Zerubbabel's work.
Jehoshaphat stationed troops in Ephraimite cities his father Asa had captured; the earlier account records Asa's reforms in cities he had taken in mount Ephraim.
Kings also recounts Ahab and Jehoshaphat going to battle at Ramoth Gilead, where Ahab is killed.
Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping Ahab, while his father Hanani had earlier rebuked Jehoshaphat's father Asa for trusting Syria. The warnings address different kings and decisions.
Jehu's rebuke of Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked follows Jehoshaphat's pledge to join Ahab in the campaign against Ramothgilead.
Jehu son of Hanani rebukes Jehoshaphat for supporting Ahab; a later notice names Jehu's writings as a source for the history of Jehoshaphat's reign.
Jehoshaphat recalls Israel sparing Ammon on its journey from Egypt; Moses had instructed the Israelites not to attack the Ammonites or take their land.
Jehoshaphat recalls that Israel did not invade mount Seir during the wilderness journey; Moses had explicitly forbidden Israel to fight Esau's descendants for their land.
Jehoshaphat's prayer recalls Israel's restraint toward Ammon, Moab, and Seir; Jephthah's earlier account likewise describes Israel avoiding Edom and Moab during its wilderness journey.
Jehaziel assures Jehoshaphat that the battle belongs to God; Hezekiah later assures Judah that the LORD will fight for them against Assyria. These are separate military crises.
Jehaziel tells Judah to stand still and see the LORD's salvation rather than fight; Moses used closely matching words before the LORD delivered Israel at the Red Sea. The events are separate.

Chronicles records Jehoshaphat joining Ahaziah in a shipbuilding venture that ended in disaster; Kings likewise records the wrecked ships but says Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's later offer of sailors.
Jehoram's marriage to Ahab's daughter explains the alliance Chronicles earlier reports between his father Jehoshaphat and Ahab's house; Jehoram consequently followed Ahab's evil ways.
Elijah's written warning condemns Jehoram for rejecting the ways of his grandfather Asa; Chronicles earlier describes Asa's removal of foreign altars, images, and groves.
Elijah's written warning contrasts Jehoram with his father Jehoshaphat; Chronicles earlier says Jehoshaphat sought the LORD and refused Baal worship.

Philistines and Arabians who had earlier brought gifts and livestock to Jehoshaphat are later named as peoples stirred up against his son Jehoram; the passages describe different actions under successive kings.
Chronicles explains that Ahaziah succeeded Jehoram because an invading band had killed his elder sons; the preceding account describes that invasion and says only Jehoahaz, the youngest, remained.
Both accounts place Israel's wounded king Joram at Jezreel after fighting Hazael of Syria at Ramah; Chronicles additionally says Judah's Ahaziah visited him there.
Kings gives the parallel account of Athaliah killing Judah's royal heirs after Ahaziah's death and continues with Jehosheba's rescue of the infant Joash.
Kings records the same destruction of Baal's temple, altars, and images after Joash's coronation, including the killing of Mattan, Baal's priest, before the altars.
Both accounts report public rejoicing and the restoration of quiet after Athaliah was killed; Kings adds that she was executed beside the king's house.
Amaziah spared the children of his father's assassins because Moses' law forbids executing children for their parents' sins; Chronicles explicitly cites this command.
Kings also records Amaziah defeating 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt; Chronicles calls the defeated people the children of Seir, while Kings adds the capture of Selah.
Chronicles names Isaiah son of Amoz as the writer of Uzziah's deeds; Isaiah's opening verse identifies him as a prophet whose visions included Uzziah's reign.
Jotham worked on the wall of Ophel, and a later passage records Manasseh strengthening Ophel's defenses; these were separate building projects under different kings.
Ahaz burned his children in the Valley of Hinnom, and the later king Manasseh made his children pass through fire there; the passages describe similar abominations in separate reigns.
Kings confirms that Ahaz made his son pass through fire in imitation of the nations' abominations; Chronicles also locates Ahaz's child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom.
Kings repeats the description of Ahaz sacrificing and burning incense at high places, on hills, and under green trees; both passages describe his idolatry.
Moses commanded Israel to destroy pagan worship sites on hills and under green trees; Ahaz instead offered sacrifices and incense in those very settings.
Chronicles reports Ahaz's defeat by the Syrian king and his captives; Isaiah places Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel in the campaign against Ahaz and Jerusalem.
Chronicles first records Ahaz closing the temple doors; Hezekiah later recalls those closed doors and the neglected lamps, incense, and offerings as he restores worship.
Hezekiah describes the temple worship neglected after its doors were closed; the earlier account explicitly records Ahaz closing the doors and damaging the temple vessels.
Hezekiah's assembly celebrated the feast of unleavened bread for seven days, as prescribed in the law; Leviticus places that feast on the fifteenth day of the first month.
Chronicles records the seven-day feast of unleavened bread under Hezekiah; Luke identifies the feast of unleavened bread as the Passover in the New Testament setting.
Kings independently describes Hezekiah removing high places, images, and groves; Chronicles records participants in his Passover reform breaking down such objects across Judah and beyond.

Hezekiah encouraged Judah not to fear Assyria because the LORD would help them; Jehoshaphat earlier told Judah not to fear an invading multitude because the battle was God's. These are separate crises.
Hezekiah tells the people God is with them against Assyria; the Assyrian spokesman later challenges that same confidence by claiming Hezekiah cannot secure their deliverance.
Chronicles says Hezekiah and Isaiah prayed to heaven during the Assyrian threat; Kings records Hezekiah praying before the LORD for deliverance from Sennacherib.
Kings expands Chronicles' brief notice of Hezekiah's life-threatening illness, prayer, God's answer, and a confirming sign; the account describes his recovery and added years.
Isaiah gives a fuller parallel account of Hezekiah's fatal illness, his prayer, God's promise of fifteen more years, and the sign granted to confirm it.

Chronicles says Hezekiah humbled himself and Jerusalem escaped immediate wrath; Jeremiah recalls Hezekiah fearing the LORD and seeking mercy when Micah prophesied judgment. The texts do not identify these as one occasion.
Kings repeats Chronicles' judgment that Manasseh practiced the same abominations as the nations God had driven out before Israel.
Kings closely parallels Chronicles: Manasseh rebuilt the high places his father removed, erected Baal altars and a grove, and worshiped the heavenly host.
Kings also says Manasseh built altars in the LORD's house, adding that he made altars to the heavenly host in its courts; both accounts contrast this with God's claim on Jerusalem.
Both histories record Manasseh's child sacrifice, divination, enchantments, and dealings with spirits; Chronicles says 'children,' while Kings says 'son.'
Manasseh later fortified Ophel, where Jotham had earlier built along the wall; these passages describe separate royal improvements to the same Jerusalem area.
Both histories record Manasseh's death, burial at his own property, and succession by Amon; Kings specifies the garden of Uzza, while Chronicles says his own house.
Kings also records the book of the law being found during temple repairs and the prophetess Huldah's response.
Kings briefly records the Passover that Josiah commanded, while Chronicles gives a fuller account of its observance.
Kings gives the parallel account of the people making Josiah's son Jehoahaz king after Josiah's death; Chronicles states the succession briefly, while Kings also mentions his anointing.

Chronicles records Nebuchadnezzar replacing the deported Jehoiachin with Zedekiah; Jeremiah confirms the appointment and identifies Zedekiah as Josiah's son and Jehoiachin's uncle, though Chronicles calls him his brother.
Chronicles explicitly describes the land's desolation and seventy years as fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy that Judah's land would be desolate and serve Babylon for seventy years.
Chronicles says the deserted land enjoyed its sabbaths during exile; Leviticus had warned that the land would rest during Israel's absence because it had not received its sabbath rests.
Ezra opens with the same account of God stirring Cyrus to proclaim the rebuilding of the temple, repeating Chronicles' closing narrative and extending it with Cyrus' words.
Isaiah names Cyrus as the ruler who would order Jerusalem and its temple rebuilt; Chronicles records Cyrus issuing a proclamation to rebuild the LORD's house in Jerusalem.
Chronicles says Cyrus' proclamation followed the fulfillment of Jeremiah's word; Jeremiah promised that after seventy years at Babylon God would visit his people and bring them back.
Chronicles closes and Ezra begins with the same report: God stirred Cyrus of Persia to proclaim the rebuilding of the LORD's house in Jerusalem.
Isaiah specifically names Cyrus as the one who would order Jerusalem and the temple rebuilt; Ezra records Cyrus issuing the decree after the exile.
Ezra identifies Cyrus' decree as fulfillment of the LORD's word through Jeremiah; Jeremiah had promised that after seventy years God would bring the exiles back.
Chronicles records Nebuchadnezzar carrying the temple vessels to Babylon; Ezra later describes Cyrus bringing those vessels out for their return.
Ezra first describes Cyrus bringing out the temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar; the later officials' letter recalls Cyrus ordering those vessels restored.
The later decree preserved in Ezra orders the return of the very gold and silver temple vessels that Cyrus brought out in the opening chapter.
Ezra and Nehemiah preserve corresponding lists of people who returned from exile; some names and numbers differ between the lists.
Ezra's returnee list includes Zerubbabel and Jeshua; these same leaders later organized rebuilding the altar and restoring sacrifices in Jerusalem.
Ezra names Jeshua son of Jozadak and Zerubbabel as leaders rebuilding the altar; Haggai addresses these leaders as Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor during the later temple work.
The worshippers' refrain at the foundation of the second temple repeats the thanksgiving that David appointed for worship before the ark: the LORD is good and his mercy endures for ever.
At the laying of the temple foundation, the worshippers sing that the LORD is good and his mercy endures for ever, the same words of thanksgiving found in this psalm.
The settlers opposing Zerubbabel say Esarhaddon king of Assyria resettled them; Kings records Esarhaddon succeeding Sennacherib, identifying the Assyrian ruler they name.
Ezra records Haggai prophesying to the returning Jews during temple rebuilding; Haggai's opening verse dates and identifies his message to Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest.
Ezra names Zechariah son of Iddo among the prophets encouraging the builders; Zechariah dates his ministry to Darius's reign and traces his ancestry through Berechiah to Iddo.
Ezra earlier shows Zerubbabel and Jeshua rebuilding the altar; the same leaders later began renewed work on God's house with the prophets supporting them.
Tatnai first questions the authority for rebuilding the temple; Darius later orders Tatnai and his associates to stay away and permit the work to proceed.
The officials' report recalls Cyrus's decree authorizing the temple's reconstruction; Ezra's opening chapter preserves that decree and its instructions.
The officials' letter reports Cyrus ordering the seized gold and silver temple vessels returned; Darius's decree repeats and confirms their restoration.
Ezra records the order to return the vessels Nebuchadnezzar carried away; Daniel describes Belshazzar using those same temple vessels at his feast before their return.
Darius's recorded decree confirms the officials' report that Cyrus had ordered the gold and silver vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar returned to Jerusalem's temple.
Darius addresses Tatnai by name in his order allowing the temple work to continue, following Tatnai's earlier challenge to the builders' authority.
The dedication of the rebuilt temple offered twelve goats for all Israel's tribes; Elijah likewise used twelve stones to represent the twelve tribes, in separate worship settings.
After the second temple was rebuilt, the returned exiles rejoiced during seven days of unleavened bread; Hezekiah's earlier assembly had also observed the seven-day feast with gladness.
Ezra lists the Nethinim among the returning families; a later return under Ezra included 220 more Nethinim, described as servants appointed to assist the Levites.
Ezra names Meremoth son of Uriah the priest among those weighing returned offerings; Nehemiah names Meremoth son of Urijah, son of Koz, among the wall repairers, apparently the same priestly worker.
Ezra's command not to marry foreign peoples' sons or daughters echoes Moses' explicit prohibition on intermarriage with the nations Israel was to displace.
Ezra wept and confessed before a great assembly over intermarriage; at a later public reading of the law, Ezra and Nehemiah addressed another weeping assembly. These are separate gatherings.
Nehemiah identifies himself as the son of Hachaliah at the start of his account; the covenant-signing list names Nehemiah the governor with the same father.
Hanani brings Nehemiah news of Jerusalem's distress; later Nehemiah appoints his brother Hanani, alongside Hananiah, to oversee Jerusalem.
Nehemiah first hears that Jerusalem's wall is broken and its gates burned; he later calls the people to rebuild those walls and end the city's disgrace.
Nehemiah asks God to remember Moses' warning about scattering the disobedient and promise to gather the repentant; Deuteronomy records that promise of restoration.
Sanballat and Tobiah first resent Nehemiah's effort to help Jerusalem; later they join others in opposing the wall repairs when they hear the breaches are closing.
Nehemiah's appeal to rebuild Jerusalem's ruined walls directly follows the report he received about their broken condition and burned gates.
Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem initially mock the rebuilding; after the wall is nearly complete, Sanballat and Geshem attempt to draw Nehemiah into a meeting intended to harm him.
Nehemiah locates rebuilding near the tower of Hananeel; Jeremiah's promise of a restored Jerusalem also names that tower as a boundary landmark.
Eliashib and the priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate near the towers of Meah and Hananeel; the dedication procession later passed those same landmarks.
Nehemiah names Meremoth son of Urijah, son of Koz, among the wall builders; Ezra mentions Meremoth son of Uriah the priest weighing the returned temple treasures, apparently the same man.
Nehemiah records repairs at the tower of the furnaces; the later wall-dedication procession passes that tower, showing its place along the completed circuit.
Both chapters locate the Nethinim, temple servants, at Ophel in Jerusalem; Nehemiah 11 additionally names Ziha and Gispa as their overseers.
Sanballat first joined Tobiah and Geshem in mocking Nehemiah's plan to rebuild; he later became angry and mocked the Jews as the wall went up.
Nehemiah dates his twelve-year governorship from Artaxerxes' twentieth through thirty-second year; he later recalls leaving Jerusalem to return to the king in that thirty-second year.
Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mocked the proposed rebuilding in Nehemiah 2; they were still opposing the project when the wall was completed except for its gates.
Sanballat mocked the Jews when rebuilding began; the later account names him among the enemies who learned that the wall's breaches had been closed.
Nehemiah and Ezra preserve corresponding lists of people who returned from exile; some names and numbers differ between the lists.
Ezra 7 introduces Ezra as a skilled scribe in Moses' law who returned from Babylon; Nehemiah later records the people asking him to read that law publicly.
Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, and other Levites helped explain God's law at the public reading; several of these names also appear among the Levites leading the later confession.
Nehemiah reports the people finding Moses' command to dwell in booths during the seventh-month feast; Leviticus states that exact requirement.
Nehemiah 8 names Levites who explained the law; Nehemiah 9 again names Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, and others among the Levites leading public confession and praise.
Nehemiah's prayer recalls God bringing Abram out of Ur of the Chaldees; Genesis describes Abram's family departing Ur on the way toward Canaan.
Nehemiah recalls God changing Abram's name to Abraham; Genesis records the name change and God's promise to make him father of many nations.
Nehemiah recalls God descending on Mount Sinai to give Israel his law; Exodus announces that the LORD would descend on Sinai before the people.
Nehemiah describes God as gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness despite Israel's rebellion; Joel uses the same distinctive description while calling for repentance.
Nehemiah's confession recalls Israel making a molten calf and crediting it with the exodus; Exodus records Aaron making the calf and the people making that claim.
Nehemiah's wall-building account places the Nethinim at Ophel; the later census again locates those temple servants there and names their overseers.
The second thanksgiving procession passed the tower of the furnaces; Nehemiah's earlier repair list names workers who restored that same tower.
The dedication procession passed the Sheep Gate and the towers of Meah and Hananeel; the earlier rebuilding account says Eliashib and the priests repaired those landmarks.
Nehemiah's public reading cites Moses' prohibition on Ammonites and Moabites entering God's congregation; Deuteronomy states that command and its stated duration.

Nehemiah recalls Balaam being hired to curse Israel but God turning the curse into a blessing; Deuteronomy expressly explains that God refused to listen to Balaam and turned the curse into a blessing.
Nehemiah recalls the Moabites hiring Balaam against Israel and God changing the curse to blessing; Joshua recounts Balak summoning Balaam and God refusing to heed him.
Nehemiah recalls Balak and Balaam's attempt to curse Israel; Micah likewise tells Israel to remember what Balak planned and Balaam answered as evidence of God's righteous acts.
Nehemiah dates his governorship through Artaxerxes' thirty-second year; later he explains that he was away from Jerusalem because he returned to the king during that year.
Esther refers to the captivity taken from Jerusalem with Jeconiah under Nebuchadnezzar; Jeremiah independently describes that deportation of King Jeconiah and Judah's leaders.
Esther is introduced as Abihail's daughter, raised by Mordecai; the later account again names her as Abihail's daughter when she and Mordecai confirm the Purim letter.
Ahasuerus previously summoned Queen Vashti wearing her crown; after Vashti was removed, he crowned Esther queen in her place. These are distinct events involving successive queens.
Mordecai first uncovered Bigthan and Teresh's plot against Ahasuerus; the royal chronicles later recorded his warning, leading the king to ask why Mordecai had not been rewarded.
Ahasuerus raised Haman above the other princes; later Haman boasted to his friends and wife about his wealth, children, and promotion by the king.
Esther openly identified Haman as the enemy threatening her people; the earlier account already calls him the Jews' enemy when Ahasuerus gives him the king's ring.
Ahasuerus first gave Haman the royal signet ring to authorize his decree against the Jews; after Haman's fall, the king took that same ring and gave it to Mordecai.
Haman's decree was published throughout the provinces to prepare for the Jews' destruction; the later counter-decree used the same empire-wide publication to authorize the Jews' defense.
Haman's first decree left Shushan perplexed; after Haman's fall and Mordecai's rise, Shushan rejoiced, showing the reversal of the Jews' fortunes.
Mordecai tells Esther's messenger about the money Haman promised for destroying the Jews; the earlier account records Haman's offer of ten thousand talents and the king's assent.
Mordecai gives Esther's messenger a copy of the decree issued at Shushan to destroy the Jews; Esther 3 records the dispatch and publication of that decree.
Ahasuerus extended his golden sceptre when Esther first approached uninvited; he extended it again when she returned to plead against Haman's decree. These are separate audiences.
Ahasuerus first offered to grant Esther's request when she approached him; at her second banquet he renewed that offer, prompting her plea for her people.
Haman was furious when Mordecai refused to bow to him; even after attending Esther's banquet, seeing Mordecai remain unmoved at the gate renewed his anger.
Haman first gathered his wife Zeresh and friends after Mordecai angered him; after he was forced to honor Mordecai publicly, he returned to tell the same circle of his humiliation.
Zeresh and Haman's friends advised him to erect gallows for Mordecai; Haman came early to ask the king for Mordecai's execution, only to find the king preparing to honor Mordecai.
Haman erected fifty-cubit gallows for Mordecai at his wife's and friends' suggestion; Harbonah later revealed the gallows, and the king ordered Haman hanged on them instead.
Haman entered the palace court intending to ask permission to hang Mordecai on gallows built the previous day, but the king called him in to discuss rewarding Mordecai instead.
Haman was ordered to parade Mordecai through Shushan as the man the king delighted to honor; later the provincial officials supported the Jews because Mordecai had become influential.
Esther invited the king and Haman to a second banquet; after Haman's humiliating errand honoring Mordecai, the king's chamberlains hurried him to that appointed banquet.
Ahasuerus first asked what Esther wished when she approached the throne; at her second banquet he repeated his offer, and Esther asked that her life and her people's lives be spared.
Harbonah told the king of the fifty-cubit gallows Haman had built for Mordecai; the earlier passage records Zeresh and Haman's friends proposing that very gallows.
Mordecai had raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter; after Haman's fall, Esther disclosed that family relationship to the king, and Mordecai was admitted into his presence.
Ahasuerus gave his signet ring to Haman when authorizing the decree against the Jews; after Haman's fall, the king took that ring and gave it to Mordecai.
The king extended his golden sceptre to Esther on her first approach to the court and again when she returned to beg him to counter Haman's scheme. The gestures belong to separate requests.
Haman's decree and Mordecai's later counter-decree were both published throughout the provinces; the second allowed Jews to defend themselves on the day originally set for their destruction.
After Haman's decree was published, Shushan was perplexed; when Mordecai emerged in royal dress following the counter-decree, the city rejoiced. The scenes mark a reversal.
Haman reluctantly dressed Mordecai in royal apparel and led him through the city to honor him; later Mordecai emerged from the king's presence wearing royal robes and a golden crown.

Mordecai's decree was addressed to provincial governors and other officials throughout the empire; when the Jews defended themselves, those same ranks of officials helped them out of fear of Mordecai.
Haman had boasted of his many children while planning Mordecai's death; after the Jews gained authority to defend themselves, they killed Haman's ten sons, though Esther 5 does not give their number.
After Haman's downfall, Mordecai appeared publicly in royal dress and a golden crown; the closing account says the king's records chronicled the greatness to which he advanced Mordecai.
Mordecai became great in the king's house and his fame spread throughout the provinces; Esther's closing account says the royal chronicles recorded his greatness and advancement.
Ezekiel explicitly names Job with Noah and Daniel as examples of righteousness, matching Job's introduction as upright, God-fearing, and one who turned away from evil.
James explicitly names Job as an example of patient endurance and points to the Lord's mercy; Job is introduced as an upright man who feared God before suffering began.
At the beginning of the book, Job offered sacrifices on behalf of his children; after his trials, God directed Job's friends to bring offerings and said Job would pray for them.
Job 2 describes another gathering before the LORD at which Satan appears among the sons of God, directly continuing the heavenly scene first described in Job 1.

Satan appears before the LORD in Job's heavenly scene; Revelation calls Satan the accuser of God's brethren before God and describes his being cast down. The passages describe different visions or events.
Job describes Satan appearing at a gathering before the LORD; Zechariah shows Satan standing to oppose Joshua the high priest as Joshua stands before the angel of the LORD. These are distinct scenes.
The LORD asks Satan where he has been in both encounters, and Satan gives the same answer about going to and fro in the earth; the second encounter occurs after Job's initial losses.
Before Job's losses, God calls him upright and one who turns from evil; after those losses, God repeats that assessment and adds that Job still holds fast his integrity.
God initially describes Job to Satan as upright and faithful; at the book's conclusion God calls Job his servant and rebukes Job's friends for not speaking rightly about him.
Satan first claims Job will curse God if his possessions are touched; after Job remains faithful, Satan claims Job will do so if his own body is afflicted.
After losing his children and possessions, Job does not sin or charge God foolishly; after his physical affliction, the book again says he did not sin with his lips.
Job's second heavenly gathering repeats the first: the sons of God present themselves before the LORD, and Satan again comes among them, before a new trial is permitted.
God's question about where Satan has been and Satan's answer recur almost word for word in the two heavenly scenes, before the second test of Job begins.
God repeats his earlier praise of Job's upright character, then adds that Job maintains his integrity despite the losses Satan was permitted to inflict.
In the first test Satan is allowed to touch Job's possessions but not his person; in the second Satan may afflict Job's body but must spare his life.
Paul quotes Eliphaz's statement that God catches the wise in their own craftiness; in Job, the words are spoken by Eliphaz.
Bildad is introduced among the three friends who come to comfort Job; in Job 8 he begins his first speech, challenging Job's response to suffering.
Both Job and Amos name the constellations Pleiades and Orion while acknowledging God's power as their maker; Amos also describes God's rule over day and night.
Job names Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades as works of God's creation; later God challenges Job about governing these constellations, emphasizing the limits of human power.
Job repeatedly speaks of his bitterness and anguish: in chapter 7 he refuses to restrain his complaint, and in chapter 10 he continues pleading directly with God.
Job acknowledges that God's hands formed him but asks why God seems to destroy him; the psalmist likewise credits God's hands with making him, then seeks understanding of God's commands.
Job describes God depriving rulers of understanding and making them wander in a pathless wilderness; Psalm 107 repeats the unusual picture of princes wandering in a wilderness without a way.
Eliphaz portrays the wicked as conceiving mischief and producing deceit; Isaiah likewise says evildoers conceive mischief and bring forth iniquity, using closely corresponding imagery.

Bildad says the wicked person's light will go out; Proverbs contrasts the joyful light of the righteous with the lamp of the wicked being extinguished. The shared imagery concerns the fate of the wicked.
Elihu describes God speaking to people through dreams in the night when deep sleep falls; Eliphaz earlier described receiving a frightening vision during that same kind of deep sleep.
Elihu accuses Job of speaking without knowledge in both speeches; the later passage repeats and intensifies his judgment of Job's words rather than introducing a new speaker.
God first answers Job from the whirlwind in chapter 38; after Job's brief response, God speaks again from the whirlwind in chapter 40, continuing his questions.
God asks Job who laid the foundations of the earth; Psalm 104 praises the LORD for laying earth's foundations, affirming the creative power behind God's question.
God questions Job about whether he can bind Pleiades or loosen Orion; Amos names the same constellations while calling people to seek the LORD who made them.
God names Pleiades and Orion when questioning Job about his power over creation; Job had earlier named those same stars as works made by God.
God's renewed answer from the whirlwind in Job 40 continues the questioning begun when he first addressed Job from the whirlwind in Job 38.
Job's three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, first came to comfort him; after their speeches, God rebukes them for not speaking rightly about him and directs them to offer sacrifices.
James points to Job's endurance and the Lord's mercy; the closing account shows how the LORD blessed Job's later life after his suffering.
Psalm 1 describes delighting in the LORD's law and meditating on it; Paul also says he delights in God's law, while acknowledging an inner struggle against sin.
Both passages compare a person who trusts and follows God to a fruitful tree planted beside water; Jeremiah adds that this tree does not fear heat or drought.
The believers quote the opening of Psalm 2 in prayer and apply its opposition to the Lord and his anointed to events surrounding Jesus.
Paul cites the declaration 'Thou art my Son' from Psalm 2 while proclaiming Jesus' resurrection.
Hebrews quotes 'Thou art my Son' from Psalm 2 to distinguish the Son from the angels.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 2's declaration to explain that Christ did not appoint himself to the honor of high priest.
Revelation uses Psalm 2's picture of ruling with a rod of iron and shattering pottery when describing authority received from Christ.
The heading of Psalm 3 places David's prayer during his flight from Absalom; 2 Samuel records Absalom entering Jerusalem with his supporters as David fled.
Paul echoes the psalm's warning about anger and sin, adding an instruction not to let the sun go down on anger; the KJV wording differs.
Paul quotes the psalm's image of an open grave to describe corrupt speech in his account of human sin.
These two psalms open with almost the same prayer that the LORD not rebuke or chasten David in anger, showing a distinctive repetition in David's pleas for mercy.
Jesus applies Psalm 8's words about children and infants to the praise offered by children in the temple.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 8's question about humanity and dominion, then discusses its significance in relation to Jesus.
Paul quotes the psalm's description of a mouth filled with cursing and deceit as part of his account of human sin.
Paul draws on Psalm 14's declaration of human corruption and the absence of those who do good in his description of universal sin.
Paul echoes Psalm 14's account of God looking for those who understand and seek him, concluding that none does good.
Peter quotes Psalm 16 and argues that David's words about not seeing corruption point to the resurrection of Christ.
Paul quotes Psalm 16's words about God's Holy One not seeing corruption and applies them to Jesus' resurrection.
Peter quotes the psalm’s promise that God’s Holy One would not see corruption as part of his argument for Jesus’ resurrection.
David asks God to hide him under the shadow of his wings for protection; in another psalm, written during his flight from Saul, David uses the same image for refuge until danger passes.
David asks God to shelter him beneath his wings in Psalm 17; in Psalm 63 he rejoices under that same protection because God has helped him.
Paul quotes David's promise to praise God among the Gentiles while explaining that Gentiles also glorify God.
Paul uses the psalm's language about a message reaching all the earth while asking whether Israel has heard the gospel; the psalm speaks of creation's witness.
Psalm 20 says the Lord saves his anointed; Psalm 28 calls the Lord the saving strength of his anointed and asks him to save his people.
Jesus speaks the opening words of Psalm 22 while on the cross, as Mark records.
Jesus speaks the opening words of Psalm 22 while on the cross, as Matthew records.
John quotes Psalm 22:18 as fulfilled when soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes and cast lots for his coat during the crucifixion.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 22's promise to declare God's name to the congregation and applies the words to Jesus.
Psalm 23 expresses confidence in dwelling in the Lord's house; Psalm 27 turns that desire into a prayer to remain there and behold his beauty.
Paul quotes the psalm's statement that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord when discussing food and conscience.
David lifts his soul to the Lord in Psalm 25; in Psalm 143 he repeats that prayer while asking God to show him the way to walk.
Both prayers lift the soul to the Lord; Psalm 25 begins by expressing trust, while Psalm 86 asks God to bring joy to his servant.
Psalm 27 asks to dwell in the Lord's house and behold his beauty; Psalm 23 expresses confidence in dwelling there through the Lord's goodness and mercy.
Both psalms ask the Lord to teach his way; Psalm 27 seeks a safe, plain path amid enemies, while Psalm 86 asks for a heart united in reverence.
Psalm 31 repeats Psalm 27's call to courage and confidence that the Lord will strengthen the heart, addressing all who hope in him.
Psalm 28 calls the Lord the saving strength of his anointed, echoing Psalm 20's assurance that the Lord saves his anointed from heaven.
Both psalms summon worshipers to give the Lord glory and strength; Psalm 29 addresses the mighty, while Psalm 96 extends the appeal to the peoples of the earth.
Psalm 96 repeats Psalm 29's call to give glory to the Lord's name and worship him in the beauty of holiness, adding a summons for all the earth to fear him.
Both psalms call God's people to give thanks at the remembrance of his holiness; Psalm 30 addresses his saints, and Psalm 97 calls the righteous to rejoice.
Jesus uses the psalm's words about committing one's spirit into God's hands as he dies on the cross.
Paul quotes David's words about forgiven sins to explain the blessing of righteousness counted apart from works.
Both psalms praise God with the psaltery and a ten-stringed instrument; Psalm 144 also calls for a new song, as Psalm 33 does in the next verse.
Psalm 33 says the Lord's counsel stands forever despite the plans of nations; Proverbs contrasts the many plans in a person's heart with the counsel of the Lord that stands.
Psalm 33 says the Lord watches those who fear him and hope in his mercy; Psalm 147 says he takes pleasure in those same people.
Peter quotes Psalm 34's instruction to guard one's tongue, turn from evil, and seek peace.
John says Jesus’ bones were not broken in fulfillment of Scripture; Psalm 34:20 says God keeps the righteous person’s bones unbroken, though John does not identify the source by name.
Jesus applies the psalm's words about being hated without cause to the hostility directed against him; Psalm 69:4 contains similar wording.
Paul quotes the psalm's statement that the wicked have no fear of God before their eyes.
Proverbs repeats Psalm 37's warning not to fret over evildoers; both immediately turn to the temporary future of the wicked.
Psalm 37 repeats Psalm 34's command to depart from evil and do good, then connects that conduct with enduring life in the land.
Psalm 37 says the wicked person's descendants will be cut off while God's faithful are preserved; Proverbs contrasts the wicked being cut off with the upright remaining in the land.
Psalm 37 urges waiting for the Lord and keeping his way rather than fearing the wicked; Proverbs forbids personal revenge and urges waiting for the Lord to save.
Psalm 38 opens with nearly the same plea as Psalm 6: David asks the Lord not to rebuke him in anger or chasten him in hot displeasure.
The closing plea of Psalm 38 asks the Lord to make haste to help; Psalm 40 repeats that urgent request while seeking deliverance from many troubles.
Psalm 70 opens by asking God to make haste to help, echoing Psalm 38's closing cry for quick rescue.
Hebrews quotes this psalm while describing Christ's coming to do God's will; the Greek quotation says a body was prepared, while the KJV psalm says ears were opened.
Jesus quotes the psalm about a trusted companion turning against the speaker in reference to his betrayal.
Psalm 42 pictures the soul thirsting for the living God like a deer for water; Psalm 84 likewise describes intense longing for the Lord's courts and the living God.
Psalm 42 asks God his rock why he has forgotten the psalmist amid oppression; Psalm 43 repeats that question while calling God his strength.
Psalm 43 repeats Psalm 42's refrain: the downcast soul is called to hope in God because praise will come again.
Psalm 43 asks why God has cast off the speaker amid oppression; Psalm 42 similarly asks why God has forgotten him while enemies cause mourning.
Psalm 43's closing call to the downcast soul to hope in God nearly repeats the same refrain at the end of Psalm 42.
Paul quotes the psalm's words about being killed all day long and counted as sheep for slaughter when discussing suffering.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 45's words about an enduring throne and anointing and applies them to the Son.
Psalm 145 repeats Psalm 48's confession that the Lord is great and greatly to be praised, then adds that his greatness cannot be fully searched out.
Both psalms declare the Lord great and greatly to be praised; Psalm 48 praises him in his holy city, while Psalm 96 calls for his greatness to be proclaimed among the nations.
Psalm 50 says God summons the whole earth from sunrise to sunset; Malachi uses that same span to declare that the Lord’s name will be great among the nations.
Psalm 50 describes God summoning the earth from sunrise to sunset; Psalm 113 uses the same worldwide span to call for praise of the Lord's name.
Paul quotes David's confession that God is justified in his words when defending God's truthfulness.
Psalm 52’s heading identifies Doeg as the man who reported David’s visit to Ahimelech; 1 Samuel introduces Doeg at Ahimelech’s sanctuary before that report.
Psalm 53 substantially repeats Psalm 14’s account of widespread corruption, the foolish denial of God, and the longing for Israel’s salvation, though some wording differs.
Romans repeats the declaration that all have turned aside and that no one does good, as Paul assembles Scripture testimony about human sin.
Both psalms thank God for delivering the speaker’s soul from death and describe walking before him in the light or land of the living.
In Psalm 57 David seeks refuge beneath God’s wings amid danger; Psalm 63 uses the same image to rejoice in the help God has already given.
Psalm 108 opens by reusing Psalm 57’s resolve to sing with a steadfast heart and its summons to instruments and public praise.
Psalm 108 repeats Psalm 57’s description of God’s mercy reaching the heavens and his truth reaching the clouds, with a small difference in wording.
Psalm 59 asks God to rescue David from enemies who rise against him; Psalm 18 looks back and praises God for delivering him from such enemies.
Psalm 108 repeats the divine declaration in Psalm 60 about dividing Shechem and measuring Succoth and continues with the same claims about Gilead and Manasseh.
Psalm 60 speaks of authority over Edom in poetic language; 2 Samuel separately records David placing garrisons in Edom, where the people became his servants.
Psalm 108 repeats Psalm 60’s figurative declarations about Moab, Edom, and Philistia and the following question about entry into Edom.
Psalm 108 repeats word for word the plea for help in trouble and the warning that human help is vain.
Psalm 17 asks God to hide the speaker beneath the shadow of his wings; Psalm 63 rejoices under those same wings because God has been his help.
Psalm 57 seeks refuge in the shadow of God’s wings during danger; Psalm 63 celebrates that same protection as a reason to rejoice.
Both psalms call the righteous and upright in heart to rejoice in the Lord, with Psalm 64 anticipating joy and Psalm 32 directly commanding it.
Both psalms tell the nations that the Lord judges peoples righteously; Psalm 67 looks for nations to rejoice, while Psalm 96 proclaims his reign.
Paul applies the psalm's language of ascending on high to Christ; the psalm speaks of receiving gifts, while Ephesians speaks of giving them.
John records the disciples recalling this psalm's words about zeal for God's house after Jesus clears the temple.
Paul quotes the psalm's words about reproaches falling upon the speaker and applies them to Christ.

Psalm 69 describes vinegar being given to the sufferer in his thirst; John records Jesus saying 'I thirst' and being offered vinegar at the crucifixion, in a passage John connects with Scripture's fulfillment.
Paul quotes David's appeal that the wicked person's table become a snare and eyes grow dark when discussing Israel's stumbling.
Peter quotes the psalm's call for a dwelling to become desolate when discussing Judas and selecting a replacement apostle.
Psalm 70 closely reproduces Psalm 40:13–17: an urgent plea for deliverance, shame for enemies, joy for those seeking God, and a final cry for help.
Psalm 71 opens with wording closely matching Psalm 31’s declaration of trust, request not to be put to shame, and plea for righteous deliverance.
Both psalms call the Lord a rock and fortress. Psalm 18 celebrates God's deliverance, while Psalm 71 asks that he remain a secure refuge.

Psalm 72 speaks of Sheba's kings bringing gifts to the king; the queen of Sheba later visits Solomon with gold, spices, and precious stones. The account illustrates royal tribute without identifying the psalm as a prediction of that visit.
Psalm 72 anticipates gifts from the kings of Sheba and other distant lands; Isaiah describes people coming from Sheba with gold and incense to praise the Lord. These are distinct prophetic settings.

Psalm 74 recalls God dividing the sea while portraying his victory in vivid sea-creature imagery; Nehemiah 9 recounts the historical crossing and the destruction of Israel's pursuers. The imagery is not a literal detail in Nehemiah.
Psalm 76 names Salem alongside Zion as God's dwelling place; Genesis calls Melchizedek the king of Salem in Abraham's day. The connection is the place name, not a shared event.
Matthew quotes the psalm's announcement of speaking in parables and connects it to Jesus teaching the crowds through parables.
The crowd recalls Scripture about bread from heaven in speaking with Jesus; Psalm 78 recounts the manna, as does Exodus 16.

Psalm 79 describes nations defiling the temple and ruining Jerusalem; Psalm 74 laments enemy destruction in God's sanctuary. Both mourn devastation of the holy place, without requiring that every detail describe the same occasion.
Psalm 79 repeats Psalm 44's distinctive complaint that God's people have become a reproach, scorn, and derision to their neighbors amid national suffering.

Psalm 81 recalls God testing Israel at the waters of Meribah; Numbers 20 names a place Meribah where the Israelites contended with the Lord. The KJV also records an earlier Meribah episode, so this need not identify one incident exclusively.

Both passages use the distinctive image of honey from the rock to describe God's provision; Deuteronomy looks back on what God gave Israel, while Psalm 81 describes what he would have given a listening people.
Jesus quotes Psalm 82's words 'Ye are gods' when responding to the accusation of blasphemy.
Psalm 83 asks God to make hostile leaders like Oreb and Zeeb; Judges records how the Ephraimites killed those two Midianite princes during Gideon's victory.
Psalm 85 anticipates the land yielding its increase through the Lord's goodness; Leviticus promises rain and fruitful harvests among the blessings of covenant obedience.
Both prayers ask the Lord to teach his way. Psalm 27 seeks guidance amid enemies, while Psalm 86 asks for a heart united in reverent obedience to God's truth.
Psalm 87 describes God's foundation in the holy mountains and his love for Zion; Psalm 48 praises Zion as the holy mountain and city of the great King.
Both psalms locate justice or righteousness and judgment at the foundation of God's throne; Psalm 89 also names mercy and truth, while Psalm 97 portrays the Lord's reign in clouds and darkness.
During Jesus' temptation, the devil quotes the psalm's promise of angelic protection, applying it to a proposed leap from the temple.
During Jesus' temptation, the devil quotes the psalm's promise of angelic protection, applying it to a proposed leap from the temple.
Paul quotes the psalm's statement that the Lord knows human thoughts are vain, applying it to the wisdom of this world.
Hebrews quotes Psalm 95's warning about the wilderness generation and uses it to urge readers not to harden their hearts toward God's voice.
Hebrews repeats Psalm 95's appeal to respond to God's voice 'To day,' applying the warning to its readers.
Both psalms open with the identical call to sing the Lord a new song; Psalm 96 calls all the earth to announce his salvation, while Psalm 98 praises his marvelous victory.
Both psalms say the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; Psalm 96 contrasts him with the nations' idols, while Psalm 145 emphasizes his unsearchable greatness.
Psalm 96 closely repeats Psalm 29's command to worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness; Psalm 96 broadens the summons to all the earth.
