Both psalms declare that God judges peoples righteously; Psalm 67 rejoices in his just rule of the nations, while Psalm 96 proclaims the Lord's reign to the nations.
Both psalms call on the sea and all it contains to rejoice before the Lord; Psalm 98 expands the picture to rivers and hills because God comes to judge the earth in righteousness.
Psalm 97 echoes Psalm 89's description of righteousness or justice and judgment as the foundation of God's throne; Psalm 97 places the words within a proclamation of his reign.
Both psalms use the distinctive command to give thanks at the remembrance of the Lord's holiness; Psalm 30 addresses his saints and Psalm 97 calls the righteous to rejoice.
Both psalms begin by calling for a new song to the Lord; Psalm 96 summons all the earth, while Psalm 98 grounds the song in God's victory and revealed salvation.
Both psalms invite the sea and everything in it to roar in praise; their surrounding verses picture creation rejoicing before the Lord as judge.
Psalm 99 remembers Moses and Samuel as people who called on God and were answered; Jeremiah invokes both as powerful intercessors while declaring that Judah’s judgment will not be averted.
Hebrews addresses the Son with Psalm 102's words about the Creator whose years endure even as the heavens and earth change.
Hebrews quotes the psalm's words about angels and ministers as part of its comparison between angels and the Son.
Both verses urge God’s people to call on his name and declare his deeds among the peoples; Isaiah places the exhortation in a song of salvation.
Both psalms recall the plagues of flies and frogs sent on Egypt; Psalm 105 lists frogs first and flies afterward, while Psalm 78 mentions flies before frogs.
Both passages recall the earth swallowing Dathan and Abiram during Israel’s wilderness rebellion; Deuteronomy also mentions their households, tents, and possessions.
Both passages recall Israel’s devotion to Baalpeor; Psalm 106 mentions joining the worship and eating sacrifices, while Hosea condemns the shameful corruption.
Psalm 106 recalls Israelites joining themselves to Baalpeor; Numbers 25 records Moses ordering the judges to put to death those involved in that worship.
Psalm 107 repeats Job’s distinctive wording that God pours contempt upon princes; the psalm adds the picture of rulers wandering in a wilderness.
Both passages portray God bringing leaders to helplessness and making them wander in a pathless wilderness; Job speaks of the chiefs of the earth, Psalm 107 of princes.
Psalm 108:1–5 reuses much of Psalm 57:7–11, including the fixed heart, awakened instruments, praise among the nations, and God’s glory above the earth; the wording has small differences.
Psalm 108 reuses Psalm 60’s declarations concerning Moab and Edom and the question of who will lead into Edom; the wording about Philistia differs.
Peter quotes the psalm's call for another to take an office while explaining why Judas's place among the apostles should be filled.
Peter quotes David's words about the Lord's right hand to proclaim that Jesus has been exalted by God.
Hebrews quotes David's words about the Lord's right hand to show the Son's distinction from the angels.
Jesus cites David's description of the Lord speaking to 'my Lord' when questioning how the Messiah can be both David's son and Lord.
Jesus quotes David's words about the Lord at God's right hand while asking how the Messiah is David's son and Lord.
Jesus quotes Psalm 110's words about the Lord at God's right hand when questioning the relationship between David and the Messiah.
Hebrews quotes the promise of a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek while discussing Christ's appointment as high priest.
Hebrews uses Psalm 110's promise of an enduring priesthood to explain Jesus' priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.
Hebrews quotes God's sworn declaration of a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek to distinguish Jesus' priesthood.
Both verses state that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; Psalm 111 continues with good understanding for those who obey his commandments, while Proverbs names knowledge of the holy.
Paul quotes the psalm's description of giving to the poor while encouraging generous giving to those in need.

Both passages use the distinctive expression “from the rising of the sun” to its setting in speaking of the Lord’s name; the psalm commands praise, while Malachi says his name will be great among the nations.
Both condemn man-made idols: Deuteronomy describes gods of wood and stone that cannot see or hear, while Psalm 115 portrays silver and gold images with powerless mouths and eyes.
The two psalms repeat the same warning that makers of powerless idols become like the idols they trust; both passages contrast idols with trust or praise directed to the Lord.
Paul quotes the psalm's words about believing and speaking to explain the faith that leads him to speak despite suffering.
Paul quotes the psalm's call for all nations to praise the Lord while explaining the Gentiles' inclusion in praise to God.
Hebrews quotes the psalm's confidence in the Lord as helper to encourage contentment and freedom from fear.
Peter quotes the psalm's rejected-stone image and applies it to Christ, contrasting those who believe with those who reject him.
Peter applies the psalm's rejected-stone image to Jesus, whom the leaders rejected but God raised from the dead.
Jesus quotes the psalm's rejected-stone image after telling the parable of the wicked tenants.
Jesus quotes the psalm's rejected-stone image after telling the parable of the vineyard tenants.
Jesus quotes the psalm's rejected-stone image to the religious leaders following the parable of the vineyard tenants.
The crowd welcomes Jesus with the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
The crowd praises Jesus as king using the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
Those welcoming Jesus repeat the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
The crowds welcoming Jesus use the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
Jesus repeats the psalm's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name while speaking about Jerusalem's future response to him.
Both speakers seek an answer to someone who reproaches them; Psalm 119 rests on trust in God’s word, while Proverbs urges a son to act wisely so his father can answer a reproach.
Both blessings say the Lord blesses his people “out of Zion”; Psalm 128 adds the hope of seeing Jerusalem flourish, while Psalm 134 identifies him as maker of heaven and earth.
Both neighboring psalms directly call on Israel to hope in the Lord; Psalm 130 gives his mercy and plentiful redemption as reasons, while Psalm 131 urges enduring hope.

Psalm 132 closely echoes Solomon’s prayer in 2 Chronicles, asking the Lord to enter his resting place with the ark and to clothe his priests and bring joy to his people; Chronicles continues by recalling David.
Both verses use the exact blessing “bless thee out of Zion”; Psalm 134 invokes the maker of heaven and earth, while Psalm 128 looks toward Jerusalem’s prosperity.
Both verses describe God causing vapors to rise from earth’s ends, making lightning for rain, and bringing wind from his treasuries; Jeremiah places this within praise of the Creator over idols.
Psalm 136 praises the Lord for bringing Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm; Exodus records God promising redemption with an outstretched arm and great judgments.
Both passages recount God bringing Israel out of Egypt “with a strong hand” and “with a stretched out arm”; Jeremiah adds signs, wonders, and great terror.
The psalm recalls Edom’s hostility during Jerusalem’s calamity; Ezekiel condemns Edom for taking vengeance on Judah and announces judgment against it.
Psalm 137 asks God to remember Edom’s part in Jerusalem’s destruction; Jeremiah delivers a separate prophecy of calamity against Edom, naming Teman, Dedan, and Bozrah.
Psalm 137 recalls Edom urging Jerusalem’s destruction; Lamentations addresses Edom after Zion’s suffering and declares that Edom’s wrongdoing will also be punished.
Paul quotes the psalm's image of poison beneath the lips as part of his description of sinful human speech.
Both psalms credit the Lord with training the speaker’s hands for battle; Psalm 18 continues with the strength to bend a bow, while Psalm 144 calls God his strength.
Both psalms urge a new song with stringed instruments; Psalm 144 promises a song upon the psaltery, while Psalm 33 calls for praise with harp and psaltery.
Both psalms declare that the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; Psalm 145 adds that his greatness cannot be searched out, while Psalm 48 locates its praise in God’s city.
Both psalms picture living creatures depending on God for food at the proper time; Psalm 145 speaks of all eyes waiting on him, and Psalm 104 of creatures waiting for their supply.
The two verses closely repeat the resolve to sing praise to the Lord for as long as the speaker lives and has being.
Both verses say God knows the stars individually and calls them by name; Isaiah adds that none is missing because of his power.
Both psalms join reverence for the Lord with hope in his mercy; Psalm 33 says his eye is on such people, while Psalm 147 says he takes pleasure in them.
Psalm 149 says the Lord delights in his people and gives salvation to the meek; Psalm 147 says he takes pleasure in those who fear him and hope in his mercy.
Both proverbs place the fear of the Lord at the start of wisdom or knowledge; Proverbs 1 contrasts it with fools rejecting instruction, while Proverbs 9 adds knowing the holy.
Both proverbs tell a son to heed his father’s instruction and not abandon his mother’s teaching; Proverbs 6 repeats the paired commands almost word for word.
Isaiah repeats Proverbs’ wording that the wicked run toward evil and hurry to shed blood; Isaiah specifies innocent blood and describes the damage left in their paths.
Proverbs 2 says wisdom delivers from the strange woman who flatters with words; Proverbs 7 repeats the warning and illustrates it with a young man drawn into her house.
Hebrews quotes Proverbs' appeal not to despise the Lord's correction and explains discipline as a sign of God's fatherly care.
Peter repeats the proverb that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, urging humility toward one another.
James quotes the proverb that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble as he calls readers to submit to God.
Both passages urge a son to keep wisdom or instruction before his eyes; Proverbs 4 adds keeping those words within his heart.
Both passages speak of the “wife of thy youth”; Proverbs encourages a husband to rejoice with her, while Malachi condemns treachery against her.
Proverbs 6 and Proverbs 24 repeat the warning that a little sleep and folded hands lead to poverty arriving like a traveler and want like an armed man.
Both proverbs tell readers to write moral instruction upon the tablet of the heart; Proverbs 7 also says to bind the commands upon the fingers, while Proverbs 3 speaks of mercy and truth.
Both passages say that instruction or wisdom protects against the strange woman who flatters with her words; Proverbs 7 develops this warning in a narrative.

Proverbs 9 calls fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom and knowing the holy understanding; Proverbs 1 calls fear of the Lord the beginning of knowledge and contrasts it with fools rejecting wisdom.
Both verses explicitly call the fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom; Proverbs 9 adds knowledge of the holy, while Psalm 111 commends doing God’s commandments.
Both proverbs say that a wise son makes his father glad; Proverbs 10 contrasts this with a foolish son bringing grief to his mother, while Proverbs 15 says a foolish man despises her.
Both proverbs contrast the failure of wealth or ill-gotten treasure with righteousness delivering from death; Proverbs 11 specifically places riches in the day of wrath.
Both proverbs call a rich man’s wealth his strong city; Proverbs 18 adds that he imagines it to be a high wall.
Peter draws on Proverbs' comparison of the righteous and the ungodly while discussing suffering and judgment.
Both proverbs commend working one's land for food and warn against following empty pursuits; Proverbs 28:19 adds the consequence of poverty.
Both proverbs say a person enjoys good from the fruit of the mouth; Proverbs 12:14 also mentions recompense for one's work.
Both proverbs contrast the righteous person's light with the wicked person's lamp going out; Proverbs 24:20 links the image to the wicked having no future reward.
Both call something a fountain of life that helps one escape the snares of death: the wise person's teaching in Proverbs 13:14 and fear of the Lord in 14:27.
Both contrast resisting correction with accepting reproof: Proverbs 13:18 speaks of shame or honor, while Proverbs 15:5 contrasts folly with prudence.
Both proverbs value upright conduct over crooked ways; Proverbs 14:2 connects uprightness with fearing the Lord, while 28:6 values it above wealth.
Both describe judgment on the wicked person's household and a favorable outcome for the upright; Proverbs 3:33 identifies God's curse and blessing.
Proverbs 16:25 repeats almost word for word the warning in Proverbs 14:12 that a path which seems right can end in death.
Both verses call something a fountain of life that turns people from death's snares: fear of the Lord here and wise teaching in Proverbs 13:14.
Both say mistreating the poor insults their Maker: Proverbs 14:31 speaks of oppression, while Proverbs 17:5 condemns mockery.
Both condemn oppressing poor people; Proverbs 14:31 calls it an offense against their Maker, while Proverbs 22:16 warns of resulting poverty.
Both commend accepting reproof and warn against rejecting correction; Proverbs 13:18 contrasts disgrace and honor, while 15:5 contrasts folly and prudence.
Both declare the sacrifice of the wicked unacceptable; Proverbs 21:27 adds that an offering made with a wicked purpose is even more offensive.
Both teach that an angry person stirs up strife; Proverbs 15:18 also praises the peacemaker who is slow to anger.
Both say a wise son makes his father glad; Proverbs 10:1 says a foolish son grieves his mother, while 15:20 says he despises her.
Both stress the value of many advisers: Proverbs 11:14 says they bring safety, while 15:22 says plans succeed through counsel.
Proverbs 14:12 states this warning almost word for word: a way may look right to a person yet lead to death.
Both teach that mistreating poor people insults their Maker; Proverbs 17:5 singles out mockery, while 14:31 speaks of oppression and showing mercy.
Both use a mother bear robbed of her cubs to picture danger; Proverbs warns about confronting a fool, while Hushai describes David's angry fighting men.
Both call a rich person's wealth a strong city; Proverbs 18:11 adds that the protective wall may exist only in the rich person's imagination.
Both prefer a poor person who lives uprightly to a dishonest person; Proverbs 19:1 contrasts crooked speech and folly, while 28:6 contrasts crooked conduct and wealth.
Both compare a king's anger to a roaring lion; Proverbs 19:12 also compares his favor to dew, while 20:2 warns against provoking him.
Both liken a king's anger to a roaring lion; Proverbs 20:2 warns against provoking him, while 19:12 contrasts his wrath with his favor.
Proverbs 27:13 repeats almost exactly the instruction to take security from someone who guarantees a stranger's debt, including the warning involving a strange woman.
Both warn that a talebearer reveals secrets; Proverbs 11:13 contrasts the person who keeps a confidence, while 20:19 warns against close dealings with a gossip.
Both condemn cursing one's parents: Exodus 21:17 prescribes death under the law, while Proverbs 20:20 warns that the offender's lamp will go out.
Both call readers to wait on the Lord rather than take matters into their own hands; Proverbs 20:22 forbids personal revenge, while Psalm 37:34 promises eventual vindication.
Proverbs 25:24 repeats almost word for word the comparison between living in a corner of the housetop and sharing a large house with a quarrelsome woman.
Proverbs 27:12 repeats almost word for word that a prudent person sees danger and takes cover while the simple continue and are punished.
Both picture a lazy person claiming a lion is outside or in the streets; Proverbs 26:13 repeats that excuse before further describing laziness.
Both condemn oppressing poor people: Proverbs 22:16 warns it leads to want, while 14:31 says such oppression insults the poor person's Maker.
Both promise that the listener's expectation will not be cut off; Proverbs 24:14 explicitly ties that hope to finding wisdom.
Both say safety is found in many counsellors; Proverbs 24:6 applies the advice especially to conducting war.
Both command readers not to fret over evildoers or envy the wicked; Psalm 37 goes on to explain their temporary success.
Both warn that showing favoritism is wrong, especially in judgment; Proverbs 28:21 adds that even a small bribe can lead a person astray.
Paul quotes Proverbs' instruction to feed and give drink to an enemy while teaching against personal revenge.
Peter repeats the proverb about a dog returning to its vomit to describe people who return to corruption after escaping it.
Proverbs 22:3 repeats this warning almost word for word: prudent people recognize danger and hide, while the simple proceed and suffer for it.
Proverbs 20:16 repeats almost exactly the instruction to take a garment as security for a stranger's debt, also mentioning the pledge involving a strange woman.
Both say an upright poor person is better than a crooked person; Proverbs 28:6 contrasts upright poverty with dishonest wealth, while 19:1 adds perverse speech and folly.
Both teach that tending one's land brings food, while chasing empty pursuits leads to loss; Proverbs 12:11 calls it foolish and 28:19 warns of poverty.
Both proverbs condemn favoritism: Proverbs 24:23 forbids partiality in judgment, while 28:21 warns that a person may compromise justice even for a piece of bread.
Both say anger stirs up strife; Proverbs 15:18 contrasts the angry person with someone slow to anger, while 29:22 adds that fury leads to transgression.
The book begins and ends with the Preacher's declaration that everything is vanity, framing the search for lasting meaning in Ecclesiastes.
Both ask what a person gains from all the labor performed under the sun; Ecclesiastes 2:22 adds the vexation of heart involved in that work.
Ecclesiastes first questions the lasting profit of labor, then describes enjoying the fruit of one's work during the life God gives as a person's portion.
Both assess human work as vanity and vexation of spirit; Ecclesiastes 2:11 specifically looks back on the Preacher's own achievements and finds no lasting profit.
Both describe work under the sun as vanity and vexation of spirit; Ecclesiastes 2:17 adds the Preacher's grief and frustration with life.
The Preacher's survey of his own accomplishments repeats his earlier conclusion that work under the sun is vanity and vexation of spirit.
These adjoining discussions present opposite outcomes of wealth: Ecclesiastes 5:19 calls the ability to enjoy it God's gift, while 6:2 describes a wealthy man denied that enjoyment.
Ecclesiastes 6:2 describes someone who has wealth but cannot enjoy it, reversing 5:19, where both wealth and the ability to enjoy it are gifts from God.
Both warn that someone who digs a pit may fall into it; Ecclesiastes adds the danger of breaking through a hedge, while Proverbs adds a rolling stone returning on its mover.
Ecclesiastes ends by repeating the Preacher's opening words that all is vanity, enclosing the book's reflections within the same refrain.
Both verses begin with an admiring declaration of the beloved's beauty and compare her eyes to doves; Song 4:1 adds the image of hair like goats on Gilead.
Song 3:5 repeats the charge to the daughters of Jerusalem, invoking gazelles and deer and urging them not to awaken love until it pleases.
Both verses proclaim mutual belonging between the lovers and mention the beloved feeding among the lilies; Song 6:3 reverses the order of the possessive statements.
Both verses open with the same line about the day breaking and shadows fleeing; Song 2:17 then calls the beloved to return, while 4:6 speaks of going to fragrant hills.
Both passages call on the beloved and compare him to a roe or young hart moving over mountains; the later verse asks him to make haste.
Song 2:7 gives the same charge to the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir or awaken love until it pleases, invoking roes and hinds of the field.
Both begin with the declaration that the beloved is fair and has doves' eyes; Song 4:1 continues with a description of her hair.
Both compare the beloved's hair to a flock of goats appearing from Gilead; Song 4:1 adds praise of her eyes, while 6:5 begins with their overwhelming effect.
Both compare the beloved's teeth to a washed flock whose members bear twins and none are barren, repeating an unusually detailed image.
Both compare the beloved's temples within her locks to a piece of pomegranate; Song 4:3 also describes her lips and speech.
Both passages repeat the line about the day breaking and shadows fleeing; Song 4:6 describes a journey to the mountain of myrrh, while 2:17 calls the beloved back.
In consecutive exchanges, the women first ask what makes the beloved special, then ask where he has gone so they can help seek him.
The women's offer to help seek the beloved follows their earlier question about what makes him special; the woman's description intervenes in Song 5:10–16.
Both verses say the lovers belong to one another and describe the beloved feeding among lilies; Song 6:3 reverses the order of the shared declaration.
The beloved’s hair is again compared to a flock of goats descending from Gilead; Song 4:1 also praises her eyes, while 6:5 says her eyes overwhelm him.
The description of the beloved’s teeth repeats the image of washed sheep bearing twins, with none barren.
Both verses compare the beloved’s temples, seen within her locks, to a piece of pomegranate.
The charge to the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir or awaken love until it pleases returns here; Song 2:7 also invokes roes and hinds.
Both verses urge the beloved to move swiftly like a roe or young hart over mountains; the places named are Bether and the mountains of spices.
Paul quotes Isaiah's warning that without a remnant, God's people would have become like Sodom and Gomorrah.
Isaiah and Micah give closely matching descriptions of the last days: the Lord’s mountain is exalted, nations seek his teaching, and weapons become tools of peace.
Both prophets say the Lord will judge among nations, swords will become plowshares, and nations will no longer learn war.
Both passages say human pride will be humbled while the Lord is exalted; Isaiah 5:16 specifically exalts him in judgment and righteousness.
Isaiah compares Judah’s open display of sin to Sodom; Genesis records that the men of Sodom were wicked and sinned greatly against the Lord.
The words “For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still” recur after descriptions of judgment in both passages.
Paul quotes Isaiah's commission describing people who hear and see without understanding while explaining his audience's response.
Jesus echoes Isaiah's warning about seeing and hearing without understanding when explaining why he speaks in parables.
Matthew quotes Isaiah's words about hearing without understanding and applies them to the crowds who hear Jesus' teaching.
John quotes Isaiah’s words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts to explain continued unbelief despite Jesus’ signs, then says Isaiah spoke of his glory.
Matthew expressly presents Jesus’ birth to the virgin Mary as fulfilling Isaiah’s sign of a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, interpreted “God with us.”
Hebrews quotes Isaiah's words about the children God has given him, applying them in its discussion of Jesus and those he calls brethren.
Matthew quotes Isaiah’s reference to Zebulun, Naphtali, and Galilee and the great light shining in darkness to explain Jesus’ ministry around Capernaum.
Paul quotes Isaiah's words that only a remnant of Israel will be saved while discussing God's dealings with Israel.
Paul quotes Isaiah's prophecy of the root of Jesse who will rule the Gentiles, connecting it to their hope in Christ.
Isaiah repeats the song at the Red Sea: the Lord is strength, song, and salvation; Isaiah also calls on people to trust him without fear.
Isaiah and the psalm both declare that the Lord is their strength, song, and salvation, repeating words also used at the Red Sea in Exodus 15:2.
Isaiah and the psalm both call people to invoke the Lord’s name and make his deeds known among the peoples.
Both prophets announce the approaching day of the Lord as destruction from the Almighty, using closely matching wording.
Isaiah describes the sun and moon losing their light in judgment; Jesus likewise speaks of their darkening after tribulation, in Mark’s account.
Isaiah describes the darkened sun, moon, and stars in his oracle against Babylon; Jesus uses corresponding heavenly signs when describing tribulation and his coming.
Both passages foretell the Lord shaking the heavens and earth in judgment; Haggai specifies the overthrow of kingdoms and military powers.
Both prophecies speak of the Lord shaking heaven and earth; Isaiah describes wrath against Babylon, while Haggai announces a future shaking of nations and the Lord’s house filled with glory.
Isaiah predicts that the Medes will rise against Babylon; Daniel recounts Babylon’s fall as its kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians.
Both prophets name the Medes in the Lord’s judgment against Babylon; Jeremiah says the Lord has stirred up their kings to destroy it.
Both Isaiah and Jeremiah compare Babylon’s coming devastation to God’s overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah.
Isaiah dates this oracle to the year King Ahaz died; Kings records Ahaz’s death and the succession of his son Hezekiah.
Both judgments on Moab describe weeping along the ascent of Luhith and the road toward Horonaim.
Both prophecies mourn Moab’s ruined vineyards at Sibmah and Jazer, including the loss of harvest joy around Heshbon and Elealeh.
Both prophets announce judgment on Damascus: Isaiah foretells its ruin, while Amos names Syria’s offenses and predicts captivity.
Isaiah 8 foretells Assyria taking the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria; Isaiah 17 similarly announces the weakening of Damascus and Ephraim.
Both passages picture survivors of judgment as a few olives left after an olive tree is shaken.
Isaiah condemns seeking familiar spirits and wizards rather than turning to God; the Egypt oracle foresees Egyptians relying on those practices when their counsel fails.
Isaiah 19 predicts Egypt falling under a harsh ruler; Isaiah 20 names Assyria as the power that will lead Egyptians and Ethiopians into captivity.
Both prophets portray Egypt’s leadership or centers as failing under judgment: Isaiah calls the princes of Noph deceived, while Ezekiel foretells judgment on Noph and its idols.
Both passages envision a highway connected with Assyria, but Isaiah 11 describes the remnant’s return while Isaiah 19 describes future travel and fellowship between Egypt and Assyria.

Isaiah 19 warns that Egypt will come under a harsh ruler; Isaiah 20 describes Assyria leading away Egyptians and Ethiopians as captives. These are related warnings concerning Egypt, not an explicit identification of the ruler.
The angel in Revelation echoes Isaiah’s doubled announcement that Babylon has fallen; Revelation adds its own accusation that Babylon corrupted the nations.

Isaiah announces, “Babylon is fallen, is fallen,” and the breaking of its idols; Revelation repeats the fall announcement in its judgment of Babylon the great. The texts do not explicitly equate the historical and apocalyptic settings.

Isaiah 21 foretells a near-term loss of Kedar’s glory; Isaiah 60 instead pictures Kedar’s flocks bringing offerings to glorify the Lord’s sanctuary. These are contrasting prophetic portrayals of Kedar, not the same event.
Paul uses Isaiah's words about eating and drinking because death is near while arguing that denying resurrection empties suffering of purpose.

Isaiah announces devastation for Tyre and its maritime trade; Joel also addresses Tyre and Sidon in judgment, specifically for taking goods and selling Judah’s people. These are related judgments, not explicitly the same event.
Isaiah’s threefold warning, “fear, and the pit, and the snare,” is repeated almost word for word in Jeremiah’s oracle against Moab; Jeremiah adds that fleeing one danger leads to another.
Paul quotes Isaiah's promise that death will be swallowed up in victory while describing the resurrection of the dead.

Isaiah 27 pictures outcasts returning from Assyria and Egypt to worship at Jerusalem; Isaiah 19 pictures Egypt, Assyria, and Israel sharing in the Lord’s blessing. Both anticipate worship connected with those nations, though the scenes differ.
Paul quotes Isaiah's warning about speaking to the people through other tongues while discussing tongues and their significance.
Peter quotes Isaiah's promise of a chosen cornerstone in Zion and applies it to faith in Christ.
Paul applies Isaiah's promise about believing in Zion's cornerstone to faith in Christ; Romans says the believer will 'not be ashamed,' while Isaiah says 'shall not make haste.'
Paul uses Isaiah’s stone laid in Zion and the promise to the believer, combining the foundation-stone wording with stumbling-stone language from another Isaiah passage.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's rebuke of people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far away, applying it to the Pharisees and scribes.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's warning that people may honor God with their lips while their hearts remain far from him, applying it to empty worship and human traditions.
Paul quotes Isaiah's warning that God will overturn human wisdom while explaining why the message of the cross confounds worldly expectations.
Isaiah 30 identifies princes at Zoan among those involved in seeking help from Egypt; Isaiah 19 calls the princes of Zoan foolish and says their counsel has misled Egypt.

Both passages name Tophet, associated with the Valley of Hinnom; Isaiah uses it as imagery for the prepared burning of a king, while Jeremiah announces the place will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter.
Isaiah 30 says Egyptian help will prove vain; Isaiah 31 explains why: Egyptians are human, not God, and their horses are flesh, not spirit. Both warn Judah against relying on Egypt.

Both passages picture a dramatic reversal in which a wilderness or Lebanon becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is regarded as a forest; Isaiah 32 explicitly connects the change with the Spirit poured out from above.

Isaiah 34 foretells a great slaughter in Bozrah and Idumea; Isaiah 63 depicts a figure coming from Edom and Bozrah with garments stained through judgment. The shared Edomite setting is notable without assuming an identical scene.
Isaiah describes Edom’s ruins filled with wild beasts, owls, and satyrs; an earlier oracle uses closely matching creatures for deserted Babylon. Both pictures signal desolation in distinct lands.

Isaiah 35 promises that the restored wilderness will receive the glory of Lebanon and see the Lord’s glory; Isaiah 60 pictures Lebanon’s trees beautifying his sanctuary. Both use Lebanon’s splendor in restoration imagery.
Isaiah and 2 Kings recount Sennacherib's invasion of Judah and the Assyrian commander's challenge to Jerusalem.
Isaiah and 2 Kings recount Hezekiah's response to Assyria's threats, Isaiah's message, and Jerusalem's deliverance.
Isaiah and 2 Kings describe Hezekiah's illness, his prayer, God's promise of healing, and the sign given to him.
Isaiah and 2 Kings recount the Babylonian envoys' visit and Isaiah's warning after Hezekiah shows them his treasures.
Isaiah predicts treasures stored by Hezekiah’s house would be carried to Babylon; 2 Kings records Nebuchadnezzar taking treasures from Judah’s royal house.
John the Baptist identifies himself as the wilderness voice described by Isaiah, calling people to prepare the Lord's way.
Luke quotes Isaiah's call to prepare the Lord's way, including the promise that all people will see God's salvation, in describing John the Baptist's ministry.
Mark introduces John the Baptist by citing Isaiah's words about a voice in the wilderness preparing the Lord's way.
Matthew applies Isaiah's wilderness-voice prophecy to John the Baptist and his call to prepare for the Lord.
Peter quotes Isaiah's contrast between fading grass and the enduring word of God while describing the lasting message preached to believers.
Paul uses Isaiah's question about knowing the Lord's mind when explaining spiritual discernment and saying that believers have the mind of Christ.
Paul quotes Isaiah's question about knowing the Lord's mind or being his counselor while praising God's unsearchable judgments.
Isaiah 41 promises a messenger who brings good tidings to Jerusalem; Isaiah 52 describes a messenger who announces peace and salvation to Zion. The later passage expands the image.
Isaiah 41 promises good tidings to Jerusalem; Nahum pictures good tidings of peace proclaimed to Judah after an enemy’s downfall. Both announce relief, but their circumstances are distinct.
Matthew names Isaiah as the prophet and applies God’s Spirit-endowed, chosen servant who brings judgment to the Gentiles to Jesus’ quiet and merciful ministry.
Isaiah describes the Lord making a way through the sea; the psalm recalls his unseen path through the waters as he led his people through Moses and Aaron. Both point to the exodus deliverance.
Both passages call on heaven and earth to sing because the Lord has acted for his people: Isaiah 44 says he redeemed Jacob, while Isaiah 49 celebrates his comfort and mercy toward the afflicted.
Isaiah names Cyrus and says Jerusalem and the temple will be rebuilt; Chronicles records the Lord stirring Cyrus to issue his proclamation, continued in the following verse.
Isaiah names Cyrus as the one who will order Jerusalem and its temple rebuilt; Ezra records Cyrus’s proclamation that the Lord charged him to build the house at Jerusalem.
Isaiah 44 calls Cyrus the Lord’s shepherd who will carry out his purpose for Jerusalem; Isaiah 45 calls him the Lord’s anointed and describes God enabling his victories.
Paul quotes Isaiah's declaration that every knee will bow and every tongue will confess, applying it to each person's accountability before God.
Isaiah names both Bel and Nebo as humbled Babylonian idols; Jeremiah likewise announces that Bel is confounded and Merodach broken when Babylon falls. The named gods are not identical in wording.
Isaiah shows Babylon’s god Bel brought low and its idols carried away; Jeremiah says the Lord will punish Bel in Babylon and expose his helplessness.
Isaiah says the Lord founded the earth and stretched out the heavens; the psalm likewise attributes the earth’s foundation and heavens to his hands.
Isaiah calls the people to leave Babylon and the Chaldeans, proclaiming their redemption; Jeremiah likewise commands them to flee Babylon and depart from the land of the Chaldeans.
Paul and Barnabas apply Isaiah's commission to be a light to the Gentiles to their mission of carrying salvation beyond Israel.
Paul quotes God's promise to hear and help in an acceptable time and urges his readers to respond to the present day of salvation.

Isaiah recalls that Abraham was one man when God called and blessed him; Genesis describes Abraham and Sarah’s old age as the Lord promised them a son. Together they clarify the unexpected beginning of the promised family.

Isaiah promises that devastated Zion will become like Eden and be filled with gladness; Joel describes a fertile land like Eden before a destructive army, then a burnt wilderness behind it. The comparison runs in opposite directions.

Isaiah invokes the Lord’s arm that cut Rahab in ancient days; Psalm 89 also says he broke Rahab and scattered his enemies with his strong arm. Both celebrate God’s past victory, without specifying an identical event in the verses themselves.
Both verses promise that the Lord’s redeemed will return to Zion singing, crowned with everlasting joy, while sorrow and sighing flee away. Their wording is nearly identical.
Paul draws on Isaiah's statement that God's name is blasphemed among the nations to rebuke those whose conduct dishonors God.
Paul quotes Isaiah's image of the beautiful feet of a messenger bringing good news while explaining the importance of preaching the gospel.
Paul echoes Isaiah's call to leave what is unclean as he urges believers to separate from idolatry and belong to God.
Paul quotes Isaiah's words about people who had not heard coming to understand, explaining his aim to preach Christ where he was not known.
John quotes Isaiah’s question “Who hath believed our report?” to describe the unbelief that persisted despite the many miracles Jesus performed.
Paul quotes Isaiah's question about who believed the report while explaining that not everyone has obeyed the gospel.
Matthew identifies Jesus' healings as fulfilling Isaiah's words about bearing human infirmities and sicknesses.
Peter applies Isaiah’s words about suffering for sins and healing through the servant’s stripes to Jesus bearing sins on the cross.
The Ethiopian official reads Isaiah’s picture of a silent sheep led to slaughter; Philip begins with that text and preaches Jesus to him.
Peter applies Isaiah's description of the servant's sinlessness and lack of deceit to Jesus while describing his suffering.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's words about being numbered with transgressors and says they must be fulfilled in him.
Paul quotes Isaiah's call for the barren woman to rejoice while discussing the children of promise through Sarah and the Jerusalem above.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's promise that people will be taught by God while explaining how those taught by the Father come to him.
Paul cites Isaiah's promise of the sure mercies of David in proclaiming the resurrection of Jesus and God's enduring promises.
Jesus cites Isaiah's designation of God's house as a house of prayer when rebuking wrongdoing in the temple.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's words about God's house being a house of prayer for all nations while confronting commerce in the temple.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's declaration that God's house is a house of prayer while driving buyers and sellers from the temple.
Isaiah names feeding the hungry and clothing the naked as acts of genuine righteousness; Ezekiel likewise identifies giving bread to the hungry and covering the naked as deeds of a just person.
Both describe being made to ride on the earth’s high places: Deuteronomy recalls the Lord’s provision for Jacob/Israel, while Isaiah promises the heritage of Jacob to those delighting in the Lord.
Paul draws on Isaiah's description of feet rushing to shed blood as part of his scriptural indictment of human sin.
Isaiah pictures people from Sheba bringing gifts and praise to Zion; Psalm 72 similarly describes kings from Sheba bringing presents to the king. Their recipients and settings are distinct.
Genesis names Nebajoth and Kedar among Ishmael’s sons; Isaiah later names the flocks of Kedar and rams of Nebaioth among offerings brought to the Lord’s sanctuary.
Isaiah 2 includes the ships of Tarshish among symbols humbled in the day of the Lord; Isaiah 60 instead pictures such ships bringing Zion’s people and gifts home. The scenes are different.
Both restoration passages speak of the glory of Lebanon: Isaiah 35 says it will adorn the transformed wilderness, while Isaiah 60 pictures its trees beautifying God’s sanctuary.
Jesus reads Isaiah’s words about the Spirit-anointed messenger proclaiming good news and liberty, then declares the Scripture fulfilled; Luke’s wording differs from Isaiah’s wording in the KJV.
Jesus reads Isaiah's proclamation of the Lord's acceptable year in the synagogue and says the Scripture is fulfilled in his listeners' hearing.
Both passages call for a highway to be prepared. Isaiah 40 announces a way for the Lord in the wilderness; Isaiah 62 calls for a cleared road and a banner for the people approaching Zion.

Amos condemns Edom’s hostility and announces judgment reaching Bozrah; Isaiah depicts a powerful figure coming from Edom, specifically Bozrah, after judgment. The scenes are related but not explicitly identical.
In both passages the Lord finds no human helper, acts by his own arm, and executes judgment. Isaiah 59 announces his intervention; Isaiah 63 presents the warrior speaking about it.
Paul quotes Isaiah's words about being found by those who had not sought God while explaining the inclusion of the Gentiles.
Paul quotes Isaiah's picture of God stretching out his hands to a disobedient people while speaking about Israel's response.
Isaiah announces God’s creation of new heavens and a new earth; John later sees a new heaven and earth after the former creation passes away.
Stephen quotes Isaiah's declaration that heaven is God's throne and earth his footstool to show that God is not confined to a man-made house.
Jesus repeats Isaiah's image of the undying worm and unquenched fire when warning about the seriousness of judgment.
At his call Jeremiah is told not to fear because the Lord will deliver him; later God renews that promise, saying opponents will fight him but not prevail.
Both passages say the Lord puts his words into a speaker’s mouth. Jeremiah describes a physical touch at his call, while Isaiah 51 gives the assurance within a message about Zion.
God first places his words in Jeremiah’s mouth; later he compares those same words to fire that will consume the people who reject them.
Jeremiah is commissioned to uproot and build nations; chapter 18 repeats those verbs and explains that a nation’s turning from or toward evil affects the announced outcome.
Jeremiah’s commission includes tearing down and building up; God later promises that just as he watched over Israel to destroy, he will watch over them to build and plant.
Huldah’s warning in 2 Kings condemns forsaking the Lord, burning incense to other gods, and worshiping the works of human hands—nearly the same charges in Jeremiah’s commission.
Jeremiah’s first message condemns abandoning the Lord and offering incense to other gods; chapter 19 repeats those offenses while announcing judgment on Jerusalem.
Jeremiah calls the Lord the fountain of living waters whom Israel has abandoned; later he again names the Lord as the fountain of living waters and says those who forsake him will be ashamed.
Deuteronomy commands Israel to destroy pagan worship sites under every green tree; Jeremiah condemns Judah for practicing idolatry on high hills and under every green tree.
Jeremiah 2 accuses God’s people of unfaithfulness on every high hill and under every green tree; Jeremiah 3 explicitly calls the same behavior Israel’s spiritual adultery.

Jeremiah portrays Judah as an unfaithful wife with many lovers; Ezekiel extends the same marriage imagery to Jerusalem’s pursuit of Assyria and Chaldea. These are prophetic comparisons, not literal marriages.
Both prophets use the command to break up fallow ground as a call to repentance. Hosea urges sowing righteousness; Jeremiah warns Judah not to sow among thorns.
Jeremiah first sounds the trumpet and calls Judah to gather inside fortified cities; later the people themselves urge one another to enter fortified cities because judgment has come.
Both warnings trace news of the northern threat through Dan: Jeremiah 4 announces danger from Dan and Ephraim, while Jeremiah 8 describes invaders’ horses heard from Dan.

Jeremiah describes the judged land as without form and void, with dark heavens, deliberately echoing Genesis’s description before creation. It is imagery for devastation, not a second creation account.
At Jeremiah’s calling God places words in his mouth; in chapter 5 those words become like fire against the disobedient people.
Jeremiah 8 repeats the accusation in chapter 6 almost word for word: from the least to the greatest, even prophets and priests deal falsely and covet gain.
Jeremiah repeats nearly word for word that the people feel no shame for their abominations and therefore will fall when the Lord visits them in judgment.
Jesus combines Isaiah's description of a house of prayer with Jeremiah's rebuke of a den of robbers when confronting conduct in the temple.
Jesus joins Isaiah's words about a house of prayer to Jeremiah's accusation that the temple has become a den of robbers.
Jesus quotes Jeremiah's image of a den of robbers, alongside Isaiah's house-of-prayer language, while cleansing the temple.
Deuteronomy warns Israel not to worship the sun, moon, and stars; Jeremiah describes Judah serving those heavenly bodies and then being exposed before them in disgrace.
Jeremiah 8 pictures the scattered survivors of judgment in places where God has driven them; Jeremiah 23 promises that God will gather the remnant of his flock from those countries.
Jeremiah 8 repeats the warning of Jeremiah 6 almost word for word: the people lack shame for their wrongdoing and will fall when the Lord judges.
Jeremiah 4 commands Judah to gather in fortified cities as danger approaches; Jeremiah 8 repeats that appeal as the people confront the consequences of their sins.
Jeremiah first asks whether Gilead has balm for his wounded people; later he tells Egypt to seek balm from Gilead but says its many medicines will not cure its wound.
Paul echoes Jeremiah's instruction to boast in the Lord rather than human strength or wisdom when rejecting human boasting.
Paul echoes Jeremiah's call to boast in the Lord while defending the proper basis for commendation.
Both passages describe the Lord making vapors rise, lightning for rain, and wind coming from his treasuries. Jeremiah uses this distinctive description to contrast the Creator with idols.
Jeremiah 51 closely repeats chapter 10’s condemnation of idol-makers as foolish and of molten images as false, now within his prophecy against Babylon.
Both verses declare that idols are vanity and works of errors that perish when God visits them. Jeremiah repeats this warning in the oracle against Babylon.
Both passages contrast worthless idols with the Lord, Jacob’s portion, who formed all things and is called the Lord of hosts. The later verse repeats the earlier declaration.
God promises Moses that he will bring Israel from Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey; Jeremiah invokes the oath to their fathers while calling Judah to obey that covenant.
The Lord renewed his oath to Abraham when he promised Isaac the land and descendants; Jeremiah recalls the ancestral land oath while calling Judah to keep its covenant.
Both passages accuse Israel of refusing to listen and following stubborn, evil hearts; Jeremiah 11 explicitly connects that disobedience with the covenant judgments.
God twice forbids Jeremiah to intercede for the people because he will not hear prayers offered on their behalf amid persistent covenant disobedience.
Jeremiah twice appeals to the Lord who examines hearts and judges righteously, entrusting his case against those seeking his harm to God.
Both prophets say that the Lord will remember the people’s iniquity and visit their sins; Hosea condemns unacceptable sacrifices, while Jeremiah rebukes their wandering.
Samuel prayed and offered a sacrifice for Israel, and the Lord answered; Jeremiah later cites Samuel alongside Moses as an intercessor whose pleading could not now avert judgment.
The psalm remembers Moses and Samuel calling on the Lord and receiving an answer; Jeremiah says that even their intercession could no longer turn aside Judah’s judgment.
Jeremiah repeats the appointed outcomes of death, sword, famine, and captivity. Chapter 15 addresses Judah’s judgment; chapter 43 applies the same categories to Egypt under Babylon.
Both warnings say that the people will serve enemies in a land they do not know, because they have kindled the Lord’s anger with a fire that will burn.
Both passages picture the faithful person as a tree planted beside water whose leaves remain green and whose fruit continues; Jeremiah adds that drought need not make it afraid.
The Lord says he searches hearts and repays people according to the fruit of their deeds; chapter 21 applies that principle to Jerusalem’s coming punishment.
Jeremiah says the Lord searches the heart and gives people according to their ways; later Jeremiah praises God whose eyes see human ways and who recompenses their deeds.
Jeremiah first calls the Lord the fountain of living waters abandoned by his people; later he says those who forsake that fountain will be ashamed.
Jeremiah 17 promises the continuing entrance of Davidic kings if Judah obeys; Jeremiah 22 separately announces that no descendant of Jeconiah will prosper on David’s throne.
Both passages condition continued Davidic kingship on obedience: Jeremiah 17 speaks of keeping the Sabbath, while Jeremiah 22 requires justice and protection of the vulnerable.

Jeremiah’s commission includes building and planting nations; his message in chapter 18 explains that announced good may change when a nation does evil, just as announced judgment may change when it repents.
Jeremiah says God can choose to build and plant a nation if its conduct warrants it; chapter 31 promises to watch over Israel and Judah to build and plant after earlier judgment.
Jeremiah urges Judah to change its evil conduct despite announced disaster; later he repeats that appeal and explicitly says God may relent from the judgment if they obey.
Jeremiah first warns that Judah’s land will become a desolation provoking astonishment and hissing; after the broken-pot sign he repeats the same warning about Jerusalem.

The Lord warns through both passages that his judgment on Jerusalem will make listeners’ ears tingle; 2 Kings announces this in connection with Manasseh’s sins, Jeremiah in connection with Judah’s idolatry.
Jeremiah twice condemns the high places of Baal where Judah burned children in sacrifice; chapter 32 also speaks of causing sons and daughters to pass through fire to Molech.
Jeremiah twice announces that Tophet and the Valley of Hinnom will be called the Valley of Slaughter because of the coming deaths and burials there.
Jeremiah repeats the warning that Judah or Jerusalem will become desolate, provoking astonishment and hissing from passersby; chapter 19 applies it after the broken jar.
Jeremiah twice condemns incense and drink offerings made on Jerusalem’s rooftops; chapter 32 connects that offense with the Chaldeans burning those houses.

Jeremiah identifies his opponent Pashur as the son of Immer and a priest; Chronicles names Immer as the head of one of the priestly divisions, offering background on the priestly name without proving individual descent.
Zephaniah son of Maaseiah serves in Zedekiah’s delegation to Jeremiah; chapter 29 also names him as the priest receiving a letter about Jeremiah and the temple officers.
Zedekiah sends Jeremiah delegations that include Zephaniah son of Maaseiah in both passages. Jeremiah 21 also names Pashur; chapter 37 names Jehucal instead.

Jeremiah 21 names Zephaniah son of Maaseiah as a priest in Zedekiah’s delegation; the account of Jerusalem’s fall names Zephaniah the second priest among those seized. The later verse does not give his father’s name.
Jeremiah tells Jerusalem that its armed resistance to the Chaldeans will fail; chapter 33 likewise describes fighting the Chaldeans amid a city filled with the slain.
Jeremiah warns that Judah’s weapons will fail against Babylon; later he says the Chaldeans will return, take Jerusalem, and burn it despite hopes for their departure.
Jeremiah warns that Zedekiah and those left in Jerusalem will be handed over to Babylon; later Zedekiah privately asks the prophet for a message and hears that he will be delivered to Babylon’s king.
Both warnings say that those remaining in Jerusalem will die by sword, famine, or pestilence, but those who go out to the Chaldeans will preserve their lives.
Jeremiah twice says that obedience would allow Davidic kings to pass through the gates in chariots and on horses; chapter 17 emphasizes Sabbath observance, chapter 22 just governance.
The Lord rejects Coniah son of Jehoiakim even if he were his signet ring; Jeremiah later records Zedekiah reigning instead of Coniah under Babylonian appointment.
Jeremiah describes Coniah as a rejected vessel cast into exile; Hosea uses the same distinctive phrase, “a vessel wherein is no pleasure,” for Israel among the nations.
Jeremiah promises that the Lord will gather his dispersed flock; the letter to the exiles repeats that God will bring those driven away back to their own land.
Both promises say the Lord will gather those he scattered among other countries and bring them home; chapter 23 pictures the returned remnant as his flock.
Jeremiah 23 names the promised righteous Davidic king “The LORD Our Righteousness”; chapter 33 repeats the name for Jerusalem while promising renewed safety.
Jeremiah twice charges Israel’s prophets with speaking in Baal’s name; chapter 23 specifies that the prophets of Samaria led the people astray.
Both verses say the Lord’s anger will not turn back until he carries out his purposes, and that the people will understand in later days; the preceding verses also describe his whirlwind.
Jeremiah again condemns prophets who claim to speak in the Lord’s name without being sent by him; chapter 23 singles out their claims of receiving dreams.
Both accounts place their events after Nebuchadnezzar deported Jeconiah and Judah’s officials and craftsmen to Babylon; the fig vision explains the plight of the deported and those left behind.
The Lord promises to build and plant the deported people when he restores them; later he uses the same words conditionally for those who remain in Judah instead of fleeing to Egypt.
Both passages date messages to the fourth year of Jehoiakim; chapter 25 also identifies it as Nebuchadrezzar’s first year, while chapter 36 introduces the writing of Jeremiah’s prophecies.
Jeremiah 1 dates the beginning of his prophetic call to Josiah’s thirteenth year; chapter 25 looks back from Jehoiakim’s reign over twenty-three years of warnings the people ignored.
Jeremiah repeatedly says the Lord spoke persistently to Judah, but the people refused to listen; chapter 25 summarizes the twenty-three years of unheeded warnings.
Both verses charge Judah with refusing to listen to the Lord’s servants, the prophets, whom he repeatedly sent with warnings.
Jeremiah’s exile letter repeats the charge that the Lord persistently sent prophets, but Judah refused to listen, first stated in chapter 25.
Jeremiah repeats that the Lord continually sent prophets whom Judah refused to hear; chapter 44 specifies their warning to stop the idolatrous practices the people continued.
Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God’s servant in announcing judgment against Judah and neighboring nations; Ezekiel says God would give Egypt to the same king after his army’s service against Tyre.
Jeremiah announces seventy years of Babylonian rule and desolation; Daniel explicitly says he learned from Jeremiah’s writings that Jerusalem’s desolations would last seventy years.
Jeremiah 25 includes desert peoples described as living “in the utmost corners”; chapter 9 uses the same distinctive designation within a wider judgment on the nations.
Jeremiah calls Babylon “Sheshach” in the nations’ judgment list and later declares that Sheshach—identified there as Babylon—has been taken.
Jeremiah again says the Lord sent his prophets persistently and that Judah would not listen; chapter 7 traces those warnings back to the exodus.
Both narratives place activity at the new gate of the Lord’s house; chapter 26 describes officials hearing Jeremiah’s case, while chapter 36 records Baruch reading Jeremiah’s scroll there.
Jeremiah twice urges Judah to amend its ways; chapter 7 specifies justice, protection of the vulnerable, and turning from idols, while chapter 26 warns that obedience can avert announced disaster.
Jeremiah quotes Micah’s prophecy almost word for word: Zion would be plowed like a field, Jerusalem become heaps, and the temple mount become wooded heights.
Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God’s servant and gives him dominion over the nations and even the beasts; the next chapter repeats that claim while announcing an iron yoke of Babylonian rule.
Jeremiah warns that prophets promising a speedy return of the temple vessels are lying; Hananiah then makes that very claim, specifying a return within two years.
Jeremiah 27 recalls Jeconiah’s removal to Babylon when distinguishing temple vessels that remained; chapter 24 records the same deportation as the setting of the fig vision.
Hananiah promises that the Lord’s temple vessels will return within two years; Jeremiah’s earlier warning calls such predictions lies and says the remaining vessels will later be brought back.
Deuteronomy warns that disobedient Israel will bear an iron yoke under enemies; Jeremiah announces that God has imposed an iron yoke of service to Nebuchadnezzar upon the nations.
Jeremiah tells Hananiah that God did not send him and that he made people trust a lie; he later makes the same accusation against Shemaiah, another false prophet.
Jeremiah says Hananiah will die for teaching rebellion against the Lord; he later judges Shemaiah for the same offense, but announces a different punishment involving his descendants.
Jeremiah promises the exiles a return after seventy years in Babylon; Ezra records Cyrus’s proclamation and explicitly says the Lord brought it about to fulfill Jeremiah’s word.
Jeremiah promises the captives a return to their homeland; chapter 23 pictures the same restoration as the Lord gathering his scattered flock into its folds.
Jeremiah promises to gather the exiles back from the countries where they were scattered; chapter 32 repeats the promise and says they will live safely in the land.
Jeremiah’s warning of rotten figs, sword, famine, and pestilence repeats the earlier fig vision’s judgment against Zedekiah and those remaining in Jerusalem.
Both passages foretell the desolation of Judah through Babylonian judgment, describing the devastation as an astonishment and a hissing among the nations.
Jeremiah repeats that the Lord sent prophets persistently but Judah refused to hear them; chapter 26 presents the warning as a condition for judgment on the temple and city.
Both verses condemn Judah for repeatedly ignoring God’s instruction; chapter 29 names the unheeded prophets, while chapter 32 says the people turned their backs despite God’s teaching.
Jeremiah rebukes Shemaiah for claiming divine authority and making people trust a lie; the earlier judgment on Hananiah uses nearly the same words, though it concerns a different prophet.
Jeremiah declares that Shemaiah taught rebellion against the Lord and would be punished; Hananiah was condemned for the same offense but received a sentence of death that year.

Both prophets use the striking promise that the Lord will break an oppressor’s yoke and burst his people’s bonds; Jeremiah speaks of Jacob’s future deliverance, while Nahum announces relief from Assyria.
Jeremiah repeats almost word for word that the Lord’s fierce anger will not turn back until he fulfills his purposes and that the people will understand in later days.
Matthew explicitly cites Jeremiah’s picture of Rachel weeping for her children to describe the mourning caused by Herod’s killing of children in Bethlehem.
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant that changes God's relationship with his people and writes his laws in their hearts.
Hebrews repeats Jeremiah's new-covenant promise of God's law written in hearts and minds, followed by the assurance that sins will be remembered no more.
Hebrews repeats Jeremiah's new-covenant promise that God will no longer remember his people's sins and iniquities.
Zedekiah imprisons Jeremiah for announcing Babylon’s capture of Jerusalem; chapter 34 records the same warning delivered directly to Zedekiah, including that the king would face Nebuchadnezzar.
Jeremiah praises God for seeing everyone’s ways and repaying their deeds; earlier he records God’s declaration that he searches hearts and rewards each person according to conduct.
Jeremiah’s prayer recalls Israel’s exodus with signs, wonders, a mighty hand, and an outstretched arm; Deuteronomy uses the same details in Israel’s confession of deliverance.
Jeremiah remembers God bringing Israel out of Egypt by his strong hand and outstretched arm; Exodus records God’s promise to redeem them with an outstretched arm and great judgments.
Jeremiah thanks God for giving Israel the land promised to the fathers, flowing with milk and honey; at the burning bush God had announced that he would bring Israel into that very land.

Jeremiah warns that Babylon will burn houses where incense was offered to Baal and other gods; chapter 19 specifically condemns incense on Jerusalem’s rooftops before announcing the city’s destruction.

Chronicles recounts Manasseh making his children pass through fire in the valley of Hinnom; Jeremiah condemns the same kind of child sacrifice at Baal’s high places there, without identifying a single ceremony.
Jeremiah twice condemns Judah for building places of child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom; chapter 7 calls the site Tophet and says such offerings were never commanded by God.
Leviticus forbids giving children to Molech; Jeremiah condemns Judah for making children pass through fire to Molech at the high places in Hinnom.
Both promises say the Lord will gather the people he scattered among the nations and return them to their land; chapter 23 calls them his flock, while chapter 32 promises safety.
Both passages promise an everlasting covenant: Isaiah recalls the sure mercies of David, while Jeremiah describes God’s enduring commitment to do his people good and keep them faithful.
Jeremiah promises to plant the restored people securely in their land; the earlier vision of good figs also says God will bring the captives back, build them, and plant them.
Both passages promise a righteous Branch from David and Judah’s safety; chapter 23 calls the king “The LORD Our Righteousness,” while chapter 33 gives that name to Jerusalem.
Jeremiah rebukes Judah for withholding the freedom required for Hebrew servants after six years; Deuteronomy directly commands their release in the seventh year.
Jeremiah names Jonadab son of Rechab as the Rechabites’ ancestor; Chronicles separately identifies the house of Rechab among the Kenite scribal families.
The Rechabites trace their refusal of wine to Jonadab son of Rechab; Kings introduces Jehonadab son of Rechab as Jehu’s companion, the same named ancestor in the historical account.
Jeremiah contrasts the Rechabites’ obedience to their father with Judah’s refusal to hear God; chapter 25 similarly recounts years of God’s repeated warnings through Jeremiah and the prophets.
Jeremiah repeats that God spoke persistently to Judah but the people refused to hear; chapter 35 contrasts that refusal with the Rechabites’ obedience to their father.
Jeremiah again charges Judah with ignoring prophets whom God repeatedly sent; chapter 44 specifies that the prophets warned against burning incense to other gods.
Both passages say the Lord continually sent prophets calling Israel to obey, but the people would not listen; chapter 35 contrasts their disobedience with the Rechabites’ faithfulness.
Both chapters date messages to Jehoiakim’s fourth year; chapter 25 dates Jeremiah’s warning to that year, and chapter 36 dates God’s instruction to write his words in a scroll.
Jeremiah is told to write his messages from Josiah’s days onward; chapter 25 states that his warnings began in Josiah’s thirteenth year and continued for twenty-three years.
Baruch son of Neriah writes Jeremiah’s dictated prophecies in chapter 36; chapter 32 names the same trusted associate as recipient of the witnessed land-purchase documents.
Elnathan son of Achbor appears among the officials who hear about Jeremiah’s scroll; chapter 26 identifies the same named official as Jehoiakim’s agent sent to bring Urijah back from Egypt.
Jeremiah states that Nebuchadnezzar installed Zedekiah in Coniah’s place; Kings records the replacement of Jehoiachin and explains that Mattaniah was renamed Zedekiah.
Jeremiah names Coniah son of Jehoiakim as the king replaced by Zedekiah; his earlier oracle had announced Coniah’s rejection and removal from royal favor.
Zedekiah sends messengers to ask Jeremiah for God’s help in both accounts; Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is named in both, but his fellow envoy differs, so they should not be treated as one delegation.
Jeremiah tells Zedekiah privately that he will be delivered to Babylon’s king; the earlier message also warned that Babylon would capture Zedekiah and the remaining people.
Zedekiah orders Jeremiah held in the court of the prison and supplied with bread; after a later imprisonment in a muddy dungeon, Jeremiah is rescued and returned to that court.
After Ebedmelech rescues Jeremiah from the dungeon, he remains in the court of the prison, where Zedekiah had earlier ordered him held and fed.
Zedekiah secretly questions Jeremiah in both encounters: in chapter 37 he asks for a word from the Lord, and in chapter 38 he swears not to hand Jeremiah over to those seeking his life.
Jeremiah repeatedly counsels Zedekiah to submit to Babylon and live; chapter 38 adds that surrender would spare the king’s household and prevent the burning of Jerusalem.
Jeremiah records Nebuzaradan deporting survivors after Jerusalem fell; the next chapter describes Jeremiah being released from chains among captives gathered at Ramah.
Jeremiah is assigned to Gedaliah after his release; the earlier account says Babylonian officers took him from prison and entrusted him to Gedaliah, without specifying identical stages of custody.
Johanan and other commanders come to Gedaliah at Mizpah; after Gedaliah’s assassination, Johanan and the remaining leaders approach Jeremiah to seek guidance.
Ishmael was among the commanders who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah; the next chapter records him returning with ten men and murdering the governor.
Both accounts identify Ishmael son of Nethaniah and ten men as Gedaliah’s killers in the seventh month; Kings also mentions the Jews and Chaldeans killed at Mizpah.
After Johanan had warned Gedaliah of Ishmael’s plot and Gedaliah dismissed the warning, Johanan and the commanders learned of Ishmael’s murders and went after him.
Johanan and the commanders pursued Ishmael after Gedaliah’s murder and recovered his captives; afterward these leaders came to Jeremiah to ask what they should do.
Johanan gathered the people rescued from Ishmael; after they sought Jeremiah’s guidance, Jeremiah summoned Johanan and the other captains to hear the Lord’s answer.
Johanan rescued the remnant from Ishmael, but later he and the other captains disobeyed the Lord’s instruction to stay in Judah and took the survivors into Egypt.
Nebuzaradan directed Jeremiah to Gedaliah and offered him a place in Judah; after Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, the survivors feared Babylonian retaliation and prepared to flee to Egypt.
Johanan and the captains who learned of Ishmael’s murders and pursued him later assembled with the rescued people to ask Jeremiah to seek the Lord’s guidance.
Johanan, the captains, and the people came to Jeremiah to request God’s direction, but afterward the same leaders refused his command to remain in Judah.
Jeremiah warned the remnant that entering Egypt would bring God’s anger and make them a curse and reproach; his later message pronounces judgment on those who chose to settle there.
Nebuzaradan left some poor people in Judah after Jerusalem fell; Jeremiah later says Johanan took the remnant left under Gedaliah’s care, along with Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt.
The remnant reached Tahpanhes in Egypt after refusing to stay in Judah; Jeremiah’s next address concerns Judeans residing at Tahpanhes and other Egyptian locations.
Both oracles name Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Noph in Egypt, but Jeremiah 44 addresses Judean refugees there, while Jeremiah 46 warns Egypt of an approaching Babylonian attack.
Jeremiah repeats that the people would not listen or turn from their wrongdoing; in chapter 44 he specifies their refusal to stop offering incense to other gods.
Before the remnant fled, Jeremiah warned they would become a curse and reproach in Egypt; after their arrival he rebukes them for provoking God by burning incense to other gods.
Jeremiah dates his personal message to Baruch to Jehoiakim’s fourth year, when Baruch wrote Jeremiah’s prophecies in a scroll; chapter 36 records the writing assignment and Baruch’s work.
Both passages mention Pharaoh Neco’s movement toward the Euphrates: Kings records Josiah’s death when he confronted Neco, while Jeremiah dates Babylon’s later defeat of Neco at Carchemish.
Jeremiah asks whether there is balm in Gilead to heal his people, but later tells Egypt that even many medicines and balm cannot cure its wound after defeat.
Jeremiah foretells Egypt’s defeat by Nebuchadnezzar and his servants; his other oracle specifically warns that Pharaoh Hophra will be handed over to those seeking his life.
Jeremiah repeats almost exactly that the Lord will correct Jacob in measure but will not leave him wholly unpunished or bring his people to a complete end.
Jeremiah describes the Philistines as the remnant of Caphtor, while Amos says that God brought the Philistines from Caphtor, explicitly connecting the people with the same origin.
Jeremiah’s earlier judgment list includes Ashkelon, Azzah (Gaza), Ekron, and other Philistine cities; his later oracle specifically announces destruction at Gaza and Ashkelon.
Both prophets lament Moab’s ruin with cries from its towns; Isaiah speaks of fugitives reaching Zoar and Horonaim, and Jeremiah records the cry of destruction at Horonaim.
The earlier song describes Moab as the people of Chemosh, whose sons and daughters were taken by Sihon; Jeremiah predicts that Chemosh, his priests, and his princes will go into captivity.
Jeremiah names Kerioth among the Moabite towns facing judgment; Amos specifically warns that God will send fire on Moab and consume Kerioth’s palaces.
Jeremiah echoes Isaiah’s lament over the vine of Sibmah, the weeping of Jazer, and the lost harvest, using the same distinctive vineyard imagery for Moab’s devastation.
Both prophecies describe cries from Heshbon and Elealeh and the drying waters of Nimrim as signs of Moab’s ruin.
Jeremiah repeats Isaiah’s exact sequence of fear, the pit, and the snare, applying the same judgment imagery specifically to Moab rather than to the whole earth.
Jeremiah predicts war and destruction at Rabbah, capital of Ammon; Ezekiel describes Babylon’s king at a crossroads deciding whether to attack Rabbah or Jerusalem.
Both prophets announce judgment on Edom: Jeremiah’s oracle begins by questioning the wisdom of Teman, while Amos specifically declares fire against Teman and Bozrah.
Jeremiah and Obadiah closely repeat that Edom’s pride has deceived it, describing its lofty dwelling in the clefts of the rock and warning that even a high nest cannot protect it.
Jeremiah compares Edom’s coming ruin to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah; Deuteronomy likewise invokes those destroyed cities to describe land devastated by God’s judgment.
Jeremiah repeats almost word for word the Lord’s counsel and the image of a flock being driven away, applying it first to Edom and then to Babylon.
Jeremiah names the kings of Elam among the nations to receive the cup of God’s judgment; this later prophecy addresses Elam directly and announces the breaking of its military strength.
Jeremiah repeats the striking judgment phrase about sending the sword after people until they are consumed; chapter 9 addresses Judah’s scattering, while chapter 49 applies the warning to Elam.
Both prophets name the Babylonian idol Bel: Isaiah pictures Bel stooping under the burden of its images, while Jeremiah announces Bel’s humiliation when Babylon falls.
Both prophecies tell people to depart from Babylon: Isaiah calls them to proclaim the Lord’s redemption of Jacob, while Jeremiah urges them to leave before Babylon’s coming judgment.
Those escaping Babylon are called to declare in Zion the Lord’s vengeance for his temple; the later chapter repeats this announcement in language of God vindicating his people.
Jeremiah reuses the lion-from-Jordan image and God’s challenge about who can stand before him, first in judgment against Edom and then against Babylon.
Both passages call for the Lord’s deliverance from Babylon to be announced in Zion, framing Babylon’s downfall as the Lord’s action for his people and temple.
Jeremiah repeats his earlier proclamation that the Lord made the earth by his power and stretches out the heavens, contrasting the Creator’s wisdom with powerless idols.
Jeremiah and the psalm use strikingly similar wording about God raising vapours from the ends of the earth, making lightning with rain, and bringing wind from his storehouses.
Jeremiah repeats his earlier condemnation of those who make idols: their molten images are false and have no breath in them.
Both passages describe idols as worthless works of error that will perish when God judges them; Jeremiah repeats the same words in his later oracle.
Jeremiah repeats that Jacob’s God is unlike idols: he formed everything, Israel belongs to him, and his name is the Lord of hosts.
Jeremiah names Ashchenaz among the kingdoms summoned against Babylon; Chronicles lists Ashchenaz as a descendant of Gomer, giving a genealogical occurrence of the uncommon name.
Jeremiah describes Nebuchadrezzar as having devoured and crushed his people; the earlier oracle calls Israel a scattered sheep, first devoured by Assyria and then injured by Babylon.
Jeremiah 25 calls the king of Sheshach to drink the cup of judgment, and Jeremiah 51 identifies Sheshach with Babylon while announcing its capture.
Kings and Jeremiah record the same siege beginning on the tenth day of the tenth month in Zedekiah’s ninth year; Kings continues through Jerusalem’s fall and its aftermath.
Both accounts date Nebuchadnezzar’s siege of Jerusalem to Zedekiah’s ninth year and describe the Babylonian army surrounding the city.
Both accounts identify Nebuzaradan arriving at Jerusalem in Nebuchadnezzar’s nineteenth year; Jeremiah says the tenth day of the fifth month, while Kings says the seventh.
Jeremiah and Kings both report the Babylonian army demolishing the walls around Jerusalem after the city’s fall.
Both accounts say the Chaldeans broke the temple’s bronze pillars, bases, and sea and carried their metal to Babylon; Jeremiah also details the temple furnishings.
Both accounts list the bronze temple utensils taken by the Babylonians, including shovels and snuffers, with some differences in the items named.
Both accounts say Nebuzaradan carried off temple objects of gold and silver, including the firepans and bowls named in Kings.
Jeremiah and Kings both say Solomon’s two pillars, the bronze sea, and other furnishings contained an immense amount of bronze; Jeremiah names twelve bronze bulls, while Kings names the bases.
Jeremiah describes a bronze pillar of eighteen cubits; Kings records Solomon making two pillars of the same height and naming them Jachin and Boaz.
Both accounts give each bronze temple pillar a height of eighteen cubits and describe its ornamentation; the measurements are not identical in every detail.
Both narratives name Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and three door keepers among the people Nebuzaradan seized.
Both accounts list an officer over soldiers, a military scribe, and sixty men seized in Jerusalem; Jeremiah names seven royal attendants, while Kings names five.
Both accounts say Evilmerodach released Jehoiachin in the thirty-seventh year of his captivity and treated him kindly; Jeremiah dates the act to the twenty-fifth day, Kings to the twenty-seventh.
Both laments picture God as an archer whose bow is aimed against his people; chapter 2 describes Zion under attack, while chapter 3 voices the suffering personally.
Both poems depict God with a drawn bow against his own people; Lamentations 2 speaks of devastation in Zion, and Lamentations 3 gives the individual lament.
Both books mention dealings with Egypt and Assyria: Hosea criticizes Ephraim’s alliance-making, while Lamentations recalls relying on those powers for bread amid hardship.
Ezekiel identifies the living creatures seen beside the Chebar in his opening vision as cherubim, linking the earlier vision of God’s glory to the later temple vision.
Ezekiel says the vision of God’s glory returning to the temple resembled the vision he had seen by the river Chebar at the beginning of the book.
Ezekiel again describes the cherubim moving straight ahead without turning, just as the living creatures moved in his first vision.
Both visions describe four faces on each creature; the later account names a cherub face where the first names an ox face.
The wheels beside the cherubim repeat the appearance of a wheel within a wheel and movement in all four directions from Ezekiel’s first vision.
In both visions the wheels move and stand with the living creatures, because the spirit of the creatures is in the wheels.
Ezekiel first hears the creatures’ wings like great waters and the voice of the Almighty; later their sound fills the outer court.
Ezekiel sees a sapphire-like throne above the creatures; at Sinai, Israel’s elders see sapphire-like pavement beneath the God of Israel. These are different visions.
Both visions place the appearance of a sapphire-like throne above the living creatures, later identified as cherubim.
Ezekiel again sees a fiery figure with brightness like amber, matching the appearance in his opening vision as he is carried to Jerusalem.
The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet when he is first commissioned and does so again when God sends him into his house.
God makes Ezekiel firm against stubborn hearers, following the earlier command not to fear their threatening words or appearance.
God repeats his command for Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel whether the people listen or refuse.
God again appoints Ezekiel a watchman and requires him to warn the wicked; failure to warn brings responsibility for their blood.
Ezekiel later expands the warning that a person who turns from righteousness to wickedness will die for that wrongdoing.
Ezekiel’s sign of rationed bread in besieged Jerusalem is echoed by God’s warning that he can break a land’s supply of bread as judgment.
Kings records Judah building high places beneath every green tree; Ezekiel later condemns the continuing pattern of worship at such sites.
Hosea describes sacrifices on hills and beneath shade trees; Ezekiel announces judgment on Israel’s idols and worshipers at those same kinds of shrines.
Jeremiah charges the people with unfaithfulness beneath every green tree; Ezekiel condemns offerings at hilltop and tree-shaded idolatrous sites.
The warning of coming disaster repeats the striking image of hands becoming feeble and knees becoming weak like water.
Both prophets say that neither silver nor gold can rescue people on the day of the LORD’s wrath.
