Ezekiel sees men facing east and worshiping the sun between the porch and altar; Joel calls priests to weep in that same temple area. The actions sharply contrast.
The linen-clothed man who reports completing his marking task in chapter 9 receives the next command to scatter fiery coals over Jerusalem.
Both descriptions say that the wheels stand and move with the creatures because their spirit is in the wheels; chapter 10 identifies them as cherubim.
Ezekiel expressly identifies the cherubim at the temple as the living creatures he had seen by the river Chebar in his opening vision.
Ezekiel states that the faces of the cherubim are the faces he saw by the Chebar, where he described the man, lion, ox, and eagle faces.
God promises to replace a stony heart with a heart of flesh and give a new spirit; the later passage adds that his Spirit will enable obedience.
God foretells catching Jerusalem’s ruler in his net and taking him to Babylon without seeing it; Kings recounts Zedekiah’s capture, blinding, and removal to Babylon.
God foretells breaking a sinful land’s bread supply; Ezekiel’s earlier siege sign applies that warning specifically to Jerusalem’s rationed food.
God calls Noah righteous before the flood; Ezekiel names Noah among the exceptionally righteous who could save only themselves in a judged land.
Job is introduced as upright and God-fearing; Ezekiel names him among the righteous who could deliver only themselves from judgment.
In two judgments pictured as an unfaithful woman’s humiliation, Ezekiel says the offenders will be stripped and left naked by those they trusted.
Chapter 16 calls Samaria Jerusalem’s older sister; chapter 23 represents Samaria as Aholah and Jerusalem as Aholibah in a second sister-city allegory.
Jeremiah and Ezekiel both cite the sour-grapes proverb and reject blaming children for their parents’ sins, affirming personal responsibility.
Ezekiel repeats that a wicked person who turns from wrongdoing and acts justly will live rather than die.
Both warnings say that a formerly righteous person who turns to wrongdoing will die for that sin; earlier righteousness does not excuse it.
Both passages call Israel to repent and turn away from sin; Ezekiel 14 specifically addresses the idols the people have embraced.
God again declares that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and urges Israel to turn from evil and live.
In both episodes elders of Israel come before Ezekiel to seek the LORD; chapter 14 exposes idolatry in their hearts, while chapter 20 recounts Israel’s rebellion.
God’s words to Moses promise to rescue Israel from Egypt and bring them to a land flowing with milk and honey, the promise Ezekiel later recalls.
Ezekiel recalls God’s promise to bring Israel from Egypt into a land flowing with milk and honey; Jeremiah recalls that the promised land was given.
Ezekiel repeats the covenant command that Israel keep the Sabbaths holy as a sign between the LORD and his people, first stated in Exodus.
Both visions speak of the mountain of Israel: Ezekiel 17 pictures a planted cedar sheltering birds, while Ezekiel 20 promises restored worship by gathered Israel.
After God gathers and restores Israel, both passages say the people will remember their former evil and loathe their sinful ways.
The fire consuming green and dry trees from south to north is followed by a sword against righteous and wicked from south to north, two images of sweeping judgment.
Ezekiel repeats the warning that fear of coming judgment will leave hands weak and knees unable to stand.
Ezekiel names Rabbah of the Ammonites as a possible route for Babylon’s sword; Jeremiah separately foretells warfare and ruin at Rabbah.
Jeremiah calls Judah not to oppress foreigners, orphans, and widows; Ezekiel later condemns Jerusalem for abusing those same vulnerable people.
Ezekiel condemns sexual relations with a sister; Leviticus explicitly forbids relations between a man and his sister, whether sharing father or mother.
Ezekiel rebukes priests for failing to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean; his later vision commands priests to teach those distinctions.
Leviticus directs Israel to distinguish clean from unclean animals; Ezekiel rebukes priests for neglecting the broader distinction between clean and unclean.
Both allegories of Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness describe enemies stripping her naked as a humiliating consequence of judgment.
Both charges say God was cast behind the people’s backs: the earlier warning addresses Jeroboam’s idolatry, while Ezekiel accuses Jerusalem of forgetting God.
Both prophets call a city a “bloody city,” but Ezekiel condemns Jerusalem while Nahum condemns Nineveh.
Ezekiel first places Rabbah of Ammon on the Babylonian king’s possible invasion route, then foretells that Rabbah will become a pasture for camels.
Ezekiel condemns Edom for taking revenge on Judah, while Jeremiah also foretells calamity for Edom, naming Teman and Dedan within the judgment.
Both chapters describe the shock caused by Tyre’s fall: the islands tremble in chapter 26, while the districts shake at the cries of her sailors in chapter 27.
Persia appears among Tyre’s hired fighters and later among the forces gathered with Gog; these are different military settings.
Genesis lists Javan, Tubal, and Meshech among Japheth’s sons; Ezekiel names the same three as peoples trading people and bronze with Tyre.
Ezekiel names Togarmah as a trading partner of Tyre and later as a northern contingent in Gog’s army; these are different roles and settings.
Genesis identifies Togarmah as a son of Gomer; Ezekiel names the house of Togarmah as a supplier of horses and mules to Tyre.
Ezekiel describes Kedar’s princes trading sheep and goats with Tyre; Isaiah later pictures Kedar’s flocks brought to honor the LORD in Zion.
Ezekiel’s earlier oracle says Tyre’s fall will make the islands tremble; his lament describes the surrounding shores shaking at the cries of her sailors.
Mourners for Tyre cast dust on their heads and sit in grief; Lamentations depicts Zion’s elders sitting on the ground with dust on their heads after Jerusalem’s fall.
The “terrible of the nations” draw swords against Tyre’s ruler and, in a separate judgment on Egypt, accompany Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign.
Genesis places the first man in Eden; Ezekiel uses “Eden the garden of God” within a figurative lament addressed to the king of Tyre, not a second account of Adam.
Both prophecies say Egyptians will be scattered among the nations as part of Egypt’s judgment; chapter 29 also specifies forty years of desolation.
Both oracles portray Egypt’s cities as desolate among devastated countries; chapter 29 adds a specified forty-year period and dispersion of the Egyptians.
Ezekiel foretells Egyptians returning to Pathros after exile; the next chapter names Pathros among Egyptian regions that will first face devastation.
Jeremiah also foretells Nebuchadnezzar entering Egypt and destroying its temples; Ezekiel specifically says Egypt will become the payment for his campaign against Tyre.
Both prophecies describe Egypt and its cities left desolate among devastated nations; Ezekiel 29 also specifies forty years of scattering.
Ezekiel repeats that God will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar: chapter 29 calls its spoil his army’s wages, while chapter 30 describes the destruction he will bring.
Pathros is marked for devastation in this judgment on Egyptian cities, yet the earlier oracle names Pathros as the land to which displaced Egyptians will later return.
The image of the proud ruler going down to the pit is developed in Ezekiel 32, where Egypt and other defeated nations are pictured among the dead.
Ezekiel 31 says Pharaoh will lie with the uncircumcised slain; chapter 32 expands that picture by naming the other fallen nations in the pit.
Both oracles place Egypt among those going down to the pit; Ezekiel 31 uses the downfall of a lofty tree, whereas chapter 32 mourns Egypt’s multitude.
Genesis names Tubal and Meshech among Japheth’s sons; Ezekiel uses these names for peoples pictured among the nations brought down in judgment, without equating them with individual ancestors.
God repeats Ezekiel’s appointment as Israel’s watchman: both passages require him to pass on God’s warnings and distinguish the hearers’ responsibility from his own.
God again promises to gather scattered Israel from the nations; Ezekiel 34 adds that he will shepherd them on their own land and mountains.
Jeremiah promises to bring Israel home from distant lands, including the vulnerable; Ezekiel portrays the same promised gathering as a shepherd bringing his flock home.
Ezekiel promises to break Israel’s oppressive yoke, deliberately recalling God’s statement that he broke their yoke when bringing them out of Egypt.
The promise of fruitful trees and productive land repeats the covenant blessing in Leviticus, which also promises rain in its season.
Both restoration promises say Israel will no longer bear the shame or reproach of surrounding nations; Ezekiel 34 also promises an end to hunger.
Ezekiel first addresses Israel’s mountains with a warning of the sword against their high places; here he addresses those same mountains with hope after foreign desolation.
Ezekiel 34 promises that restored Israel will no longer bear the nations’ shame; this oracle repeats that relief while speaking directly to the land.
Ezekiel repeats God’s promise to replace a stony heart with a heart of flesh and give a new spirit so his people will obey his commands.
Both restoration oracles say Israel will remember its former sins and loathe those deeds, showing repentance alongside God’s promised return of the people.
Both prophecies compare the renewal of ruined land to Eden: Isaiah promises comfort for Zion’s wilderness, and Ezekiel foresees rebuilt, inhabited cities.
Paul applies God’s promise to dwell among his people to believers as God’s temple, echoing Ezekiel’s covenant words, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”
Ezekiel 39 resumes the oracle introduced in chapter 38, again naming Gog as the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal and declaring God’s opposition to him.
Genesis lists Magog, Tubal, and Meshech among Japheth’s sons; Ezekiel uses these names in describing the land and peoples associated with Gog, without identifying Gog as a person in that genealogy.
The command to prophesy against Gog in chapter 39 repeats the opening of chapter 38, including God’s opposition to Gog, ruler associated with Meshech and Tubal.
Both instructions require Ezekiel to look, listen, and pay close attention to what is shown or said concerning the temple, so that its details are faithfully conveyed.
The east-facing gate measured at the start of the temple vision appears again when Ezekiel is brought to an east-facing gate to see God’s glory returning.
Ezekiel 40 describes the east-facing gateway of the visionary complex; chapter 44 returns to the outward east gate and finds it closed, explaining that God entered by it.
First Kings records Solomon appointing Zadok priest in place of Abiathar; Ezekiel later singles out the sons of Zadok for priestly service at the altar.
Both passages reserve close altar ministry for priests descended from Zadok; chapter 43 specifically directs them to receive the bullock for the altar’s sin offering.
Ezekiel 40 identifies the sons of Zadok as priests entrusted with the altar; chapter 44 explains their continuing privilege to approach God because they kept charge of the sanctuary.
Solomon’s temple is described as sixty cubits long and twenty wide, while Ezekiel measures a forty-by-twenty-cubit temple room; these are different plans, not identical dimensions.
Both regulations require priests to leave their holy ministry garments in designated chambers and put on other clothing before entering the outer court among the people.
The eastward gate measured in Ezekiel 40 provides architectural context for the eastward approach in chapter 43, where the glory of Israel’s God returns.
Ezekiel sees God’s glory enter from the east; in the next vision scene, the outward east-facing gate is closed because the Lord God of Israel has entered by it.
The priests descended from Zadok are entrusted with the altar in Ezekiel 40; chapter 43 assigns those priests the first sin offering during the altar’s dedication.
The altar ordinance assigns the sin offering to priests descended from Zadok; the following chapter explains that these priests may approach God because they remained faithful when others strayed.
Ezekiel returns to the outward east-facing gate after seeing God’s glory enter by the east; the gate is now shut because the Lord has entered through it.
Both passages distinguish the faithful sons of Zadok from Levites who went astray; chapter 44 grants them ministry near God, and chapter 48 assigns them a consecrated land portion.

Both instructions guard the holiness of the outer court: priests change out of their ministering garments before meeting people, while offerings are cooked in designated chambers rather than carried outside.
Ezekiel condemns earlier priests for failing to distinguish holy from profane and clean from unclean; the future priests are expressly commanded to teach those distinctions.
Ezekiel first requires a holy offering of land when Israel’s inheritance is divided; the closing land description confirms that the tribal territories are allotted as inheritances.
Both sanctuary-cleansing instructions apply blood from a sin offering to the altar’s corners; chapter 45 also names the doorposts of the house and inner-court gate.
The prince’s festival grain offering of an ephah per bull or ram with a hin of oil per ephah reappears in the instructions for Sabbath and new-moon offerings; the occasions differ.
The Sabbath grain-offering rule repeats the ephah for a ram and hin of oil per ephah specified for the prince’s festival offerings; the two commands concern different occasions.
Chapter 44 forbids priests from bringing their holy garments into the outer court; chapter 46 similarly confines preparation of holy offerings to priestly chambers to avoid sanctifying the people.
Both boundary descriptions locate Zedad near the northern edge of the promised land; Numbers approaches it from the entrance of Hamath, while Ezekiel begins from the great sea by Hethlon.
The southern border is repeated almost word for word: from Tamar by the waters of strife at Kadesh to the river or valley leading toward the great sea.
Ezekiel identifies Zadok’s descendants as the priests entrusted with the altar; the later allotment reserves a holy land portion for those same faithful priests.
Both descriptions trace the southern border through Tamar and the waters of strife at Kadesh toward the great sea; chapter 47 goes on to describe the western border.
Daniel places Nebuchadnezzar’s siege of Jerusalem in Jehoiakim’s third year; Chronicles also recounts Nebuchadnezzar taking Jehoiakim and temple vessels toward Babylon, without giving that same year.
Both passages place Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign against Judah during Jehoiakim’s reign; Kings adds that Jehoiakim served him for three years before rebelling.
Both accounts say Nebuchadnezzar took vessels from the Lord’s house to Babylon and placed them in a pagan temple; Daniel names the destination as Shinar.
The three Judean youths renamed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in chapter 1 are later appointed by Nebuchadnezzar to govern affairs in Babylon province.
Daniel is given the Babylonian name Belteshazzar in chapter 1; Nebuchadnezzar later identifies him by both names and says that the name reflects the king’s god.
God gives Daniel exceptional understanding in visions and dreams; Ezekiel’s oracle ironically compares the proud prince of Tyre with Daniel’s renowned wisdom, without proving the king was wiser.
Daniel 1 says he continued until the first year of Cyrus; chapter 10 dates another revelation to Cyrus’s third year, showing Daniel still received visions later.
Daniel 1 places his service as continuing into Cyrus’s first year; Daniel 6 confirms that he prospered under both Darius and Cyrus.
Both Babylon’s king and Egypt’s Pharaoh are troubled by dreams they want explained; Pharaoh summons Joseph, while Nebuchadnezzar demands an interpretation from his wise men.
Daniel’s ability to understand visions and dreams is explicitly attributed to God in chapter 1; chapter 2 shows God revealing Nebuchadnezzar’s secret to him in a night vision.
Chapter 1 records Daniel receiving the name Belteshazzar; Nebuchadnezzar uses that same name when asking him to reveal and interpret his dream.
The three men Daniel secured government posts for in Babylon province are later accused of refusing to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s image and face the fiery furnace.
The officials accuse Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego of defying the image decree while acknowledging that the king had previously appointed them over Babylon province.
Nebuchadnezzar’s praise closely repeats the psalm’s declaration that God’s kingdom lasts forever and his dominion endures through every generation.
Nebuchadnezzar calls Daniel Belteshazzar and connects the name with his own god; the earlier account records when the Babylonian name was assigned.
Nebuchadnezzar identifies Daniel as master of the magicians and capable of interpreting dreams; the queen later recalls that same standing and ability to Belshazzar.
The watcher’s decree that Nebuchadnezzar would live among beasts and be wet with dew is recalled when Daniel later describes the king’s actual humiliation to Belshazzar.
The queen recalls Daniel’s exceptional spirit and appointment over Babylon’s wise men; Nebuchadnezzar’s own words show him relying on Daniel because other interpreters failed.
The queen names Daniel as Belteshazzar while recalling his skill at explaining mysteries; chapter 1 records the Babylonian name first given to him.
Daniel’s excellent spirit and wisdom are remembered before Belshazzar; under Darius he is promoted above other officials for that same excellent spirit.
Daniel announces that Babylon will pass to the Medes and Persians; Isaiah had earlier predicted that God would stir up the Medes against Babylon.
Darius the Median takes Babylon’s kingdom at the end of chapter 5; chapter 6 immediately describes how he organized its government under 120 princes.
Daniel says Darius the Median received Babylon’s kingdom after Belshazzar’s death; chapter 9 identifies Darius as a Mede and describes his first year as king over the Chaldeans.
The queen praises Daniel’s excellent spirit and interpretive wisdom under Belshazzar; Darius later prefers him above other officials because of that same excellent spirit.
Both accounts describe royal decrees under the law of the Medes and Persians as unalterable, though Daniel concerns a ban on petitions and Esther concerns Vashti’s removal.
Daniel 6 records his prosperity under Darius and Cyrus, while the earlier account says he continued in service into Cyrus’s first year; both trace his service into the Persian period.
When questioned by the high priest, Jesus identifies himself as the Son of man and uses Daniel’s distinctive image of coming with the clouds of heaven; Mark also mentions the right hand of power.
Jesus describes the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and glory, drawing on the imagery of Daniel’s heavenly figure who receives everlasting dominion.
Jesus tells the high priest that he will see the Son of man coming in heaven’s clouds, echoing Daniel’s vision; Jesus also speaks of sitting at the right hand of power.
Daniel’s vision places him at Shushan in Elam; Esther later identifies Shushan as the palace where Ahasuerus reigned. These are distinct settings involving the same named royal center.
Daniel sees himself at Shushan by the Ulai in a vision, while Nehemiah later reports being at Shushan the palace; both name the same royal location in different periods.
Gabriel is named as the one commanded to explain Daniel’s vision; in Luke he identifies himself to Zacharias as the angel sent to announce John’s birth. These are separate appearances.
Gabriel, named in Daniel as the interpreter of a vision, is later sent by God to Nazareth to announce Jesus’ birth to Mary; the messages and recipients are different.
Daniel expressly says he learned from Jeremiah’s writings that Jerusalem’s desolations would last seventy years; Jeremiah had foretold seventy years of Babylonian domination and desolation.
Daniel identifies the visiting Gabriel as the one seen in his earlier vision; Daniel 8 names Gabriel when he is told to make Daniel understand that vision.
Gabriel comes to Daniel while he prays and offers understanding; in Luke Gabriel identifies himself as the angel sent from God with a message for Zacharias. The encounters are distinct.
Daniel 1 says his service continued to Cyrus’s first year, while this vision is dated to Cyrus’s third year; the later date shows Daniel still receiving revelations after the earlier milestone.
Daniel is called Belteshazzar when receiving this revelation under Cyrus; chapter 1 recounts the Babylonian official giving him that name.

Daniel first sees a man clothed in linen by the Hiddekel; chapter 12 again describes a linen-clothed man above a river, now answering when the predicted events will end. The text does not explicitly identify the figure.
In two separate visions Daniel falls into a deep sleep with his face to the ground, then is touched and raised; the strikingly repeated sequence connects his experiences.
Michael appears as a chief prince aiding the heavenly messenger in chapter 10 and as the great prince standing for Daniel’s people during future trouble in chapter 12.
Michael helps the messenger opposed by the prince of Persia; Jude names Michael as the archangel in a separate dispute concerning Moses’ body. The events should not be conflated.

Michael aids the messenger amid conflict involving Persia in Daniel; Revelation describes Michael and his angels fighting the dragon. Both depict Michael in heavenly conflict, but not the same battle.

The messenger predicts the arrival of the prince of Grecia after conflict involving Persia; Daniel’s earlier vision explicitly identifies the goat as the king of Grecia, joining the visions’ Greek focus.
The speaker recalls strengthening Darius the Mede in his first year; Daniel 9 dates Daniel’s study of Jeremiah and prayer to the first year of Darius, described as of Median descent.

Both prophecies unusually mention ships coming from Chittim, but Numbers depicts an attack on Asshur and Eber while Daniel describes ships opposing a king and prompting his withdrawal; the events are not explicitly equated.
Daniel 12 repeats the removal of the daily sacrifice and setting up of the desolating abomination from chapter 11, then specifies a period of 1,290 days.
Daniel predicts the sanctuary’s defilement, removal of the daily sacrifice and an abomination that makes desolate; Jesus explicitly cites Daniel’s abomination of desolation in warning his listeners.
Daniel 10 calls Michael “your prince,” and Daniel 12 identifies him more fully as the great prince standing for Daniel’s people during a time of trouble.

Daniel depicts Michael standing for his people during a time of trouble; Revelation depicts Michael leading angels against the dragon. Both name him in a heavenly conflict setting without equating the events.
Daniel says the dead will awaken, some to everlasting life and others to shame; Jesus similarly distinguishes a resurrection of life from a resurrection of damnation.
Daniel is told to seal the words until the time of the end; an earlier vision likewise tells him to shut up a vision because it concerns many days ahead.
Daniel sees a linen-clothed man by the river in chapter 10; chapter 12 again places a man clothed in linen above the river and records a question about when the wonders will end.
The removal of the daily sacrifice and establishment of the desolating abomination repeat the wording of Daniel 11; chapter 12 adds a specified span of 1,290 days.
Paul quotes Hosea's promise that those once called 'not my people' will be called children of the living God.
Peter applies Hosea’s words about those once “not my people” receiving mercy and becoming God’s people to the believers he addresses.
Paul cites Hosea's promise that God will call those who were not his people his people, applying it in his discussion of God's calling.

Hosea says Israel will return and seek the Lord and David their king; Jeremiah likewise foresees Israel and Judah returning together to seek the Lord and renew their covenant. Jeremiah does not mention David here.
Hosea condemns sacrifices and incense on hills and beneath leafy trees; Ezekiel likewise identifies high places and trees where Israel offered incense to idols, adding a judgment scene.
Hosea forbids going to Gilgal amid Israel’s unfaithfulness; later he specifically describes bull sacrifices and altars at Gilgal, showing the practices behind that warning.
Hosea warns Judah not to join Israel at Gilgal; later he identifies Gilgal as a center of Israel’s wickedness and a reason for expulsion.
Hosea rebukes Ephraim for turning to the Assyrian king Jareb for healing; later he says Israel’s calf will be carried to Assyria as a present to Jareb, bringing shame rather than help.
Jesus quotes Hosea's declaration that God desires mercy rather than sacrifice when defending his disciples against criticism.
Jesus quotes Hosea's call for mercy rather than sacrifice when explaining why he eats with publicans and sinners.
Hosea likens Israel’s failure to return to God to a deceitful bow; the psalm uses the same distinctive image of Israel turning aside and acting unfaithfully like their fathers.
Hosea condemns the calf made by Israel and associated with Samaria; later he describes the people mourning the calves of Bethaven when their glory is taken away.
Hosea twice recalls Israel’s sin in the days of Gibeah: chapter 9 calls it deep corruption, and chapter 10 says the people have sinned since those days.
Hosea invokes the notorious corruption at Gibeah; Judges recounts the outrage committed there against a Levite’s concubine. The cited account provides historical context for Hosea’s warning.
Both prophets condemn worship associated with Gilgal: Hosea calls it a source of Israel’s wickedness, while Amos warns the people not to seek Gilgal because it will go into captivity.
Hosea identifies Gilgal as a center of wickedness, then specifies that people sacrificed bulls and built numerous altars there. The later verse gives substance to the earlier charge.
Hosea warns Judah not to go to Gilgal, a place associated with Israel’s unfaithful worship; later he says Israel’s wickedness in Gilgal brings judgment and expulsion.
Jesus echoes Hosea's words about people calling on mountains and hills to cover them while warning of coming suffering.
Matthew applies Hosea's words about God calling his son out of Egypt, originally spoken about Israel, to Jesus' return from Egypt.
Hosea 4 warns against visiting Gilgal; Hosea 12 identifies sacrifices of bulls and many altars at Gilgal as part of the condemned practice.
Paul draws on Hosea's words addressing death and the grave while proclaiming victory over death through Christ; his wording differs from Hosea's KJV text.
Joel repeats the call to consecrate a fast and gather a solemn assembly, expanding the invitation in chapter 2 to include elders, children, and newlyweds.
Joel and Isaiah use nearly identical words to announce that the day of the LORD is near and will come as destruction from the Almighty; Isaiah develops the warning of wrath.
Peter identifies the Pentecost outpouring of the Spirit as Joel’s prophecy that God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, followed by prophecy, dreams, and visions.
Peter quotes Joel's promise that God will pour out his Spirit even on male and female servants when explaining the events of Pentecost.
Peter repeats Joel's prophecy of wonders involving blood, fire, and smoke while explaining the outpouring of the Spirit.
Peter quotes Joel's warning that the sun will darken and the moon turn to blood before the day of the Lord.
Peter quotes Joel's promise that whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved as part of his Pentecost sermon.
Paul directly quotes Joel's promise that whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved in his teaching about calling on the Lord.
Joel anticipates the LORD restoring Judah and Jerusalem from captivity; Jeremiah explicitly promises to restore Israel and Judah to the land given to their fathers.

Joel repeats almost word for word the darkening of the sun and moon and the stars withdrawing their light. Chapter 2 adds an earthquake and trembling heavens; chapter 3 places the signs near the day of the LORD.

Amos opens with Joel’s distinctive image of the LORD roaring from Zion and speaking from Jerusalem. Amos emphasizes mourning in the land, while Joel describes shaking heavens and refuge for God’s people.
Amos dates his prophecy during the reign of Uzziah king of Judah; Chronicles records Uzziah’s accession and reign. Chronicles does not record the earthquake Amos mentions.
Amos dates his words to two years before an earthquake during Uzziah’s reign; Zechariah later recalls an earthquake in Uzziah’s days as a remembered example of flight.
Amos repeats Joel’s distinctive description of the LORD roaring from Zion and speaking from Jerusalem, applying it at the opening of his warnings concerning the nations.
Amos predicts that fire will consume the palaces of Benhadad in Damascus; Jeremiah repeats this unusually specific combination of Damascus, fire, and Benhadad’s palaces.
Amos says the people of Syria will be carried captive to Kir; Kings records Assyria’s capture of Damascus and the deportation of its people to Kir, naming the destination explicitly.

Amos first says Syria’s people will go into captivity to Kir; later the LORD recalls bringing the Syrians from Kir. The two statements use the same place in opposite movements and must not be treated as the same journey.
Amos condemns Gaza for handing captives over to Edom and predicts fire against it; Zephaniah also foretells Gaza’s desolation but provides a different setting and outcome for the Philistine coast.
Amos condemns Edom for pursuing his brother without mercy; Ezekiel condemns Edom for taking vengeance against Judah. Both identify hostility toward related Israelites as grounds for judgment.
Amos condemns Edom for pursuing his brother with the sword; Joel likewise predicts Edom’s desolation for violence against Judah and the shedding of innocent blood.

Moses calls Israel Edom’s brother and recounts Edom’s armed refusal to allow passage. Amos later condemns Edom’s continued violence against his brother, but the passages do not identify one identical incident.
Amos predicts fire upon Moab’s palaces at Kerioth; Jeremiah explicitly says Kerioth is taken in his separate prophecy of Moab’s fall. Both name the same Moabite city in judgment.
Amos invites witnesses to see oppression in Samaria; in the next chapter he directly accuses wealthy women on Samaria’s mountain of oppressing the poor and crushing the needy.
Amos warns that the LORD will punish Israel’s altars at Bethel; Kings later records Josiah destroying the altar and high place at Bethel established by Jeroboam.
Amos ironically invites Israel to continue transgressing at Bethel and Gilgal through its offerings; Hosea warns Judah not to join Israel’s corrupt worship at Gilgal or Bethaven.
Amos compares God’s past judgments on Israel to his overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, whose destruction Genesis describes.

Amos compares the overthrow suffered by parts of Israel with God’s overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah; Isaiah uses the same destruction as an image of Babylon’s future judgment. The subjects and settings differ.
Stephen quotes Amos' rebuke of Israel's idolatry in the wilderness, recalling the worship of false gods after the exodus.
Amos warns comfortable leaders who trust in Samaria; earlier he condemned the wealthy in Samaria for oppressing the poor.
Amos points to Hamath as a warning to Israel; the Assyrian spokesman later invokes Hamath’s inability to resist Assyria, in a different historical setting.
Amos names Calneh among cities Israel should examine; Genesis identifies Calneh as one of the cities at the beginning of Nimrod’s kingdom.
In the plumbline vision God says he will no longer pass by Israel; he repeats that warning in the vision of the summer fruit.
Amaziah calls Bethel the king’s sanctuary; Kings records Jeroboam’s altar, calf worship, and appointed priests at Bethel.
Amos says he was a herdsman before God called him to prophesy; the book’s opening likewise identifies him among the herdsmen of Tekoa.
God’s warning in the summer-fruit vision that he will no longer pass by Israel repeats his declaration in the earlier plumbline vision.
Amos condemns merchants who would buy the needy for silver and shoes, repeating his earlier charge that Israel sold the righteous and the poor for these prices.
Amos repeats the image of the land rising and sinking like Egypt’s flood, linking his warning of judgment to God’s power over the land.
Amos condemns those who swear by false worship associated with Samaria and Beersheba; earlier he warned Israel not to seek Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba instead of the LORD.
James cites Amos' promise to restore David's fallen dwelling when discussing Gentiles turning to God; Acts follows wording that differs from Amos in the KJV.
Obadiah announces judgment against Edom; Amos gives a specific reason for Edom’s punishment: violence against his brother and relentless anger.
Obadiah’s call to rise against Edom is reinforced by Ezekiel’s prophecy of Edom’s punishment for taking vengeance against Judah.
Obadiah announces judgment against Edom; Joel likewise foretells Edom’s desolation because of violence against the people of Judah.
Obadiah and Jeremiah both rebuke Edom’s pride in its high rocky strongholds and warn that its apparent security cannot prevent its downfall.
Obadiah says Esau’s hidden treasures will be searched out; Jeremiah likewise says God will uncover Esau’s secret places so he cannot hide.
Obadiah foretells the defeat of Teman’s warriors within Edom; Ezekiel also predicts Edom’s devastation reaching Teman.
Kings identifies Jonah son of Amittai as the prophet whose word concerned Israel’s restored border; Jonah opens by naming the same prophet before his mission to Nineveh.
Jonah is sent to Nineveh, the city whose early building Genesis records; the passages describe the same place in different periods.
God first commands Jonah to warn wicked Nineveh; at the book’s close he explains his concern for the many people and animals living there.
Jonah is sent to warn wicked Nineveh, while Nahum later introduces an oracle of judgment against that same city; these are distinct prophetic messages.
Jesus explicitly compares Jonah’s three days and three nights in the great fish with the Son of man’s three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
After the LORD prepared a fish to swallow Jonah, he commanded that same fish to release him onto dry land.
The Ninevites believed God and repented at Jonah’s warning; Jesus later cites their repentance to rebuke his own generation.
Jonah admits he knew God was gracious, merciful, and slow to anger; Joel uses closely matching words to urge sinners to return to God.
Jonah appeals to God’s mercy and patience while protesting Nineveh’s reprieve; the psalm praises God with the same gracious-and-slow-to-anger description.
At the end of Jonah, God expresses compassion for the Nineveh he had originally commanded Jonah to confront because of its wickedness.
Micah and Hosea both date their ministries to Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, while Hosea also names Uzziah and an Israelite king.
Micah and Isaiah both name Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah among the kings of Judah during their ministries, showing their overlapping periods.
Micah dates his ministry partly to Hezekiah’s reign; Jeremiah records elders recalling Micah the Morasthite prophesying during Hezekiah’s reign.
Micah identifies Samaria as a center of Israel’s transgression; Amos specifically condemns oaths associated with Samaria’s false worship.
Micah’s lament repeats David’s distinctive words about not announcing disaster in Gath; David spoke of Saul and Jonathan’s deaths, while Micah laments Judah’s coming distress.
Jeremiah records elders quoting Micah’s warning that Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become heaps, in a debate over Jeremiah’s fate.
Micah and Isaiah use nearly identical words to picture many nations going up to the LORD’s house at Zion to learn his ways.
Micah and Isaiah both foresee the LORD judging among nations and their swords and spears being remade into farming tools, ending warfare.
Micah pictures each person safely sitting beneath a vine and fig tree; Kings uses that same image to describe Judah and Israel’s security during Solomon’s reign.
The chief priests and scribes quote Micah’s prophecy of a ruler from Bethlehem to answer Herod’s question about where the Christ would be born.
Micah recalls Balak king of Moab’s dealings with Balaam; Numbers records Balak sending for Balaam to curse the people who had come out of Egypt.
Micah calls Israel to remember the journey from Shittim to Gilgal; Joshua narrates their departure from Shittim, crossing the Jordan, and encampment at Gilgal.
Micah calls for justice, mercy, and humble walking with God; Moses likewise asks Israel what the LORD requires, including love, obedience, and walking in his ways.
Jesus describes divisions between fathers, mothers, children, and in-laws, closely echoing Micah’s picture of conflict within a household.
Jesus repeats Micah’s divisions between son and father, daughter and mother, and household members, applying the language to the cost of following him.
Nahum opens with a prophecy against Nineveh; Zephaniah specifically foretells Assyria’s destruction and Nineveh becoming desolate.
Nahum describes Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon withering before the LORD; Isaiah likewise names these three regions as the land languishes in judgment.
Nahum and Isaiah both proclaim good tidings and peace through a messenger whose feet are seen upon the mountains; Nahum addresses Judah, while Isaiah speaks of Zion.
Paul quotes Habakkuk's warning about an astonishing work that people would not believe, applying it as a warning to his listeners.
Paul quotes Habakkuk's statement that the just shall live by faith while contrasting faith with reliance on the law.
Hebrews draws on Habakkuk's statement about the just living by faith while encouraging perseverance.
Paul quotes Habakkuk's declaration that the just shall live by faith while introducing the righteousness of God revealed in the gospel.
Habakkuk pictures God coming from Teman and Paran in glory; Moses describes the LORD shining from Sinai, Seir, and Paran when blessing Israel.
Habakkuk says God gives him feet like a deer’s and enables him to walk on high places, repeating the striking picture found in David’s song in Samuel.
Habakkuk’s picture of deer-like feet and walking on high places closely repeats the wording of Psalm 18, where David praises God for strength and sure footing.
Zephaniah dates his words to Josiah’s reign; Chronicles records Josiah’s accession and his early efforts to seek God and remove idolatry.
Zephaniah places his prophecy in the reign of Josiah son of Amon; Jeremiah also began receiving the LORD’s word during Josiah’s reign, specifically in its thirteenth year.
Zephaniah warns that those under judgment will build houses without living in them and plant vineyards without enjoying their fruit; Isaiah reverses both losses in a promise of restored security.

Mark and Matthew repeat Jesus’ promise that whoever endures to the end will be saved; Matthew 24 places it among his predictions of deception, persecution, and increasing lawlessness.
Both accounts refer to Daniel’s abomination of desolation and direct people in Judaea to flee to the mountains; Mark says it stands where it ought not, while Matthew specifies the holy place.
Jesus says in both accounts that the days of extraordinary distress are shortened for the elect, otherwise no flesh would be saved; Mark adds that the Lord chose those elect.
Both accounts warn that false Christs and false prophets will perform signs and wonders to mislead, if possible, even the elect; Matthew calls the signs great, while Mark uses the word seduce.

Mark foretells a darkened sun and moon after tribulation, closely echoing Isaiah’s cosmic darkness language within Isaiah’s judgment oracle against Babylon; the passages do not explicitly identify one event.
Jesus predicts the Son of man coming in clouds with power and glory, then tells the high priest that he will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power and coming in heaven’s clouds.
Both Gospel accounts say the Son of man will be seen coming in the clouds with power and great glory; Matthew additionally describes the sign in heaven and mourning among the earth’s tribes.
Mark and Matthew say the Son of man sends angels to gather his elect from the four winds; Matthew mentions a great trumpet, while Mark describes the gathering as extending from earth to heaven.
Jesus uses the same fig-tree lesson in both accounts: new leaves show summer is near, just as the predicted signs indicate that the time is near, even at the doors.
Mark and Luke both record Jesus saying this generation will not pass until the foretold things take place; Luke says all will be fulfilled, while Mark says all these things will be done.
Jesus declares in both accounts that this generation will not pass before the things foretold occur; Mark says they will be done, while Matthew says they will be fulfilled.
Jesus states that no one knows the day or hour except the Father; Mark explicitly names the Son among those who do not know, while Matthew’s KJV wording names the angels but not the Son.
Mark and Matthew recount Judas arranging with the chief priests to betray Jesus; Matthew specifies thirty pieces of silver.
Mark and Matthew recount preparations for the Passover meal and Jesus' words over the bread and cup before his arrest.
Jesus quotes Zechariah's warning about striking the shepherd and scattering the sheep, applying it to his disciples' coming desertion.
Mark and Matthew recount Jesus praying at Gethsemane and finding his disciples asleep shortly before his arrest.
Mark and Matthew recount Judas arriving with an armed crowd, identifying Jesus with a kiss, and Jesus being arrested.
Mark and Matthew recount Peter denying Jesus three times and then weeping, although some narrative details differ.
Mark and Matthew both identify Simon of Cyrene as the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross on the way to Golgotha.
Mark and Matthew recount darkness during the crucifixion, Jesus' death, and the centurion's response, with differing details.
Jesus speaks the opening words of Psalm 22 from the cross, using the psalmist's cry of abandonment.
Mark and Matthew recount Joseph of Arimathea requesting Jesus' body and laying it in a tomb.
Mark and Matthew describe women visiting Jesus' tomb and receiving news that he has risen; they differ in details of the encounter.
Luke addresses his ordered account to Theophilus; Acts opens by addressing Theophilus again and referring back to a former account of what Jesus began to do and teach.

God tells Abraham that Sarah will bear a son named Isaac; an angel later tells Zacharias that Elisabeth will bear a son named John. Both are distinctive announcements naming sons before birth, but they concern different families and promises.
The angel foretells John’s ministry in the spirit and power of Elias; John later denies being Elias when questioned and identifies himself instead as the wilderness voice preparing the Lord’s way.
The angel says John will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elias; Jesus later identifies John as the expected Elias, linking John’s preparatory ministry to that promise.
The angel predicts John will come in the spirit and power of Elias; Jesus says Elias has already come unrecognized, and the disciples understand that he means John the Baptist.
Luke locates Mary in Nazareth of Galilee before Jesus’ birth; in John, some question whether the Christ could come from Galilee, even as others point to Bethlehem and David’s lineage.

Luke identifies Nazareth in Galilee as the city where Gabriel visits Mary; Matthew later records Joseph settling his family in Nazareth after their return from Egypt, supplying a later episode in the family’s story.
Gabriel tells Mary that she will bear a son and call him Jesus; an angel separately tells Joseph the same name and explains that he will save his people from their sins.
Zacharias speaks of bringing light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, echoing Psalm 107’s exact description of people sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

Luke uses almost the same words to describe John growing strong in spirit and Jesus growing strong; the two verses refer to different children, and Luke adds wisdom and God’s grace to Jesus’ description.
Luke describes Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, while Matthew begins his account with Jesus already born there and the visit of wise men later in the narrative.
Luke cites the law that every firstborn male is holy to the Lord when describing Jesus being presented at Jerusalem.
Luke quotes Isaiah's words about preparing the Lord's way, applying them to John the Baptist's ministry.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descending, and the heavenly voice; Luke places the scene amid people being baptized.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus being tempted by the devil in the wilderness, but arrange the final two temptations differently.
Jesus quotes Moses' teaching that life depends on more than bread when responding to the devil's temptation.
Jesus draws on Moses' instruction to fear and serve the LORD when rejecting the devil's demand for worship.
The devil quotes Psalm 91's promise of angelic protection in an attempt to persuade Jesus to throw himself down from the temple.
Jesus quotes Moses' command not to tempt the LORD when rejecting the devil's challenge at the temple.
Jesus reads Isaiah's words about the Spirit-anointed messenger bringing good news and liberty and applies the passage to his ministry; Luke's wording differs from Isaiah's KJV text.
Jesus reads Isaiah's proclamation of the acceptable year of the Lord but stops before Isaiah's announcement of the day of vengeance.

Luke describes Jesus teaching from Simon’s fishing boat immediately before the miraculous catch and the disciples’ departure to follow him; Matthew gives the related call of Simon and Andrew while they are fishing, without narrating Luke’s boat teaching or catch.
Simon reports fishing all night without a catch before Jesus directs a great catch in Luke; John recounts a separate post-resurrection night without fish followed by a catch at Jesus’ instruction.
Luke and Mark describe the leper’s request and Jesus’ immediate cleansing; Mark adds Jesus’ compassion and records that the man widely publicized the healing despite instructions.
Luke and Matthew recount a leper asking Jesus to make him clean if he wills; Jesus touches and cleanses him, and Matthew includes the instruction to show himself to the priest.
In the same healing of a paralyzed man, Jesus asks whether it is easier to declare sins forgiven or command the man to walk; Mark and Luke preserve this striking question almost word for word.
Luke names Levi, a tax collector whom Jesus tells to follow him; Matthew describes the corresponding call at the tax booth but names the man Matthew, a difference worth showing plainly.
After criticism for eating with publicans and sinners, Jesus compares the sick person’s need for a physician to the sinners he came to call; Mark includes both sayings together.

Jesus answers objections to eating with publicans and sinners by saying the sick need a physician; Matthew adds a call to understand mercy rather than sacrifice and repeats Jesus’ mission to call sinners.

Mark recounts the same question about why John’s and the Pharisees’ disciples fast while Jesus’ do not; Jesus likens his presence to a bridegroom at a wedding and foretells fasting after his departure.
Matthew records John’s disciples asking why Jesus’ disciples do not fast; Jesus answers that wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them, as in Luke.
Both accounts use a new patch on an old garment to illustrate the mismatch; Matthew says the patch worsens the tear, while Luke adds that cutting the patch damages the new garment.
Jesus recalls David receiving the consecrated bread from the priest when explaining his disciples' actions on the Sabbath.
Jesus applies Malachi's promise of a messenger preparing the way to John the Baptist; the quoted wording differs from Malachi's KJV text.
Luke and Matthew describe Jesus calming a storm after his disciples fear they will perish on the lake.
Luke and Mark recount Jesus raising Jairus's daughter and healing a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus healing a woman suffering from bleeding and raising the daughter of a synagogue ruler, with different details of the father's request.
Luke and Mark recount Jesus feeding about five thousand men with five loaves and two fish and gathering twelve baskets of leftovers.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus feeding about five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, followed by twelve baskets of leftovers.
Luke and Matthew record Peter identifying Jesus as the Christ, although Matthew includes further dialogue not recorded by Luke.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus' transfiguration, when Moses and Elijah appear and a voice speaks from the cloud; their accounts differ in details.
A lawyer repeats Moses' command to love God wholeheartedly while answering Jesus' question about what is written in the law.
The lawyer also repeats Leviticus' command to love one's neighbor as oneself when answering Jesus.
Jesus teaches his disciples to ask God for daily bread in both prayers; Luke says “day by day,” while Matthew says “this day.”
Both prayers ask God for forgiveness and deliverance from temptation; Luke speaks of sins and forgiving everyone indebted to us, while Matthew speaks of debts and debtors.
Jesus repeats the invitation to ask, seek, and knock, promising that requests are answered and doors opened; Luke places it after the story of a friend requesting bread.
Jesus uses the same two examples of a father refusing to give a stone instead of bread or a serpent instead of a fish; Luke adds a third example involving an egg and a scorpion.
Jesus argues in both passages that if imperfect parents give good gifts, the heavenly Father will give to those who ask; Luke specifies the Holy Spirit, while Matthew says good things.
Jesus answers the charge of casting out devils by Beelzebub with the same divided-kingdom and divided-house reasoning in both Gospels.
Jesus asks in both accounts how Satan’s kingdom could stand if Satan were divided against himself, answering the charge that his power came from Beelzebub.
Jesus states in both accounts that anyone not with him is against him, and whoever does not gather with him scatters; Matthew adds the word “abroad.”
Jesus gives the same warning about an unclean spirit leaving, returning to an orderly house, and bringing seven worse spirits; Matthew explicitly applies the illustration to that wicked generation.
Luke repeats Jesus’ candle illustration: light is placed on a candlestick for people entering to see it, not hidden under a covering. The sayings occur in different contexts within Luke.
Jesus uses the same picture of the eye as the body’s light: a single eye brings light, while an evil eye leaves the body in darkness.
Jesus rebukes Pharisees in both accounts for carefully tithing herbs while neglecting more important duties; Luke mentions judgment and love of God, while Matthew names judgment, mercy, and faith.
Luke records Jesus condemning religious leaders’ love of prominent synagogue seats and public greetings in two distinct warnings; the later passage specifically addresses scribes.
Jesus traces the shedding of righteous blood from Abel to Zacharias in both passages and says judgment will fall on this generation; Matthew identifies Zacharias as son of Barachias.
Luke repeats Jesus’ warning that what is hidden will become known, first after a lamp illustration and later in a warning against the Pharisees’ hypocrisy.
Both passages say hidden things will be revealed and words spoken privately made public; Matthew places the saying among Jesus’ instructions not to fear opponents.
Jesus reassures his followers in both passages that every hair of their heads is numbered and that they are worth more than many sparrows; the preceding verses give different sparrow prices.
Jesus promises to acknowledge those who confess him and reject those who deny him; Luke says this happens before God’s angels, while Matthew says before his Father in heaven.

Both accounts distinguish speaking against the Son of man from blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, which Jesus says will not be forgiven; Matthew expands the statement to this world and the world to come.
Jesus tells his disciples in both passages not to worry about food or clothing, reminding them that life is more than food; Matthew next points to birds as evidence of the Father’s care.
Jesus asks the identical question in both accounts: can anyone, by worrying, add even one cubit to his stature?
Jesus directs listeners to lilies that neither toil nor spin, yet outshine Solomon’s clothing; Matthew adds that God also clothes the short-lived grass.
Jesus tells his followers to seek God’s kingdom rather than be consumed by needs, promising that necessities will be added; Matthew explicitly adds seeking God’s righteousness first.
Jesus says exactly the same thing in both passages: the heart follows wherever one’s treasure is placed.
Jesus gives almost identical instructions in both Gospels to be ready because the Son of man comes at an hour people do not expect.
Jesus warns in both passages that his coming will bring division even within families; Luke calls it division, while Matthew speaks of a sword and names family relationships.
Jesus lists the conflicts of parents, children, and in-laws in language closely echoing Micah’s depiction of enemies within one’s own household.
The two Gospels give virtually identical kingdom parables: a woman hides leaven in three measures of meal until all the dough is leavened.

Jesus urges entry through the narrow gate in both teachings; Luke emphasizes the need to strive before the door is shut, while Matthew contrasts the narrow path to life with the broad way to destruction.
Jesus uses the Psalm’s exact command to “depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity” in a warning to those excluded from the kingdom; the Psalmist addresses evildoers after the Lord hears his prayer.

Both passages describe Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom while others are excluded with weeping and gnashing of teeth; Matthew speaks during the centurion encounter, while Luke answers a question about salvation.
Both accounts record Jesus lamenting Jerusalem’s rejection of the prophets, comparing his desired protection to a hen gathering her young, and foretelling the city’s desolate house.
Jesus repeats the Psalm’s blessing, “Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the LORD,” as words Jerusalem will one day say; the Psalm originally voices a welcome in the Lord’s name.
Both passages raise whether healing is lawful on the sabbath; Luke’s patient has dropsy and Jesus asks the question, while Matthew’s patient has a withered hand and others ask it to accuse him.
Jesus repeats the exact principle that the self-exalting will be humbled and the humble exalted; Luke 14 applies it to choosing a seat, while Luke 18 concludes the Pharisee-and-publican parable.
Jesus teaches in both passages that whoever exalts himself will be humbled and whoever humbles himself will be exalted; Matthew places the saying in his rebuke of status-seeking religious leaders.

Both banquet parables send servants into the highways to bring in additional guests after the first invitations fail; Luke describes a great supper, while Matthew describes a wedding feast with different details.

Jesus repeats the image of salt that has lost its taste and is fit only to be thrown away; Matthew addresses his disciples as salt of the earth, while Luke links the saying to the cost of discipleship.
The Pharisees object in both passages to Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners; Matthew describes a meal, while Luke 15 introduces parables spoken in response to a later complaint.
Jesus tells of a shepherd leaving ninety-nine sheep to seek one that is lost in both accounts; Luke emphasizes joy over repentance, while Matthew stresses the Father’s care for the little ones.
The father in Jesus’ parable runs to embrace and kiss his returning son, closely recalling Esau running to embrace and kiss Jacob; these are separate reconciliations, not the same event.
Jesus repeats almost word for word that no one can serve two masters: devotion to God and to mammon cannot be combined; Luke addresses stewardship while Matthew teaches about earthly treasures.
Jesus teaches in both passages that divorcing and remarrying involves adultery; Matthew explicitly gives an exception for fornication, while Luke states the warning without that qualification.
Both passages warn against causing little ones to stumble and say a millstone around the offender’s neck and drowning would be better; Mark explicitly calls them little ones who believe in Jesus.
Jesus compares faith to a mustard seed in both sayings; Luke describes commanding a sycamine tree into the sea, while Matthew describes moving a mountain after a failed healing.
Jesus says the kingdom of God is “within you” (also glossed “among you”) in Luke; in Matthew he says his casting out devils by God’s Spirit shows that the kingdom has come unto his hearers.
Jesus likens the Son of man’s appearing to lightning shining across the sky in both passages; Matthew specifies east to west, while Luke describes one part of heaven to another.
Jesus compares the days of the Son of man to Noah’s days in both Gospels; Matthew adds ordinary eating and marrying before the flood, while Luke goes on to compare Lot’s days.

Jesus teaches the same reversal concerning life in both passages; John contrasts loving life in this world with keeping it unto eternal life, while Luke places the saying after his warning about Lot’s wife.
Jesus repeats the paradox that those trying to save their lives lose them, but those losing their lives preserve them; Mark specifies losing life for Jesus and the gospel.
Jesus says in both passages that clinging to life leads to losing it, while losing life leads to finding it; Matthew adds the words “for my sake.”
Jesus describes one person taken and another left in both accounts; Luke first pictures two men in one bed, while Matthew gives people in a field and women grinding at a mill.
Jesus uses virtually the same saying about eagles gathering where a body or carcass lies; Luke answers the disciples’ question “Where?” while Matthew places it amid signs of his coming.
Luke and Matthew recount a wealthy man's question about eternal life and his sorrowful response to Jesus' instruction about possessions.
Jesus repeats the command to honor father and mother when responding to a ruler's question about eternal life.
Jesus repeats the command against killing when answering a ruler's question about eternal life.
Jesus repeats the command against adultery when answering a ruler's question about eternal life.
Jesus repeats the command against stealing when answering a ruler's question about eternal life.
Jesus repeats the command against bearing false witness when answering a ruler's question about eternal life.
Luke and Mark describe Jesus restoring sight to a blind beggar near Jericho; Luke introduces the encounter as Jesus approaches, while Mark places it as he leaves.
Luke and Matthew recount Jesus' entry into Jerusalem riding a young donkey and receiving the crowd's praise.
The crowd's praise at Jesus' entry echoes Psalm 118's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name, while Luke calls him the King.
Jesus describes the temple as a house of prayer, drawing on Isaiah's promise about God's house.
Jesus uses Jeremiah's expression 'den of robbers' to condemn how the temple is being treated.
Jesus quotes the psalm's image of the rejected stone becoming the chief cornerstone while confronting the religious leaders.
The Sadducees cite Moses' law about a surviving brother marrying his brother's widow in a question intended to challenge resurrection.
Jesus refers to God's words to Moses at the burning bush, naming Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as part of his answer about resurrection.
Jesus quotes David's words in Psalm 110 about the Lord addressing 'my Lord' and uses them to ask how the Christ can be David's son.
Luke and Mark describe the same poor widow putting two mites into the temple treasury; Mark adds that the two mites make a farthing.
Jesus declares in both accounts that the widow gave more than the wealthy because she contributed all she had to live on, while others gave from abundance.
Jesus predicts nation rising against nation and kingdom against kingdom in both discourses; Mark groups these conflicts with earthquakes and famine as the beginnings of sorrows.
Mark repeats Jesus’ warning that this generation will not pass until these things happen; Luke says “till all be fulfilled,” and each follows it by affirming that his words will endure.
Jesus says in both accounts that this generation will not pass before the announced events are fulfilled; both immediately affirm the lasting truth of his words.
Luke says Jesus taught by day in the temple before spending nights on the Mount of Olives; at his arrest in Matthew, Jesus recalls that he sat teaching daily in the temple without being seized.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's words about being numbered among transgressors and says the scripture must be fulfilled in him.
Luke and Matthew describe Jesus praying shortly before his arrest; Luke places the scene at the Mount of Olives, while Matthew names Gethsemane.
Luke and Matthew recount Judas arriving with a crowd to betray Jesus and the confrontation that follows, with different details.
Luke and John recount Peter's three denials of knowing Jesus during the events surrounding Jesus' arrest, though the settings and details vary.
Luke and Matthew recount Peter denying Jesus three times and later weeping; Matthew also records Peter's recollection of Jesus' prediction.
Luke and Matthew both identify Simon of Cyrene as the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross; Matthew's passage continues through the crucifixion.
Jesus echoes Hosea's words about people calling on mountains and hills in distress, although Luke reverses the order of 'fall' and 'cover' in the KJV.
Jesus uses the psalmist's words about committing his spirit into God's hands as he dies on the cross.
Luke and Matthew recount Joseph of Arimathea receiving Jesus' body and placing it in a tomb.
Luke and John describe the discovery that Jesus' tomb was empty; their accounts differ in which visitors and disciples they describe.
Luke and John recount the risen Jesus appearing among his gathered disciples, greeting them and showing evidence of his identity.
John the Baptist applies Isaiah's words about preparing the Lord's way to his own ministry as a voice crying in the wilderness.
After Jesus clears the temple, his disciples remember the psalm's words about zeal for God's house.
Jesus compares his coming lifting up to Moses lifting up the bronze serpent in the wilderness so those who looked to it might live.

John describes Jewish reluctance to deal with Samaritans; 2 Kings recounts Assyria resettling Samaria with peoples from several lands and describes their mixed worship, providing earlier regional history without claiming to explain every later attitude.

The Samaritan woman observes that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans; Peter later describes Jewish restrictions on associating with people of another nation and says God corrected his understanding.
The Samaritan woman is surprised that Jesus, a Jew, asks her for water; Matthew records Jesus earlier directing the Twelve not to enter Samaritan towns on that particular mission.
John returns to Cana and explicitly recalls Jesus turning water into wine there; the earlier passage recounts that wedding sign, distinct from the later healing of a nobleman’s son.
Jesus promises everlasting life to those who believe in both passages; John 5 adds hearing his word, believing the Father who sent him, escaping condemnation, and passing from death to life.
Jesus says in both discourses that his works bear witness to him; John 5 emphasizes that the Father assigned those works, while John 10 says he does them in the Father’s name.
John and Matthew recount Jesus feeding about five thousand men with five barley loaves and two fish, though Matthew does not specify the loaves were barley.
John and Matthew recount Jesus approaching the disciples' boat while walking on the sea; Matthew also describes Peter stepping onto the water.
The crowd cites Scripture about bread from heaven, recalling the manna given to Israel and the wording preserved in Psalm 78.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's promise that God's people will be taught by him while explaining who comes to Jesus.
John records a claim that the Messiah must come from David’s family and Bethlehem; Luke reports Joseph’s Davidic lineage and Jesus’ birth while they were in Bethlehem.
People questioning Jesus’ origin appeal to Scripture about Bethlehem; in Matthew, the chief priests and scribes answer Herod by quoting Micah’s Bethlehem ruler prophecy.

John’s crowd appeals to Scripture that the Messiah comes from David’s line and Bethlehem; Micah foretells a ruler for Israel coming from Bethlehem Ephratah, though the verse itself does not explicitly name David.
Some leaders ask rhetorically whether any rulers or Pharisees have believed in Jesus; John later reports that many chief rulers did believe but concealed it because they feared the Pharisees.

Nicodemus, previously identified as the man who visited Jesus by night, questions the council’s treatment of Jesus here; he later brings spices for Jesus’ burial, and John again recalls his night visit.

Leaders dismiss Galilee as a source of prophets, yet Matthew portrays Jesus ministering in Galilee and quotes Isaiah’s promise of a great light there; the prophecy concerns light, not a claim that every prophet must arise there.
Jesus repeats “I am the light of the world” in both passages; John 8 promises light of life to followers, while John 9 says it before giving sight to a man born blind.
Jesus calls himself “the light of the world” in John, while in Matthew he calls his disciples “the light of the world” and tells them not to hide their good works.
Jesus says the Father bears witness to him in John 8; John 5 first discusses the limits of his own testimony, then names John, his works, and the Father as witnesses.
Before healing the man born blind, Jesus again declares that he is the light of the world; John 8 expands the same claim with the promise that those who follow him will have the light of life.
Jesus quotes Psalm 82's words 'Ye are gods' in response to the charge of blasphemy; the psalm addresses those receiving God's judgment or word.
John first introduces Lazarus as Mary and Martha’s sick brother; after Jesus raises him, witnesses to that miracle speak about it as crowds gather to meet Jesus.
John introduces Lazarus while he is sick; after Jesus raises him, a crowd comes not only to see Jesus but also to see Lazarus alive.
John names Mary and Martha as Lazarus’s sisters in Bethany; Luke separately recounts Martha welcoming Jesus and Mary sitting at his feet, without naming Lazarus or the village.
John identifies Lazarus’s sister Mary by her anointing of Jesus and wiping his feet with her hair; the next chapter narrates that very act at Bethany.
John and Matthew describe Jesus' public entry into Jerusalem on a donkey amid the crowd's praise, though they supply different details.
The crowd welcoming Jesus uses Psalm 118's blessing on the one who comes in the Lord's name.
John draws on Zechariah's description of Zion's king arriving on a donkey and applies it to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem; the KJV wording differs.
John quotes Isaiah's question about who believed the report to explain the unbelief he describes despite Jesus' signs.
John uses Isaiah's warning about blinded eyes and hardened hearts to explain the unbelief he has described; his wording especially reflects Isaiah 6:10.
Jesus applies the psalm's description of betrayal by a trusted companion to the betrayal he is about to face.
Philip asks Jesus to show the Father after years of following him; John earlier recounts Jesus calling Philip, who then told Nathanael he had found the one foretold in Scripture.
Jesus tells Philip that the Father dwelling in him does the works; earlier Jesus said he did not speak on his own but spoke what the Father commanded him.
Jesus promises to answer requests made in his name; later he says his disciples will ask the Father in his name and that the Father himself loves them.
Jesus promises to do what his disciples ask in his name so that the Father is glorified; in Matthew he promises that believing prayer will receive an answer, without using the phrase “in my name.”
Jesus says the prince of this world is coming but has no claim on him; earlier he announced that the prince of this world would be cast out in the judgment of the world.
Jesus uses the psalms' words about being hated without cause when explaining the world's rejection of him; similar language also appears in Psalm 69:4.
Jesus says the prince of this world has been judged; earlier he declared that the prince of this world would be cast out as judgment came upon the world.
Jesus promises that the Father will grant requests made in his name; in Matthew he promises an answer to prayer offered in faith, without explicitly mentioning his name.
John and Luke recount Peter denying that he knew Jesus during the events surrounding Jesus' arrest, though they describe different details of the setting.
John quotes Psalm 22:18 as fulfilled when soldiers divide Jesus’ garments and cast lots for his seamless coat at the crucifixion.
John says Scripture was fulfilled when Jesus' legs were not broken; the Passover law forbids breaking the lamb's bones, though other scriptures contain similar wording.
John applies Zechariah's words about looking upon the one who was pierced to Jesus after his side was pierced; the KJV wording differs.
John and Luke recount the discovery of Jesus' empty tomb, but give different details about the visitors and what they saw.
John and Luke describe the risen Jesus appearing among his gathered disciples and showing that he was alive, with different details of the encounter.
John names the sons of Zebedee among the disciples at Jesus’ later resurrection appearance; Matthew identifies these brothers as James and John when Jesus first called them.

In both fishing accounts Peter and the others have caught nothing after a night’s work before a remarkable catch; Luke describes an earlier encounter, while John describes the risen Jesus at the shore.
Jesus addresses Peter as “Simon, son of Jonas” when commissioning him to feed his lambs; earlier he called him “Simon Barjona” after Peter confessed him as the Christ.
John again describes the disciple whom Jesus loved alongside Peter; earlier Mary Magdalene ran to Peter and that same unnamed disciple after finding the empty tomb.
Peter quotes Psalm 109 about another taking a person's office while explaining the need to replace Judas among the apostles.
Peter applies Psalm 69's words about a deserted dwelling to Judas when explaining his place among the apostles.
Peter quotes Joel's prophecy of the outpouring of God's Spirit and the coming day of the Lord, identifying the Pentecost events with Joel's words.
Peter repeats Joel's promise that God would pour out his Spirit on male and female servants as part of his explanation of Pentecost.
Peter repeats Joel's prophecy of wonders in heaven and signs on earth, including blood, fire, and smoke.
Peter repeats Joel's description of the sun turning dark and the moon to blood before the great day of the Lord.
Peter quotes Joel's promise that whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.
Peter quotes David's psalm about God's presence and not allowing his Holy One to see corruption, applying it to Jesus' resurrection.
Peter quotes David's words about the Lord inviting 'my Lord' to sit at his right hand while explaining Jesus' exaltation.
Peter quotes Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet from among the people and applies it to Jesus.
Peter warns of the consequence of refusing the promised prophet, drawing on Moses' warning that God would require an account of those who would not listen.
Peter recalls God's promise that all families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, a promise also stated in Genesis 12:3.
Peter refers to God's promise that blessing would come to all nations through Abraham's seed; Genesis 22:18 expresses that promise directly.
Peter applies the psalm's picture of the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone to Jesus, whom the leaders rejected.
The believers quote Psalm 2 about nations and rulers opposing the Lord and his anointed while praying after threats against them.
The captain of the temple appears among those confronting the apostles in Acts 4; in Acts 5 he is named again as the authorities puzzle over the apostles’ disappearance from prison.
Peter says Jesus was killed and hanged on a tree and that God raised him; Peter repeats both the death and resurrection in his later testimony to Cornelius.
Acts introduces Gamaliel as a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law who counsels the council; Paul later says he was educated at Gamaliel’s feet.
Philip is selected among the seven in Jerusalem; years later Acts explicitly calls Philip the evangelist “one of the seven” when Paul’s companions stay at his home.
Philip is chosen among the seven in Jerusalem; after believers are scattered, Philip preaches Christ in Samaria and many see healings and hear his message.
Stephen recounts God's instruction that Abraham leave his country and relatives, recalling God's call recorded in Genesis.
Stephen recalls God's prediction that Abraham's descendants would live in a foreign land and be oppressed before God judged their oppressors.
Stephen quotes God's instruction to Moses to remove his shoes because the ground where he stands is holy.
Stephen repeats Moses' promise of a prophet whom God would raise up from among Israel's people.
Stephen cites Amos' condemnation of Israel's wilderness idolatry while rebuking the council; the wording and names differ between Acts and the KJV of Amos.
Stephen quotes Isaiah's words describing heaven as God's throne and earth as his footstool while explaining that God is not confined to a building.
The Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah's description of one led like a sheep to slaughter; Philip uses the passage to preach Jesus to him.
Acts 22 retells Saul's encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, first narrated in Acts 9, with additional details in Paul's testimony.
Acts 26 retells Saul's encounter with Jesus on the Damascus road as Paul defends himself before Agrippa, adding details not given in Acts 9.
Paul's testimony in Acts 22 recounts the light from heaven, Jesus' words, and his resulting blindness during the Damascus-road encounter in Acts 9.
Peter recounts his visit to Cornelius and the Gentiles receiving the Holy Spirit when defending his actions to believers in Jerusalem.
Peter's explanation in Acts 11 retells the vision of the sheet containing animals that he received while praying in Joppa.
Peter recalls the Holy Spirit falling upon Cornelius's household while he was speaking, as first described in Acts 10.
Acts 11 records Peter explaining to believers in Jerusalem why he entered Cornelius's house and how God gave the Holy Spirit to Gentiles.
Peter retells the sheet-and-animals vision from Acts 10 while explaining why he visited Gentiles.
Peter retells how the Holy Spirit came upon Cornelius's household as he began speaking, referring back to the event in Acts 10.
Herod kills James, identified in Acts as John’s brother; Matthew earlier names James and John as Zebedee’s sons and describes Jesus calling them from their fishing boat.
Peter credits the Lord for sending an angel to rescue him from Herod’s prison; Daniel likewise says God sent his angel to protect him in the lions’ den, in a separate rescue.
Peter goes to the house of Mary, identified as John Mark’s mother; later Barnabas wants to take this same John Mark on another missionary journey, causing a disagreement with Paul.
After his release Peter asks believers to tell James; later James speaks in the Jerusalem council, showing his continuing leadership within the church.
Paul quotes Psalm 2's words, 'Thou art my Son,' as he proclaims God's fulfillment of the promise concerning Jesus.
