Peter repeats the command to be holy because God is holy, a command given to Israel in Leviticus.
Peter repeats the command to be holy because God is holy, as stated in this passage of Leviticus.
Peter quotes Isaiah's comparison of human life to withering grass and God's enduring word while speaking of the preached gospel.
Peter quotes Isaiah's promise of a chosen cornerstone in Zion and applies it to those who believe in Christ; Isaiah's KJV says 'shall not make haste,' while Peter says 'shall not be confounded.'
Peter quotes the psalm's rejected stone becoming the head of the corner and applies the image to Christ.
Peter uses Isaiah's description of the servant who committed no violence and had no deceit in his mouth to describe Jesus' sinlessness; Peter's wording focuses on deceit and sin.
Peter quotes Psalm 34's counsel to restrain evil speech, pursue peace, and trust the Lord's attention to the righteous.
Peter draws on Proverbs' contrast between the righteous and the wicked when asking about the fate of the ungodly; his KJV wording differs substantially from the proverb.
Peter quotes the proverb about God resisting the proud and giving grace to the humble while urging believers to submit to one another.
Peter recalls hearing the Father declare Jesus his beloved Son on the holy mountain; Matthew records that voice during Jesus’ transfiguration.
Peter quotes the proverb about a dog returning to its vomit as an image of people returning to wrongdoing; he adds a separate saying about a washed sow.
Peter looks forward to new heavens and a new earth according to God’s promise; Isaiah explicitly announces God’s creation of new heavens and a new earth.
John says Cain killed his brother because his works were evil; Genesis directly narrates Cain rising against Abel in the field and killing him.
John contrasts Cain’s evil deeds with Abel’s righteousness; Hebrews calls Abel righteous and says his sacrifice was offered by faith.
John cites Cain’s murder of his brother as an example of evil; Jude invokes “the way of Cain” in condemning corrupt teachers.
Both Jude and Peter cite the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah as a warning, explicitly describing those cities as an example of judgment.
Jude points to Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of judgment by fire; Genesis records the Lord raining brimstone and fire on those cities and overthrowing them.
Jude names Michael the archangel disputing with the devil over Moses’ body; Revelation describes Michael and his angels fighting the dragon, a separate conflict.
Jude warns against following Cain's way; John identifies Cain's murder of his brother as the result of his evil works.
Jude condemns those who pursue Balaam's error for reward; Peter likewise describes people who followed Balaam because he loved the wages of unrighteousness.
Jude condemns Balaam's error for reward, while Revelation describes the teaching of Balaam as leading Israel into idolatrous eating and sexual sin.
Jude identifies Enoch as the seventh from Adam; Genesis traces his place in Adam's family line and records that Enoch walked with God and was taken by God.
Jude names Enoch as the seventh from Adam and recounts his prophecy; Hebrews describes Enoch's faith and how God took him without his seeing death.
The 'Alpha and Omega' title from Revelation's opening returns in the new-creation vision, where the one speaking promises living water freely.
The Lord calls himself 'Alpha and Omega' and 'the beginning and the ending' at Revelation's opening; the title is repeated near the book's close with 'the first and the last.'
Revelation names Laodicea among the seven churches to receive John's book; Paul had earlier instructed believers to exchange and read letters with the church there.
Revelation uses Psalm 2's image of ruling with a rod of iron and shattering pottery in its promise concerning those who overcome.
John's six-winged living creatures cry 'Holy, holy, holy' before God's throne, echoing the six-winged seraphim and the same threefold praise in Isaiah's vision.
Revelation calls the one worthy to open the sealed book 'the Lion of the tribe of Juda'; Hebrews states that Jesus descended from Judah.
The sealed tribes include Simeon, Levi, and Issachar; Genesis lists these three among Leah's sons and thus identifies their ancestry.
In both throne-room scenes, praise is directed to God on the throne and to the Lamb; Revelation 7 focuses on the redeemed multitude's cry of salvation, while chapter 5 records universal praise.
Revelation repeats God's promise to wipe away every tear: chapter 7 addresses the multitude led by the Lamb, while chapter 21 describes the end of death and sorrow.
The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the Euphrates; the sixth vial later dries up the same river for kings from the east, but these are different judgments.
John eats a little book that tastes sweet as honey but makes his belly bitter; Ezekiel also eats a scroll sweet as honey before receiving a charge to speak God's words.
The heavenly announcement that the Lord and his Christ will reign for ever echoes Israel's song after the sea crossing: 'The LORD shall reign for ever and ever.'
Revelation describes the male child who will rule the nations with a rod of iron, drawing on Psalm 2's picture of the ruler breaking the nations with an iron rod.
Revelation shows Michael fighting in heaven; Daniel describes Michael as one of the chief princes who helped during resistance from the prince of Persia.
Michael fights the dragon in Revelation; Daniel calls Michael the great prince who stands for his people during a time of extraordinary trouble and deliverance.
Revelation depicts Michael leading angels against the dragon; Jude also names Michael in a dispute with the devil, but Jude's dispute concerns Moses' body and is a different event.
John sees Satan cast down from heaven after a heavenly battle; Jesus also speaks of seeing Satan fall from heaven like lightning, without identifying the visions as the same occasion.
The dragon cast out of heaven is explicitly called the Devil and Satan; later an angel seizes that same dragon and confines him to the bottomless pit for a thousand years.
The beast in Revelation is given a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; Daniel sees a little horn with a mouth speaking great things, a distinctive visionary parallel.
Revelation's beast is allowed to wage war on the saints and overcome them, matching Daniel's description of the horn making war with the saints and prevailing.

John sees the Lamb standing on mount Sion with 144,000 people; Hebrews speaks of believers coming to mount Sion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, but does not identify the groups or scenes as identical.
The angel's cry 'Babylon is fallen, is fallen' repeats Isaiah's distinctive announcement of Babylon's fall, applying the same wording in Revelation's later vision.
The sixth vial dries up the Euphrates to prepare a way for kings of the east; the earlier sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at that river, a distinct judgment.
A vial-bearing angel offers to show John the great harlot's judgment; later, an angel described in the same way offers to show him the bride, the Lamb's wife, forming a deliberate contrast.
Revelation 17 depicts the kings of the earth committing fornication with Babylon and people becoming drunk with its wine; chapter 18 repeats the charge and adds the merchants' wealth.
The woman called Babylon wears purple and scarlet with gold, precious stones, and pearls; the lament for Babylon's fall repeats those exact luxury materials.
Chapter 18 repeats the earlier angel's announcement that Babylon made the nations drink the wine of her fornication, while expanding on the kings' and merchants' involvement.
The statement that Babylon's kings committed fornication and nations drank her wine repeats the earlier description of the woman and her influence over the earth.
The merchants lament Babylon's loss of purple, scarlet, gold, precious stones, and pearls, echoing the earlier description of the woman's extravagant clothing.
The heavenly praise celebrates God avenging the blood of his servants upon Babylon, echoing Moses' song that God will avenge the blood of his servants.
John describes heavenly voices like many waters and mighty thunderings in both visions; chapter 19 announces God's reign, while chapter 14 also mentions harpers.
Revelation describes the rider ruling the nations with a rod of iron, echoing the royal rule over nations pictured in Psalm 2:9.
The rider in Revelation 19 rules the nations with a rod of iron; the earlier promise to the conqueror uses the same image and says authority is received from the Father.
Both visions identify the dragon as the old serpent, the Devil and Satan; chapter 12 shows him cast to earth, while chapter 20 describes his later binding.
John’s judgment scene echoes Daniel’s heavenly court: the books are opened before judgment, though the two visions differ in their surrounding details.
Revelation 21 repeats the promise from chapter 7 that God will wipe away every tear, adding that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will pass away.
The voice in both passages declares, “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end”; Revelation 22:13 adds “the first and the last.”
Both visions begin with one of the seven vial-bearing angels inviting John to see a woman; one reveals Babylon’s judgment, the other the Lamb’s bride, the holy Jerusalem.
John twice falls before an angel to worship, and twice the angel refuses, calls himself a fellowservant, and commands John to worship God.
Revelation 22:13 repeats the exact titles “Alpha and Omega” and “the beginning and the end” from 21:6, adding “the first and the last.”
Moses tells frightened Israel to stand still and see the LORD's salvation; centuries later Judah receives similar words in a different battle.
At Sinai a cloud covers the mountain as the LORD’s glory appears; Numbers later describes the cloud covering the tabernacle when the LORD’s glory appears during Korah’s rebellion.
Numbers provides for Joshua to seek God’s guidance through the priestly Urim; later Saul receives no answer from God, including by Urim, when facing the Philistines.
Joshua 13:33 repeats the reason stated here for Levi receiving no territorial allotment: the LORD God of Israel was the Levites' inheritance.
Joshua places the valley of Hinnom along Benjamin's boundary; Kings later locates Topheth in that valley, where Josiah stopped child sacrifice to Molech.
Joshua assigns Zelah to Benjamin; Samuel later identifies Zelah in Benjamin as the burial place of Saul and Jonathan.
Hebron, named among the cities of refuge, was also given to Aaron's descendants as a Levitical city.
Joshua recalls Balak summoning Balaam to curse Israel; Numbers narrates Balak's fear of Israel and the messengers he sent with that request.
Judges names several towns whose inhabitants Asher failed to expel; Joshua's allotment includes Achzib, Aphek, Rehob, and Sidon, though not every town in Judges appears in that list.
Gideon recalls that Ephraim captured and killed Oreb and Zeeb, the Midianite leaders whose deaths were reported after the battle.
The Nazirite law explains the vow of dedication and the ban on cutting hair; Samson is designated a Nazirite from the womb, unlike the ordinary time-limited vow.
Ruth begins the genealogy of Perez with his son Hezron; Chronicles also names Perez as Tamar and Judah's son and lists Hezron among his descendants.
Chronicles traces Samuel's ancestral family through Elkanah, Jeroham, and the line of Toah; 1 Samuel uses variant forms Elihu and Tohu in Samuel's ancestry.
Samuel told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal for his arrival and sacrifices; Saul later waited there but offered the sacrifice himself before Samuel arrived.
David took refuge at Engedi; Chronicles identifies Hazazontamar, where an enemy force gathered in Jehoshaphat's day, as Engedi.
Joshua lists Maon and Carmel among Judah's hill-country towns; Nabal lived in Maon and sheared his flocks in Carmel.
Joshua names Shunem among the towns of Issachar; the Philistines later camp there before their battle against Saul.
Jattir, whose inhabitants receive a share of David's recovered spoil, is listed among Judah's hill-country towns.
David sends a gift to Hormah, the town Judges says was named after Judah and Simeon destroyed Zephath.
Beeroth, home of Ishbosheth’s captains Baanah and Rechab, appears among the towns allotted to Benjamin in Joshua.
Joshua lists Giloh among Judah’s towns; it is the hometown from which Absalom summons David’s counselor Ahithophel.
Enrogel, where Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited to send word to David, also marks a point on Benjamin’s boundary in Joshua’s land description.
David buries Saul and Jonathan in Zelah, in Benjamin’s territory; Joshua lists Zelah among the cities allotted to Benjamin.
Enrogel appears both as the place where Jonathan and Ahimaaz waited to relay news during Absalom’s revolt and as the landmark beside Adonijah’s later sacrificial feast; these are different events.
The Philistine army gathers near Socoh and Azekah, towns Joshua lists among the settlements allotted to Judah.
Joshua lists Keilah among Judah's towns; Samuel later reports a Philistine attack on its threshing floors, which David moves to defend.
David hides in the wilderness of Ziph while Saul hunts him; Joshua identifies Ziph among Judah's towns, providing geographical context.
God reminds Jeroboam that he raised him to rule Israel; the later rebuke of Baasha uses similar words and explicitly condemns him for following Jeroboam's sin.
Ahijah foretells the cutting off of Jeroboam's household; Baasha later kills its remaining members, explicitly carrying out the prophetic judgment.
The judgment pronounced on Ahab's family repeats the distinctive threat once spoken against Jeroboam's family; these are judgments on different dynasties.
The later sentence against Ahab's house explicitly compares its destruction to the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha, connecting the three royal judgments.
Joshua lists Gibbethon in Dan's territorial allotment; Kings later describes it as a Philistine-held city under Israelite siege when Baasha killed Nadab.
God tells Baasha that he raised him to rule Israel, deliberately echoing the earlier words spoken to Jeroboam when God made him ruler.
God announces that Baasha's descendants will be cut off just as Jeroboam's were; the earlier prophecy describes the destruction of Jeroboam's house.

The warning that Ahab's male descendants would be cut off repeats the judgment previously pronounced against Jeroboam's house; the next verse explicitly compares Ahab's dynasty with Jeroboam's and Baasha's.
Joshua lists Shunem within Issachar's territory; Kings later places the hospitable Shunammite woman at Shunem, adding the town's tribal-geographical setting.

The sons of the prophets appear as a group receiving food from Elisha at Gilgal and later as a group asking him for larger living quarters. The passages show distinct activities of Elisha's prophetic community.

The judgment against Ahab's descendants uses the same dynastic-cutoff wording previously pronounced against Jeroboam's house. The following verse explicitly likens Ahab's house to Jeroboam's and Baasha's.
Chronicles credits Sherah with building Upper Bethhoron; Joshua names Upper Bethhoron in the eastern boundary description of Ephraim's inheritance.
Chronicles credits Sherah with building Lower Bethhoron; Joshua places Lower Bethhoron along the western side of Ephraim's inherited territory.
Azariah tells Asa that the LORD will be found by those who seek him and forsake those who forsake him, repeating the distinctive warning David gave Solomon.
Chronicles calls Jericho the 'city of palm trees' when Israelite captives were returned there; Deuteronomy uses the same identifying title for Jericho.
Nehemiah records the tower of Hananeel on Jerusalem's rebuilt wall; Zechariah later uses the same landmark in a prophecy describing Jerusalem's future extent.
Ezra lists descendants of Arah among the returning exiles; Nehemiah names Shechaniah son of Arah as Tobiah's father-in-law, but does not establish their precise genealogical relationship.
Nehemiah lists Kirjatharba among villages inhabited by Judah's people; Joshua identifies Kirjatharba as Hebron, formerly named for Arba.
Bildad predicts that Job's enemies will be clothed with shame; the psalmist uses the same striking image when asking God to disgrace his adversaries. These are different speakers and settings.
The heading of Psalm 6 specifies 'Sheminith'; Chronicles uses the same musical term for harps played by Levites accompanying the ark. Neither passage explains the term in detail.
Both psalms describe joy and safety for people who trust in the LORD and know or love his name; Psalm 5 emphasizes God's defense of those who take refuge in him.
The headings of Psalms 12 and 6 both specify 'Sheminith' as a musical direction, although the psalms' prayers address different troubles.
Psalm 12's heading calls for 'Sheminith'; Chronicles describes Levites playing harps 'on the Sheminith,' providing a distinct musical context for the term.
David asks how long God will hide his face in Psalm 13; in Psalm 22 he similarly cries out about feeling forsaken and unanswered. These are separate laments expressing prolonged distress.
Both psalms use the words 'rejoice in thy salvation': Psalm 20 celebrates God's deliverance of his anointed, while Psalm 9 praises God for rescuing the afflicted.
Psalm 33 urges praise with harp and psaltery; Psalm 92 likewise names these instruments, adding a ten-stringed instrument and a solemn sound.
Psalm 49 joins speech from the mouth with meditation of the heart in wisdom; Psalm 19 asks that both the mouth's words and the heart's meditation be acceptable to God.
Both headings place David under threat, but they describe different dangers: Philistines seized him at Gath in Psalm 56, while Saul watched his house to kill him in Psalm 59.
The headings place both psalms amid Saul’s pursuit of David, but Psalm 57 names his flight to a cave and Psalm 59 the watching of his house.
Psalm 62 says the soul waits upon God for salvation; Psalm 40 remembers waiting patiently until the Lord heard and rescued the speaker.
Psalm 65 describes God stilling both raging seas and the tumult of peoples; Isaiah likens noisy, rushing nations to great waters and says God rebukes them.
Psalm 100 repeats Psalm 66’s invitation for all lands to make a joyful noise to the Lord, opening a call to worship.
Both psalms call the whole earth to make a joyful noise, and Psalm 98 expands the command with rejoicing and singing praise.
Psalm 67 asks God to be gracious and make his face shine on his people; Psalm 80 asks him to restore them and make his face shine so they may be saved.
Both prayers ask God to look down from heaven and behold his afflicted people; Psalm 80 asks him to visit his ravaged vine, while Isaiah appeals to his mercy and power.
Both psalms summon worshippers to make a joyful noise to the Lord; Psalm 81 calls Israel to sing to the God of Jacob, while Psalm 100 invites all lands to come with glad singing.
Both psalms speak of God giving his people the finest wheat; Psalm 81 describes a blessing Israel missed through disobedience, while Psalm 147 celebrates the Lord's care for Jerusalem.
Both verses pronounce the person who trusts in the Lord blessed; Jeremiah expands the statement through the image of a tree sustained by water despite drought.
Both verses praise God for delivering the speaker's soul from death or the grave; Psalm 86 emphasizes God's great mercy, while Psalm 56 anticipates walking before God in the light of life.

Psalm 89 foretells the Davidic king calling God his rock of salvation; in David's song in 2 Samuel 22, he praises the living Lord as the God of his rock and salvation. The speakers and settings differ.
Both psalms specify the harp, psaltery, and an instrument of ten strings in their descriptions of musical praise to the Lord.

Psalm 92 compares the righteous to flourishing trees, including a cedar of Lebanon; Hosea uses renewed growth, deep roots, and Lebanon's beauty to picture restored Israel. These are related images in different settings.

Both passages call for a new song to the Lord in view of his saving work made known beyond Israel; Isaiah summons praise from the ends of the earth, while Psalm 98 celebrates a victory seen by the nations.
Both psalms call all the earth to make a joyful noise to the Lord; Psalm 98 celebrates his revealed salvation, while Psalm 100 invites worship with gladness.
Psalm 100 invites all lands to make a joyful noise to the Lord; Psalm 98 uses the same invitation after proclaiming salvation seen by the ends of the earth.
Both psalms urge joyful praise in God’s presence; Psalm 95 joins singing with thanksgiving to the rock of salvation, while Psalm 100 calls all lands to serve with gladness.
Psalm 105:1 repeats the invitation recorded in David’s song when the ark was brought to Jerusalem: give thanks, call on the Lord, and make his deeds known among the people.
Psalm 106 repeats the refrain from David’s song in Chronicles: give thanks to the Lord because he is good and his mercy endures forever.
Psalms 106 and 107 begin with the same call to thank the Lord because he is good and his mercy endures forever; each then recounts acts of deliverance.

Both psalms begin with the identical call to thank the Lord for his goodness and enduring mercy; Psalm 136 repeats that mercy refrain in every verse, while Psalm 118 calls Israel and others to respond.
Both passages affirm that darkness cannot conceal anything from God: the psalm says night is as light to him, while Daniel praises him for knowing what is in darkness and revealing hidden things.
Both psalms ask God to bring the speaker out of distress for the sake of his name; Psalm 142 pictures imprisonment, while Psalm 143 asks God to preserve his life.
Both prayers ask God to answer quickly and not hide his face; Psalm 143 adds that the psalmist’s spirit is failing and he fears descending to the pit.
Both psalms use the prayer “I lift up my soul unto thee”; Psalm 143 couples trust with a request for guidance, while Psalm 86 asks God to gladden his servant.
Both verses use the distinctive promise of the finest wheat for God’s people; Psalm 147 portrays it as a blessing upon Jerusalem, while Psalm 81 describes what God would have given Israel.
Both verses command a new song to the Lord and widen its audience: Isaiah calls those at the ends of the earth and the sea to sing, while Psalm 149 calls for praise in the congregation of saints.
Both proverbs warn that greedy gain harms its pursuer or household; Proverbs 1 describes greed taking the lives of those who pursue it, while Proverbs 15 says it troubles one’s house.

Both proverbs condemn a son who brings shame to his parents; Proverbs 10 contrasts him with a son who gathers during harvest, while Proverbs 19 describes wasting his father and driving away his mother.
Both warn that greed harms those close to it: Proverbs 1:19 says greedy gain takes life, while 15:27 says it troubles one's household.
Both describe a son who brings shame on his family; Proverbs 17:2 contrasts him with a wise servant, while 19:26 specifies mistreatment of his parents.
Both use a refining pot for silver and furnace for gold; Proverbs 17:3 says the Lord tests hearts, while 27:21 compares a person being tested by praise.
Both say honor is unsuitable for a fool; Proverbs 19:10 also says it is even less fitting for a servant to rule princes.
Both speak of a son who brings shame: Proverbs 19:26 describes driving away parents, while 17:2 contrasts such a son with a wise servant.
Both contrast the upright with workers of wickedness and say destruction awaits the wicked; Proverbs 21:15 also speaks of the just person's joy in judgment.
Both mention the refining pot for silver and furnace for gold; Proverbs 27:21 applies the comparison to praise, while 17:3 says the Lord tries hearts.
Both proverbs contrast a dangerous attitude with trusting the Lord: pride stirs conflict in Proverbs 28:25, while fear of people traps them in 29:25.
Both connect a king's secure throne with righteous rule: Proverbs 25:5 calls for removing wicked advisers, while 29:14 emphasizes faithful judgment for the poor.
Both say there is more hope for a fool than for someone with a particular fault: speaking rashly in Proverbs 29:20 and thinking oneself wise in 26:12.
Both commend trusting the Lord over harmful human attitudes: Proverbs 29:25 warns against fearing people, while 28:25 warns about a proud heart that provokes conflict.
Both mention oppression of the poor: Ecclesiastes observes corrupted justice and officials above officials, while the psalm declares that the Lord will arise for the needy.
The Song names Shenir and Hermon together among northern mountain heights; Deuteronomy identifies Shenir as the Amorite name for Mount Hermon.
Both headings identify Isaiah son of Amoz and Judah and Jerusalem as his subject; Isaiah 1:1 also names the kings during whose reigns he prophesied.
Isaiah pictures trees rejoicing over the fall of Babylon’s king; Ezekiel pictures the trees of Eden comforted when Assyria is brought down.
Both passages say the Lord of hosts has purposed judgment that humbles pride; Isaiah 14 insists no one can overturn his decision.

Genesis names Tarshish and Kittim among Javan’s descendants; Isaiah’s maritime prophecy names ships of Tarshish and news from Chittim, showing the later use of both names without identifying the ships’ precise origin.
Both judgments depict ruined places occupied by cormorants and bitterns: Isaiah speaks against Edom, while Zephaniah describes Nineveh’s desolation. The imagery is parallel, not the same destruction.

Isaiah 41 promises trees, including fir and pine, planted in the desert; Isaiah 60 brings fir, pine, and box trees to beautify God’s sanctuary. The repeated tree list serves two different promises of renewal.
Isaiah attributes the founding of earth and spreading of heaven to the Lord; Hebrews quotes Psalm 102 to declare the Lord the maker of both, contrasting creation’s change with his permanence.
Isaiah 48 calls the Lord Israel’s Redeemer and the Holy One who guides his people; Isaiah 54 calls him Zion’s Maker, husband, Redeemer, and Holy One of Israel.
Both passages introduce the Lord as Israel’s Redeemer and Holy One; Isaiah 43 speaks of his action against Babylon, while Isaiah 48 emphasizes his teaching and guidance.

Both contrast trust in the Lord with misguided human conduct: Isaiah promises inheritance of his holy mountain rather than refuge in powerless companions, while Proverbs contrasts trust with proud strife. The outcomes differ.
Both passages say that the isles wait for the Lord. Isaiah 42 describes their waiting for his law, while Isaiah 60 pictures distant islands joining Zion’s restoration.
Isaiah 41 promises that the Lord will plant trees, including fir, pine, and box, in the desert; Isaiah 60 names those same three kinds as gifts that will beautify his sanctuary.
Genesis describes merchants carrying balm from Gilead; Jeremiah’s question about balm in Gilead draws on the region’s association with that healing substance.
Both passages say that passersby will be astonished and hiss at a devastated city; chapter 19 concerns Jerusalem, while chapter 50 applies the same warning to Babylon.
Jeremiah compares both Coniah and Moab to a vessel in which no one takes pleasure; the same image expresses rejection, though the judgments concern different peoples.
Jeremiah compares Jerusalem’s corrupt prophets to Sodom and Gomorrah; Isaiah likewise addresses Judah’s rulers and people by those cities’ names when condemning their sin.
Jeremiah identifies Micah as the Morasthite who spoke during Hezekiah’s reign; the opening of Micah likewise names his hometown and includes Hezekiah among the kings of his ministry.
Jeremiah foresees returned worshipers praising God because he is good and his mercy endures forever; the same thanksgiving formula appears in the song recorded in Chronicles.
Johanan warns Gedaliah that Ishmael, sent by the Ammonite king, intends to kill him; after Ishmael kills Gedaliah, he takes the survivors captive and heads toward the Ammonites.
Johanan had warned Gedaliah that Ishmael intended to murder him on behalf of the Ammonite king; Ishmael later killed Gedaliah and carried away the people remaining at Mizpah.
Both texts portray God with a prepared bow and arrows, but the psalm speaks of judgment on unrepentant persecutors, while Lamentations describes the sufferer as the target.
Genesis names Sheba and Dedan as sons of Raamah; Ezekiel later lists Sheba and Raamah among merchants supplying Tyre with spices, stones, and gold.
Both passages picture great trees reacting to a ruler’s downfall: Ezekiel’s trees of Eden are comforted at Pharaoh’s fall, while Isaiah’s cedars rejoice over Babylon’s king.
Daniel says God sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths; Peter later says God sent an angel to free him from Herod’s custody. These are separate rescues with the same stated divine means.
Daniel’s prayer for ruined Jerusalem repeats Hezekiah’s striking appeal for God to incline his ear and open his eyes, though Hezekiah faced Assyria and Daniel pleaded after Jerusalem’s fall.
Both prophecies picture God spreading a net over those he judges: Hosea speaks of Ephraim’s pursuit of foreign powers, while Ezekiel addresses a ruler brought captive to Babylon. The targets differ.

Hosea calls Israel an unwanted vessel among the nations; Jeremiah uses the same distinctive “vessel wherein is no pleasure” phrase of Coniah before describing his exile. These are different judgments.
Hosea and Jeremiah use the same distinctive warning: because the people persist in sin, the LORD will remember their iniquity and visit their sins. Hosea also warns of a return to Egypt.
Hosea predicts fire against Judah’s cities and palaces; Amos specifically says the LORD will send fire upon Judah to consume Jerusalem’s palaces. Both warn of judgment on Judah.
Amos names Judah and Jerusalem in the warning that fire will devour their palaces, closely echoing Hosea’s prediction that God will send fire against Judah’s cities and palaces.
Amos describes the LORD as the one who treads upon the high places of the earth; Micah uses the same distinctive language when announcing his coming judgment.
Micah names Achzib among the towns affected by Judah’s trouble; Joshua lists Achzib among the towns in Judah’s inheritance.
Micah says people lie in wait for blood; Proverbs uses the same striking phrase to describe the wicked, while contrasting them with the upright.
Micah waits for the God of his salvation despite trouble; the psalmist likewise calls God his salvation and says he waits on him throughout the day.
Micah says his enemy will be trampled like street mire; Zechariah later uses the same distinctive image of trampling enemies in battle, but in a separate prophecy.
Nahum calls Nineveh a bloody city full of lies and robbery; Ezekiel uses the same cry, “Woe to the bloody city,” against Jerusalem in a different judgment oracle.
Nahum threatens to expose Nineveh’s shame by uncovering her skirts; Jeremiah uses almost identical language against Jerusalem, a distinct object of judgment.
Habakkuk rejoices in the God of his salvation even if crops and livestock fail; Micah likewise resolves to wait for the God of his salvation amid distress.

Zechariah sees Satan standing at Joshua the high priest’s right hand to oppose him; the psalm likewise places an adversary at a man’s right hand, using the same striking position but in a different setting.

Zechariah says the ephah will be taken to Shinar; Daniel also uses the name Shinar for the land where Babylon’s king brought temple vessels, helping identify the region without claiming the two events are the same.

Zechariah says Judah’s fighters will trample enemies like mire in the streets; Micah predicts his enemy will be trodden down like street mire, using a distinctive image without describing the same battle.
Luke places the priest Zacharias in the reign of Herod king of Judaea, while Matthew dates Jesus’ birth to Herod’s reign; both accounts anchor the birth narratives in that ruler’s time.
Both accounts compare God’s kingdom to a tiny mustard seed that grows large enough for birds to lodge in its branches; Luke calls it a great tree, while Mark speaks of great branches.
Luke and Matthew tell the same mustard-seed kingdom parable: a seed planted by a man grows into a tree sheltering birds, though Luke says garden and Matthew says field.
Jesus tells a man to rise and carry his bed in both passages, but John describes a man disabled for thirty-eight years at Bethesda, while Matthew describes a paralytic whose sins Jesus forgives.
Peter says Satan filled Ananias’s heart to lie about the land money; John says Satan entered Judas as he moved toward betraying Jesus. These are different acts involving Satan, not the same event.

Paul calls the household of Stephanas the firstfruits of Achaia, while Romans calls Epaenetus the firstfruits of Achaia; these are differently named people, and the verses do not explain the distinction.
Paul addresses churches in Galatia and elsewhere says he gave those same churches instructions about collecting for the saints.
Both openings name Paul and Timothy together, writing to different congregations—Colosse and Philippi—showing their shared work in these letters.
Both Thessalonian letters open with the same three senders—Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy—addressing the church in Thessalonica.
Paul describes the lawless one's deceptive signs as Satan's work; Revelation calls Satan the deceiver of the whole world, without identifying the scenes as the same event.
Paul says he left Trophimus sick at Miletum; Acts earlier names Trophimus among the companions who traveled with Paul into Asia.
The messages to Philadelphia and Smyrna both mention people who claim to be Jews but are called 'the synagogue of Satan'; the promises to the two churches differ.

Both visions feature a rider on a white horse, but the first rider carries a bow and receives a crown, while the later rider is named Faithful and True and bears many crowns; the text does not say they are the same rider.
Revelation calls the city where Jesus was crucified 'Sodom' in a spiritual sense; Jeremiah likewise compares the wickedness of Jerusalem's prophets and inhabitants to Sodom.
Both visions present a rider on a white horse; Revelation 19 names its rider Faithful and True, unlike the crowned bowman of the first seal in Revelation 6, whose identity is not stated.
